title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
author: Daniel Kahneman
honesty: every page was read by one of the readers; gists and claims are paraphrases, not quotations; page numbers are PDF pages; the PDF itself is not in the repo

pages.gist: Front matter: blank page with no text.

pages.section: Front matter (blank pages, dedication, table of contents for Introduction, Parts I–III)
pages.gist: Front matter: nearly blank, a single stray character only.

pages.section: Front matter (blank pages, dedication, table of contents for Introduction, Parts I–III)
pages.gist: Front matter: dedication to Amos Tversky.

pages.section: Front matter (blank pages, dedication, table of contents for Introduction, Parts I–III)
pages.gist: Front matter: contents page listing the Introduction and Part I 'Two Systems' (chapters 1-9, from 'The Characters of the Story' to 'Answering an Easier Question').

pages.section: Front matter (blank pages, dedication, table of contents for Introduction, Parts I–III)
pages.gist: Front matter: contents continued, listing Part II 'Heuristics and Biases' (chapters 10-18: small numbers, anchors, availability, Tom W, Linda, causes vs statistics, regression, taming predictions) and the start of Part III 'Overconfidence' (chapters 19-21).

pages.section: Table of contents (end) and Introduction (opening, Origins)
pages.gist: Front matter: table of contents listing chapters 22-34 (end of Part III Overconfidence, Part IV Choices) and the Part V heading.

pages.section: Table of contents (end) and Introduction (opening, Origins)
pages.gist: Front matter: table of contents listing chapters 35-38 (Two Selves), Conclusions, appendices, acknowledgments, notes and index.

pages.section: Table of contents (end) and Introduction (opening, Origins)
pages.gist: Introduction: the book aims to give a vocabulary (like medical diagnostic labels) for systematic errors called biases, e.g. the halo effect, and notes that most impressions arise silently without conscious access.

pages.section: Table of contents (end) and Introduction (opening, Origins)
pages.gist: Intuitions are usually right but we are often confident when wrong and outside observers spot our errors better; Origins: Kahneman and Tversky found even they lacked intuition for reliability of small-sample results.

pages.section: Table of contents (end) and Introduction (opening, Origins)
pages.gist: Expert statisticians overestimated replication odds with small samples and advised too few observations; the authors studied first-come intuitive answers and noticed predictions are governed by resemblance to stereotypes, introducing the Steve example.

pages.section: Introduction (origins of heuristics and biases; Where we are now)
pages.gist: Steve the librarian/farmer problem shows people judge by resemblance and ignore base rates; the availability heuristic is introduced with the letter-K experiment and the politicians-adultery example.

pages.section: Introduction (origins of heuristics and biases; Where we are now)
pages.gist: The 1974 Science article challenged assumptions of rationality by tracing errors to cognitive machinery rather than emotion; availability plus media coverage shapes which issues seem important.

pages.section: Introduction (origins of heuristics and biases; Where we are now)
pages.gist: Self-demonstrations made readers see their own biases; luck plays a large role in success stories; the work turned to decisions under risk (coin bet win $130/lose $100) leading to prospect theory.

pages.section: Introduction (origins of heuristics and biases; Where we are now)
pages.gist: Accurate expert intuition comes from prolonged practice and is recognition (Klein's firefighters, Simon's chess masters), but not all professional intuition reflects true expertise.

pages.section: Introduction (origins of heuristics and biases; Where we are now)
pages.gist: The Ford-stock executive illustrates the affect heuristic and substitution of an easier question; when intuition fails, slow System 2 thinking takes over, and System 1/System 2 are introduced.

pages.section: Introduction ("What Comes Next" overview of the five parts); Part 1 title page; Part 1 "Two Systems" title; Chapter 1 "The Characters of the Story" (opening)
pages.gist: Roadmap of the book's parts: two systems and associative memory, why statistical thinking is hard, overconfidence and hindsight, prospect theory with framing and isolated choices, and the experiencing vs. remembering selves.

pages.section: Introduction ("What Comes Next" overview of the five parts); Part 1 title page; Part 1 "Two Systems" title; Chapter 1 "The Characters of the Story" (opening)
pages.gist: Rest of the roadmap: the concluding chapter's three distinctions, how organizations can improve their judgments, and the two reprinted articles in the appendixes.

pages.section: Introduction ("What Comes Next" overview of the five parts); Part 1 title page; Part 1 "Two Systems" title; Chapter 1 "The Characters of the Story" (opening)
pages.gist: Part 1 title page (front matter for the part); no substantive content.

pages.section: Introduction ("What Comes Next" overview of the five parts); Part 1 title page; Part 1 "Two Systems" title; Chapter 1 "The Characters of the Story" (opening)
pages.gist: Title page for 'Two Systems'; no substantive content.

pages.section: Introduction ("What Comes Next" overview of the five parts); Part 1 title page; Part 1 "Two Systems" title; Chapter 1 "The Characters of the Story" (opening)
pages.gist: Chapter 1 opens by contrasting how automatically you read an angry face and predict her next move (fast thinking) with the 17 × 24 problem, which you see as needing effort.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 1: The Characters of the Story (Two Systems; Plot Synopsis; start of Conflict)
pages.gist: The 17×24 exercise shows slow thinking as deliberate, effortful, memory-straining work with bodily signs such as pupil dilation; System 1 and System 2 are defined, and System 1 is named the hero that produces the impressions behind System 2's beliefs.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 1: The Characters of the Story (Two Systems; Plot Synopsis; start of Conflict)
pages.gist: Lists automatic System 1 activities, some innate and some learned through practice (such as a chess master's moves or matching a stereotype), and notes that many of them are involuntary and that the two systems share control of attention.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 1: The Characters of the Story (Two Systems; Plot Synopsis; start of Conflict)
pages.gist: Lists System 2 activities, which all need attention; System 2 can program System 1 by setting a search 'set', and attention is a limited budget, so effortful tasks interfere with each other.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 1: The Characters of the Story (Two Systems; Plot Synopsis; start of Conflict)
pages.gist: The invisible gorilla study shows we can be blind to the obvious and blind to our own blindness; plot synopsis: System 1 makes suggestions, System 2 mostly endorses them, and System 2 is mobilized when System 1 has no answer or something surprising happens.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 1: The Characters of the Story (Two Systems; Plot Synopsis; start of Conflict)
pages.gist: System 2 monitors behavior and errors and usually has the last word; System 1 is efficient but has systematic biases (it substitutes easier questions, is weak at logic and statistics) and cannot be turned off; introduces the Stroop-like conflict exercise.

pages.section: Part I, Ch.1 "The Characters of the Story" (Conflict, Illusions, Useful Fictions, Speaking of) and start of Ch.2 "Attention and Effort"
pages.gist: A Stroop-like exercise shows the conflict between an intended task and an automatic response; System 2 handles self-control; the Müller-Lyer illusion is introduced.

pages.section: Part I, Ch.1 "The Characters of the Story" (Conflict, Illusions, Useful Fictions, Speaking of) and start of Ch.2 "Attention and Effort"
pages.gist: Knowing the Müller-Lyer lines are equal does not stop you seeing them as unequal, so the fix is to recognize the pattern and distrust the impression; a therapist's warning about charming patients with many failed treatments is a cognitive illusion of the same kind.

pages.section: Part I, Ch.1 "The Characters of the Story" (Conflict, Illusions, Useful Fictions, Speaking of) and start of Ch.2 "Attention and Effort"
pages.gist: Cognitive illusions are hard to overcome because System 1 cannot be turned off and constant vigilance is impractical, so the compromise is to spot high-risk situations and try harder when stakes are high; the two systems are useful fictions that describe rather than explain.

pages.section: Part I, Ch.1 "The Characters of the Story" (Conflict, Illusions, Useful Fictions, Speaking of) and start of Ch.2 "Attention and Effort"
pages.gist: Agent-style stories are easier to understand and remember, and short labels use less working memory, which is why the systems get nicknames; closes with 'Speaking of' phrases such as 'slow down and let System 2 take control'.

pages.section: Part I, Ch.1 "The Characters of the Story" (Conflict, Illusions, Useful Fictions, Speaking of) and start of Ch.2 "Attention and Effort"
pages.gist: Ch.2 opens: System 2 is effortful and lazy, so System 1 often guides choices; the Add-1 task pushes effort to its limits, and pupil dilation tracks how hard the mind is working (Hess).

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 2: Attention and Effort (pupillometry, law of least effort, System 2 capabilities)
pages.gist: Hess's finding that pupils index mental effort leads to Kahneman and Beatty's pupillometry studies, showing an inverted-V of effort during Add-1/Add-3, with subjects giving up when overloaded.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 2: Attention and Effort (pupillometry, law of least effort, System 2 capabilities)
pages.gist: Casual conversation needs almost no effort compared with the tasks studied; at peak effort subjects missed a flashed letter K about half the time; System 2 has limited capacity like an electricity meter, but it protects its top-priority task when overloaded.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 2: Attention and Effort (pupillometry, law of least effort, System 2 capabilities)
pages.gist: Spare attention goes to the priority task, System 1 takes over in emergencies, skill and talent lower effort, the law of least effort, and a ranking of tasks by how much effort they take.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 2: Attention and Effort (pupillometry, law of least effort, System 2 capabilities)
pages.gist: Only System 2 can follow rules, compare several attributes, combine stereotypes with base rates and hold task sets; switching tasks is effortful, and attention control predicts pilot performance beyond intelligence.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 2: Attention and Effort (pupillometry, law of least effort, System 2 capabilities)
pages.gist: Time pressure plus memory load makes thinking hardest; people avoid overload by splitting tasks into easy steps and writing intermediate results down; chapter ends with 'Speaking of' examples.

pages.section: Chapter 3: The Lazy Controller (The Busy and Depleted System 2; The Lazy System 2)
pages.gist: Kahneman's walking pace shows System 2 has a natural speed; pushing past it (e.g. computing 23×78 while walking) competes for one limited effort budget shared by self-control and deliberate thought.

pages.section: Chapter 3: The Lazy Controller (The Busy and Depleted System 2; The Lazy System 2)
pages.gist: Task switching and speeded mental work are aversive (law of least effort); flow is effortless concentration; cognitive load makes people yield to temptation and judge superficially.

pages.section: Chapter 3: The Lazy Controller (The Busy and Depleted System 2; The Lazy System 2)
pages.gist: Baumeister's ego depletion: successive acts of self-control drain a shared pool, with lists of depleting tasks and signs of depletion; depletion is partly a loss of motivation.

pages.section: Chapter 3: The Lazy Controller (The Busy and Depleted System 2; The Lazy System 2)
pages.gist: Depletion differs from cognitive busyness, can be offset by incentives and glucose; Israeli parole judges' approvals fall from ~65% after meals to near zero before the next break, so they fall back on the default.

pages.section: Chapter 3: The Lazy Controller (The Busy and Depleted System 2; The Lazy System 2)
pages.gist: System 2 monitors System 1 lazily: the bat-and-ball puzzle draws an appealing wrong answer (10¢) from more than 50% of elite students, which points to overconfidence in intuition and a failure to check cheap answers.

pages.section: Chapter 3 "The Lazy Controller" (end: Intelligence, Control, Rationality; Speaking of Control); start of Chapter 4 "The Associative Machine"
pages.gist: The flowers syllogism shows that a believable conclusion makes people accept unsound arguments, and the Michigan/Detroit murder question shows that facts people know often fail to come to mind unless they search memory on purpose.

pages.section: Chapter 3 "The Lazy Controller" (end: Intelligence, Control, Rationality; Speaking of Control); start of Chapter 4 "The Associative Machine"
pages.gist: Failing these mini-tests comes from lazy System 2 monitoring, not lack of ability ('engaged' vs lazy); Mischel's marshmallow-style delay experiment links self-control to later intelligence and executive control.

pages.section: Chapter 3 "The Lazy Controller" (end: Intelligence, Control, Rationality; Speaking of Control); start of Chapter 4 "The Associative Machine"
pages.gist: Attention training raises executive control and IQ scores; Frederick's Cognitive Reflection Test shows that intuitive responders are impulsive (63% prefer $3,400 now over $3,800 next month); Stanovich separates algorithmic intelligence from rationality.

pages.section: Chapter 3 "The Lazy Controller" (end: Intelligence, Control, Rationality; Speaking of Control); start of Chapter 4 "The Associative Machine"
pages.gist: CRT-type questions predict susceptibility to bias better than IQ does; the 'Speaking of Control' examples cover flow, ego depletion leading to standard procedures, lazy System 2 and weak delay of gratification.

pages.section: Chapter 3 "The Lazy Controller" (end: Intelligence, Control, Rationality; Speaking of Control); start of Chapter 4 "The Associative Machine"
pages.gist: Chapter 4 opens with 'Bananas Vomit': associative activation automatically creates a causal story, emotions, bodily reactions and primed associations, all mutually reinforcing and coherent.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 4: The Associative Machine (Associative coherence, The Marvels of Priming, Primes That Guide Us)
pages.gist: System 1 makes associative coherence out of an unexpected word pair. It builds a causal story, judges the threat and gets ready for what comes next. Hume's three principles of association lead into associative memory as a network of linked ideas, most of them active without our awareness.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 4: The Associative Machine (Associative coherence, The Marvels of Priming, Primes That Guide Us)
pages.gist: Priming: seeing EAT makes SO_P read as SOUP, and activation spreads like ripples. Bargh's Florida effect shows old-age words making students walk more slowly, without their knowing (the ideomotor effect).

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 4: The Associative Machine (Associative coherence, The Marvels of Priming, Primes That Guide Us)
pages.gist: Priming runs both ways: walking slowly primes thoughts of old age, a forced smile or frown changes emotion, and nodding or shaking the head changes agreement. A school used as a polling station raised support for school funding.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 4: The Associative Machine (Associative coherence, The Marvels of Priming, Primes That Guide Us)
pages.gist: Money primes make people more self-reliant, selfish and distant, while reminders of death make authoritarian ideas more appealing. The Lady Macbeth effect links moral guilt to a wish to wash the body.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 4: The Associative Machine (Associative coherence, The Marvels of Priming, Primes That Guide Us)
pages.gist: Cleansing is specific to the body part used to lie (phone vs. email). Priming effects are robust but not necessarily large, yet small shifts can tip outcomes. System 2 wrongly thinks it is in charge, and an honesty-box study with pictures of eyes vs. flowers is introduced.

pages.section: Part I, Ch. 4 The Associative Machine (end: priming, Speaking of Priming) and Ch. 5 Cognitive Ease (start: illusions of remembering, illusions of truth)
pages.gist: Honesty-box results: posters of watching eyes nearly tripled contributions compared with flower posters; System 1 is the 'stranger within' that produces impressions, impulses and many systematic errors without awareness.

pages.section: Part I, Ch. 4 The Associative Machine (end: priming, Speaking of Priming) and Ch. 5 Cognitive Ease (start: illusions of remembering, illusions of truth)
pages.gist: 'Speaking of Priming' example sentences: coherence comes from the mind, people primed to find flaws find them, System 1 builds a story and System 2 believes it.

pages.section: Part I, Ch. 4 The Associative Machine (end: priming, Speaking of Priming) and Ch. 5 Cognitive Ease (start: illusions of remembering, illusions of truth)
pages.gist: Opens Cognitive Ease: System 1 keeps a set of dials, one running from easy to strained; clear fonts, repetition, priming and good mood cause ease, and poor fonts, complex wording and bad mood cause strain.

pages.section: Part I, Ch. 4 The Associative Machine (end: priming, Speaking of Priming) and Ch. 5 Cognitive Ease (start: illusions of remembering, illusions of truth)
pages.gist: Under ease people are casual and trusting; under strain they are vigilant and make fewer errors but are less creative. Illusions of remembering: made-up names seen once later feel famous because ease of perception feels like familiarity (Jacoby, 'Becoming Famous Overnight').

pages.section: Part I, Ch. 4 The Associative Machine (end: priming, Speaking of Priming) and Ch. 5 Cognitive Ease (start: illusions of remembering, illusions of truth)
pages.gist: Ease of perception and the feeling of familiarity work in both directions. Illusions of truth: familiarity gets mistaken for truth, so repetition, even of part of a statement, makes falsehoods believable; the section on writing persuasive messages begins.

pages.section: Chapter 5 "Cognitive Ease": How to Write a Persuasive Message; Strain and Effort; The Pleasure of Cognitive Ease; Ease, Mood, and Intuition
pages.gist: Making a message believable through cognitive ease: legibility, high contrast, bright colors, simple language rather than pretentious words, and rhyming aphorisms that are judged more insightful.

pages.section: Chapter 5 "Cognitive Ease": How to Write a Persuasive Message; Strain and Effort; The Pleasure of Cognitive Ease; Ease, Mood, and Intuition
pages.gist: Sources with easy-to-pronounce names get more weight (Artan vs Taahhut); fluency does not rescue obvious nonsense, but people can't trace their feeling of ease to its source; cognitive strain mobilizes System 2; the CRT is introduced.

pages.section: Chapter 5 "Cognitive Ease": How to Write a Persuasive Message; Strain and Effort; The Pleasure of Cognitive Ease; Ease, Mood, and Intuition
pages.gist: A hard-to-read font cut CRT errors from 90% to 35% because strain engages System 2; cognitive ease brings faint smiles; fluent stock names and tickers do better; the mere exposure effect is introduced.

pages.section: Chapter 5 "Cognitive Ease": How to Write a Persuasive Message; Strain and Effort; The Pleasure of Cognitive Ease; Ease, Mood, and Intuition
pages.gist: Zajonc's Michigan newspaper study: words shown more often were rated more positive, even when people saw them without knowing it; mere exposure acts as a learned safety signal (shown in chicks too).

pages.section: Chapter 5 "Cognitive Ease": How to Write a Persuasive Message; Strain and Effort; The Pleasure of Cognitive Ease; Ease, Mood, and Intuition
pages.gist: Remote Association Test: people sense in 2 seconds that a word triad is linked before finding the link; ease cues raise 'linked' judgments; good mood more than doubles intuitive accuracy, while sad mood drops it to chance; mood clusters with System 1 or System 2 reliance.

pages.section: Ch. 5 Cognitive Ease (end, 'Speaking of Cognitive Ease'); Ch. 6 Norms, Surprises, and Causes (Assessing Normality; start of Seeing Causes and Intentions)
pages.gist: Good mood loosens System 2 vigilance; a coherent word triad produces a slight smile, and attributing the good feeling to music removes the sense of coherence, so emotion drives coherence judgments.

pages.section: Ch. 5 Cognitive Ease (end, 'Speaking of Cognitive Ease'); Ch. 6 Norms, Surprises, and Causes (Assessing Normality; start of Seeing Causes and Intentions)
pages.gist: 'Speaking of Cognitive Ease' quotes: don't dismiss a plan because of a hard font, re-check repeated claims, familiarity breeds liking, and be extra careful in a good mood.

pages.section: Ch. 5 Cognitive Ease (end, 'Speaking of Cognitive Ease'); Ch. 6 Norms, Surprises, and Causes (Assessing Normality; start of Seeing Causes and Intentions)
pages.gist: Ch. 6 opens: System 1 maintains a model of what is normal; surprise shows what we expect, split into active and passive expectation; the first Jon coincidence.

pages.section: Ch. 5 Cognitive Ease (end, 'Speaking of Cognitive Ease'); Ch. 6 Norms, Surprises, and Causes (Assessing Normality; start of Seeing Causes and Intentions)
pages.gist: A single event makes a repeat feel normal (Jon, burning cars), and norm theory says later odd events pull earlier ones from memory into one causal story (wincing soup eater); start of the Moses illusion.

pages.section: Ch. 5 Cognitive Ease (end, 'Speaking of Cognitive Ease'); Ch. 6 Norms, Surprises, and Causes (Assessing Normality; start of Seeing Causes and Intentions)
pages.gist: The Moses illusion shows coherent associations hide errors; the brain detects violations of norms within 0.2 s; shared category norms make communication work; the section on seeing causes begins (Fred's anger).

pages.section: Ch. 6 Norms, Surprises, and Causes (Seeing Causes and Intentions; Speaking of Norms and Causes); Ch. 7 A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions (Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt; A Bias to Believe and Confirm)
pages.gist: System 1 automatically builds causal stories; the Hussein-capture bond headlines show an 'explanation' that fits opposite outcomes explains nothing, and the wallet/pickpocket recall shows associative coherence filling in causes.

pages.section: Ch. 6 Norms, Surprises, and Causes (Seeing Causes and Intentions; Speaking of Norms and Causes); Ch. 7 A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions (Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt; A Bias to Believe and Confirm)
pages.gist: Michotte's launching displays and Heider-Simmel's shapes show causality and intention are perceived directly by System 1 from infancy; causal thinking is misapplied where statistical reasoning is needed, which System 1 cannot do.

pages.section: Ch. 6 Norms, Surprises, and Causes (Seeing Causes and Intentions; Speaking of Norms and Causes); Ch. 7 A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions (Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt; A Bias to Believe and Confirm)
pages.gist: Kahneman explains the two systems are useful agent-metaphors, then 'Speaking of' examples: repetition makes things feel normal, consider the full range not just the average, and people demand causal stories for bad luck.

pages.section: Ch. 6 Norms, Surprises, and Causes (Seeing Causes and Intentions; Speaking of Norms and Causes); Ch. 7 A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions (Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt; A Bias to Believe and Confirm)
pages.gist: Chapter 7 opens: jumping to conclusions is efficient when likely correct and cheap, risky when unfamiliar, high-stakes and time-pressed; ambiguous figures (A B C / 12 13 14) and 'bank' are resolved by context without awareness.

pages.section: Ch. 6 Norms, Surprises, and Causes (Seeing Causes and Intentions; Speaking of Norms and Causes); Ch. 7 A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions (Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt; A Bias to Believe and Confirm)
pages.gist: System 1 bets on one interpretation guided by recent context and drops alternatives, doubt belongs to System 2; Gilbert's experiment shows busy System 2 fails to 'unbelieve' false statements, and associative memory drives confirmation bias.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 7 "A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions": confirmation bias, Halo Effect, Decorrelate Error, WYSIATI
pages.gist: People test hypotheses by looking for evidence that confirms them (positive test strategy), which makes extreme events seem more likely; the halo effect is introduced with the Joan-generosity example and Asch's Alan/Ben trait orderings.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 7 "A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions": confirmation bias, Halo Effect, Decorrelate Error, WYSIATI
pages.gist: Order matters because the halo effect gives first impressions too much weight; Kahneman found this in his own essay grading and switched to scoring one question at a time across all students with earlier scores hidden, which made his grading feel less consistent but was the better method.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 7 "A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions": confirmation bias, Halo Effect, Decorrelate Error, WYSIATI
pages.gist: The 'decorrelate error' principle: averaging independent judgments cancels out errors (the pennies-in-a-jar crowd estimate, keeping witnesses apart), so meetings should collect a written position from each member before discussion; WYSIATI is introduced.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 7 "A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions": confirmation bias, Halo Effect, Decorrelate Error, WYSIATI
pages.gist: System 1 works only with ideas that are already active and judges a story by how coherent it is, not by how much or how good the data is; it jumps to conclusions (Mindik as a leader), and this is named WYSIATI.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 7 "A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions": confirmation bias, Halo Effect, Decorrelate Error, WYSIATI
pages.gist: In the one-sided legal evidence study, people who heard only one side judged more confidently even though they knew they were missing the other side; WYSIATI is said to explain overconfidence and framing effects (90% survival vs 10% mortality).

pages.section: Ch.7 A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions (end: WYSIATI examples, Speaking of); Ch.8 How Judgments Happen (Basic Assessments, Sets and Prototypes, start of Intensity Matching)
pages.gist: Finishes WYSIATI applications (framing, base-rate neglect via Steve the librarian) and 'Speaking of' examples: halo from one presentation, decorrelating errors via independent judgments, decisions based on one consultant's report.

pages.section: Ch.7 A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions (end: WYSIATI examples, Speaking of); Ch.8 How Judgments Happen (Basic Assessments, Sets and Prototypes, start of Intensity Matching)
pages.gist: Opens Ch.8: System 2 directs attention to questions while System 1 continuously generates basic assessments that get substituted for harder questions, aided by cross-dimension translation and the mental shotgun; introduces Todorov's face-reading of dominance and trustworthiness.

pages.section: Ch.7 A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions (end: WYSIATI examples, Speaking of); Ch.8 How Judgments Happen (Basic Assessments, Sets and Prototypes, start of Intensity Matching)
pages.gist: Todorov's studies: brief-exposure competence ratings of faces predicted ~70% of election winners; this is a judgment heuristic, three times stronger among uninformed, TV-heavy voters; System 1 routinely computes similarity, causality, availability.

pages.section: Ch.7 A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions (end: WYSIATI examples, Speaking of); Ch.8 How Judgments Happen (Basic Assessments, Sets and Prototypes, start of Intensity Matching)
pages.gist: Not every attribute is assessed automatically: a glance shows towers are equal height but not that block counts match—counting requires System 2; introduces average line length question (Figure 8).

pages.section: Ch.7 A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions (end: WYSIATI examples, Speaking of); Ch.8 How Judgments Happen (Basic Assessments, Sets and Prototypes, start of Intensity Matching)
pages.gist: System 1 registers averages fast but not sums since categories are represented by prototypes; Exxon Valdez willingness-to-pay ($80/$78/$88 for 2,000/20,000/200,000 birds) shows scope neglect; introduces intensity matching.

pages.section: Ch. 8 "How Judgments Happen" (intensity matching, the mental shotgun, Speaking of Judgment) → Ch. 9 "Answering an Easier Question" (substituting questions)
pages.gist: System 1 can match intensity across unrelated scales (crime to loudness, Julie's early reading to height, income or GPA). Predicting by this kind of matching feels natural but is statistically wrong. The section on the mental shotgun begins.

pages.section: Ch. 8 "How Judgments Happen" (intensity matching, the mental shotgun, Speaking of Judgment) → Ch. 9 "Answering an Easier Question" (substituting questions)
pages.gist: The mental shotgun: System 1 computes more than it is asked to. In one study, mismatched spelling slowed rhyme detection (VOTE–GOAT). In another, sentences that could be true as metaphors slowed literal true/false judgments.

pages.section: Ch. 8 "How Judgments Happen" (intensity matching, the mental shotgun, Speaking of Judgment) → Ch. 9 "Answering an Easier Question" (substituting questions)
pages.gist: The irrelevant computation disrupts the main task. Shotgun plus intensity matching explains why we have intuitions about things we know little about. 'Speaking of Judgment' examples: judging attractiveness, judging dominance from a face, letting liking a product color a judgment of the firm's finances.

pages.section: Ch. 8 "How Judgments Happen" (intensity matching, the mental shotgun, Speaking of Judgment) → Ch. 9 "Answering an Easier Question" (substituting questions)
pages.gist: Chapter 9 opens: we are rarely stumped because, when no quick answer is found to a hard target question, System 1 answers an easier heuristic question instead (substitution). This is the core of the heuristics and biases approach.

pages.section: Ch. 8 "How Judgments Happen" (intensity matching, the mental shotgun, Speaking of Judgment) → Ch. 9 "Answering an Easier Question" (substituting questions)
pages.gist: Pólya's deliberate substitution is contrasted with involuntary substitution caused by the mental shotgun. Table 1 pairs target questions with heuristic questions (dolphin emotion for donations, current mood for life happiness, anger for punishment, looking like a winner for political future).

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 9 "Answering an Easier Question" (mental shotgun, intensity matching, 3-D heuristic, mood heuristic for happiness, affect heuristic, Speaking of Substitution); start of Characteristics of System 1 table
pages.gist: Mental shotgun plus intensity matching give ready answers to easy heuristic questions, which lazy System 2 often endorses without noticing the target question was swapped; introduces the 3-D heuristic.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 9 "Answering an Easier Question" (mental shotgun, intensity matching, 3-D heuristic, mood heuristic for happiness, affect heuristic, Speaking of Substitution); start of Characteristics of System 1 table
pages.gist: Corridor illusion (Figure 9): equal-sized figures look different because the perceived 3-D size substitutes for 2-D size on the page.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 9 "Answering an Easier Question" (mental shotgun, intensity matching, 3-D heuristic, mood heuristic for happiness, affect heuristic, Speaking of Substitution); start of Characteristics of System 1 table
pages.gist: Substitution is automatic and predictably biased; German student survey shows asking about dates first makes the dating-happiness correlation jump from about zero to very high.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 9 "Answering an Easier Question" (mental shotgun, intensity matching, 3-D heuristic, mood heuristic for happiness, affect heuristic, Speaking of Substitution); start of Characteristics of System 1 table
pages.gist: Students substitute a ready answer (love-life happiness) for general happiness; any mood-altering prior question has the same effect (WYSIATI); Slovic's affect heuristic: likes and dislikes drive beliefs about risks and benefits.

pages.section: Part I, Chapter 9 "Answering an Easier Question" (mental shotgun, intensity matching, 3-D heuristic, mood heuristic for happiness, affect heuristic, Speaking of Substitution); start of Characteristics of System 1 table
pages.gist: In attitudes System 2 acts as an apologist that seeks confirming information; 'Speaking of' examples on substitution and affect; opens the table of System 1 characteristics.

pages.section: End of Part 1 (Characteristics of System 1 table); Part 2 title "Heuristics and Biases"; Chapter 10 "The Law of Small Numbers" (opening)
pages.gist: Summary list of System 1 traits: automatic impressions, coherence, cognitive ease, causal inference, believing/confirming, halo, WYSIATI, norms/prototypes, intensity matching, mental shotgun, substitution, prospect-theory traits, loss aversion and narrow framing.

pages.section: End of Part 1 (Characteristics of System 1 table); Part 2 title "Heuristics and Biases"; Chapter 10 "The Law of Small Numbers" (opening)
pages.gist: Part divider page: 'Part 2'; no substantive content.

pages.section: End of Part 1 (Characteristics of System 1 table); Part 2 title "Heuristics and Biases"; Chapter 10 "The Law of Small Numbers" (opening)
pages.gist: Part title page: 'Heuristics and Biases'; no substantive content.

pages.section: End of Part 1 (Characteristics of System 1 table); Part 2 title "Heuristics and Biases"; Chapter 10 "The Law of Small Numbers" (opening)
pages.gist: Kidney-cancer county puzzle: both lowest and highest incidence counties are rural, tempting causal stories; System 1 finds causes even in purely statistical facts; urn-sampling setup begins.

pages.section: End of Part 1 (Characteristics of System 1 table); Part 2 title "Heuristics and Biases"; Chapter 10 "The Law of Small Numbers" (opening)
pages.gist: Urn arithmetic (small samples give extreme results far more often) explains the county pattern as a sampling artifact; nothing causal to explain; knowing the law of large numbers isn't the same as applying it.

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases, Ch. 10 "The Law of Small Numbers" (The Law of Small Numbers; A Bias of Confidence Over Doubt; Cause and Chance)
pages.gist: Knowing large samples are more precise isn't the same as grasping that small samples give extreme results more often; researchers routinely choose samples by intuition, risking ~50% failure to confirm true hypotheses.

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases, Ch. 10 "The Law of Small Numbers" (The Law of Small Numbers; A Bias of Confidence Over Doubt; Cause and Chance)
pages.gist: Even statistically sophisticated researchers chose too-small samples ('belief in the law of small numbers'); recommendation to replace impression with computation; people are insensitive to sample size in a poll example.

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases, Ch. 10 "The Law of Small Numbers" (The Law of Small Numbers; A Bias of Confidence Over Doubt; Cause and Chance)
pages.gist: System 1 doesn't grade degrees of belief or sustain doubt (WYSIATI), favoring certainty and coherence; causal thinking makes us misjudge random sequences like BBBGGG vs BGBBGB.

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases, Ch. 10 "The Law of Small Numbers" (The Law of Small Numbers; A Bias of Confidence Over Doubt; Cause and Chance)
pages.gist: All birth sequences are equally likely yet regular ones seem non-random; examples of London bombing clusters and Israeli squadron losses show seeing causes in chance; Kahneman advised accepting luck.

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases, Ch. 10 "The Law of Small Numbers" (The Law of Small Numbers; A Bias of Confidence Over Doubt; Cause and Chance)
pages.gist: Hot hand in basketball is an illusion; intuition misclassifies random as systematic (advisers, CEOs); Gates Foundation's small-schools investment rested on a small-sample artifact.

pages.section: Ch. 10 The Law of Small Numbers (end); Ch. 11 Anchors (anchoring as adjustment, anchoring as priming)
pages.gist: Small schools only look better because they vary more; people trust what a message says more than how reliable it is, and they wrongly give causes to chance results. Ends with 'Speaking of' examples on small samples.

pages.section: Ch. 10 The Law of Small Numbers (end); Ch. 11 Anchors (anchoring as adjustment, anchoring as priming)
pages.gist: Page is almost blank (a single letter 'P'), probably a chapter break, with no substantive content.

pages.section: Ch. 10 The Law of Small Numbers (end); Ch. 11 Anchors (anchoring as adjustment, anchoring as priming)
pages.gist: Chapter 11 opens with the rigged wheel-of-fortune experiment (spins of 10 or 65 led to estimates of 25% or 45%) and defines the anchoring effect, including the Gandhi age and house listing price examples.

pages.section: Ch. 10 The Law of Small Numbers (end); Ch. 11 Anchors (anchoring as adjustment, anchoring as priming)
pages.gist: Anchoring comes from two mechanisms, one per System; the System 2 'anchor-and-adjust' process stops too early (line-drawing, speeding off the highway, the teenager's loud music).

pages.section: Ch. 10 The Law of Small Numbers (end); Ch. 11 Anchors (anchoring as adjustment, anchoring as priming)
pages.gist: Adjustment is deliberate and effortful (head shaking/nodding; less adjustment under memory load or alcohol), so insufficient adjustment is a lazy System 2. Anchoring also works as suggestion or priming (Gandhi at 144).

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 11 "Anchors": Anchoring as Priming Effect, The Anchoring Index, Uses and Abuses of Anchors, Anchoring and the Two Systems, Speaking of Anchors
pages.gist: Anchoring as priming: anchors selectively activate compatible memories (Mussweiler & Strack temperature/car-brand studies); introduces the measurable anchoring index via the redwood experiment.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 11 "Anchors": Anchoring as Priming Effect, The Anchoring Index, Uses and Abuses of Anchors, Anchoring and the Two Systems, Speaking of Anchors
pages.gist: Anchoring index computed (55% typical); real-estate agents anchored 41% while denying it; willingness-to-pay for seabirds swings $20 to $143 with $5/$400 anchors; real-world examples in auctions and trading.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 11 "Anchors": Anchoring as Priming Effect, The Anchoring Index, Uses and Abuses of Anchors, Anchoring and the Two Systems, Speaking of Anchors
pages.gist: Random anchors (wheel of fortune, SSN digits, loaded dice for experienced judges) work as strongly as informative ones; arbitrary rationing ('limit 12 per person') doubles purchases; first-mover list price in negotiation.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 11 "Anchors": Anchoring as Priming Effect, The Anchoring Index, Uses and Abuses of Anchors, Anchoring and the Two Systems, Speaking of Anchors
pages.gist: Negotiation defenses: refuse outrageous anchors, 'think the opposite' by searching arguments against the anchor; damages caps can raise small awards; System 2 works on data System 1 retrieves and cannot detect the anchor's influence.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 11 "Anchors": Anchoring as Priming Effect, The Anchoring Index, Uses and Abuses of Anchors, Anchoring and the Two Systems, Speaking of Anchors
pages.gist: Anchoring arises from associative activation regardless of truth (WYSIATI); assume any number on the table has anchored you and mobilize System 2 when stakes are high; 'Speaking of Anchors' examples (business plans as best-case anchors).

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases — Ch. 12 The Science of Availability (opening sections incl. 'The Psychology of Availability')
pages.gist: Blank/section-divider page (only a stray character); no content.

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases — Ch. 12 The Science of Availability (opening sections incl. 'The Psychology of Availability')
pages.gist: Introduces the availability heuristic—judging a category's frequency by the ease with which instances come to mind—and shows ease is sensed without retrieving any instances (letter-set example).

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases — Ch. 12 The Science of Availability (opening sections incl. 'The Psychology of Availability')
pages.gist: Availability substitutes ease-of-retrieval for frequency; lists bias sources (salience, dramatic events, personal/vivid experience), recommends questioning impressions, and describes spouses' self-assessed contributions summing to over 100%.

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases — Ch. 12 The Science of Availability (opening sections incl. 'The Psychology of Availability')
pages.gist: Credit-allocation bias is debiasable by noting there is usually more than 100% credit to go around; introduces Schwarz's experiment pitting number of instances recalled against ease of recall (list 6 vs 12 assertive acts).

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases — Ch. 12 The Science of Availability (opening sections incl. 'The Psychology of Availability')
pages.gist: Ease of retrieval beats quantity: listing 12 assertive acts lowers self-rated assertiveness, frowning reduces fluency, and listing more arguments/advantages lowers confidence; the effect can reverse when people go by content.

pages.section: Ch. 13 The Science of Availability (end, incl. 'Speaking of Availability'); Ch. 13 Availability, Emotion, and Risk (start: Availability and Affect)
pages.gist: Ease-of-retrieval effects are really an 'unexplained unavailability' heuristic: low fluency counts only when it is surprising, and giving people a spurious explanation (e.g., background music) cancels the effect; System 1 sets expectations and finds causes for surprises.

pages.section: Ch. 13 The Science of Availability (end, incl. 'Speaking of Availability'); Ch. 13 Availability, Emotion, and Risk (start: Availability and Affect)
pages.gist: Personally involved people (family history of heart disease) judge by the content and number of recalled instances rather than fluency; lists conditions that increase reliance on ease of retrieval (cognitive load, good mood, novice knowledge, faith in intuition, feeling powerful).

pages.section: Ch. 13 The Science of Availability (end, incl. 'Speaking of Availability'); Ch. 13 Availability, Emotion, and Risk (start: Availability and Affect)
pages.gist: 'Speaking of Availability' examples: risk underestimated due to few media stories, conspiracies after spy movies, CEO overconfident after a streak of successes.

pages.section: Ch. 13 The Science of Availability (end, incl. 'Speaking of Availability'); Ch. 13 Availability, Emotion, and Risk (start: Availability and Affect)
pages.gist: Kunreuther: after disasters people buy insurance and protect, then complacency returns as memory fades; protections are sized to the worst disaster experienced; Slovic/Lichtenstein/Fischhoff cause-of-death survey shows accidents and tornadoes overestimated vs strokes and asthma.

pages.section: Ch. 13 The Science of Availability (end, incl. 'Speaking of Availability'); Ch. 13 Availability, Emotion, and Risk (start: Availability and Affect)
pages.gist: Media coverage biased toward novelty and emotion distorts frequency estimates; the affect heuristic substitutes 'how do I feel about it?' for 'what do I think about it?', linked to Damasio's view that emotion guides decisions.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 13 "Availability, Emotion, and Risk" (affect heuristic end; The Public and the Experts; availability cascades; Speaking of Availability Cascades)
pages.gist: Messages about a technology's benefits lowered its perceived risk (and vice versa) without relevant evidence; Slovic on public vs. experts and his claim that risk is not objective.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 13 "Availability, Emotion, and Risk" (affect heuristic end; The Public and the Experts; availability cascades; Speaking of Availability Cascades)
pages.gist: Choice of risk measure shapes the evaluation ('defining risk is an exercise in power'); Sunstein's counter-view favoring expert cost-benefit analysis; introduction of the availability cascade.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 13 "Availability, Emotion, and Risk" (affect heuristic end; The Public and the Experts; availability cascades; Speaking of Availability Cascades)
pages.gist: Availability cascade mechanics (availability entrepreneurs, media feedback, dissenters ignored) illustrated with Love Canal and the Alar scare.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 13 "Availability, Emotion, and Risk" (affect heuristic end; The Public and the Experts; availability cascades; Speaking of Availability Cascades)
pages.gist: Probability neglect—small risks are ignored or overweighted; terrorism as an availability cascade; Kahneman reconciles Slovic and Sunstein: combine expert knowledge with public emotions.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 13 "Availability, Emotion, and Risk" (affect heuristic end; The Public and the Experts; availability cascades; Speaking of Availability Cascades)
pages.gist: Closing 'Speaking of' examples: all-benefit-no-cost enthusiasm as affect heuristic; media-inflated nonevent as availability cascade.

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases, Ch. 14 "Tom W's Specialty" (Predicting by Representativeness; The Sins of Representativeness)
pages.gist: Opens the Tom W puzzle: with no specific information, ranking his likely field should follow base rates, the proportion of students in each field, like drawing marbles from an urn.

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases, Ch. 14 "Tom W's Specialty" (Predicting by Representativeness; The Sins of Representativeness)
pages.gist: Gives Tom W's personality sketch, which comes from tests of uncertain validity, and asks readers to rank fields by how similar he is to each stereotype. The usual order puts computer science first and social science last.

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases, Ch. 14 "Tom W's Specialty" (Predicting by Representativeness; The Sins of Representativeness)
pages.gist: Tom W was built as an 'anti-base-rate' character who fits small fields. Psychology students who knew the base rates were asked for likelihood, and even the statistician Robyn Dawes guessed 'computer scientist' without thinking of base rates.

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases, Ch. 14 "Tom W's Specialty" (Predicting by Representativeness; The Sins of Representativeness)
pages.gist: 114 statistically trained graduate students ranked fields by probability exactly as they ranked them by similarity, so the substitution was complete. A probability question fires a 'mental shotgun', and System 1 answers with an effortless impression of representativeness.

pages.section: Part II Heuristics and Biases, Ch. 14 "Tom W's Specialty" (Predicting by Representativeness; The Sins of Representativeness)
pages.gist: In Moneyball, scouts picked players by how they looked while Beane used past statistics. Representativeness is often better than chance, but leaning on it alone leads to sins such as overpredicting low-base-rate events (the PhD reading the NYT on the subway).

pages.section: Ch. 14 "Tom W's Specialty" (Sins of Representativeness; How to Discipline Intuition; Speaking of Representativeness) and Ch. 15 "Linda: Less Is More" (opening)
pages.gist: Base rates beat stereotype fit (shy poetry lover is likelier a business student); base-rate use rises with 'think like a statistician' and frowning, showing base-rate neglect stems from System 2 laziness; introduces second sin: insensitivity to evidence quality.

pages.section: Ch. 14 "Tom W's Specialty" (Sins of Representativeness; How to Discipline Intuition; Speaking of Representativeness) and Ch. 15 "Linda: Less Is More" (opening)
pages.gist: Untrustworthy evidence should be treated like no evidence, so stay close to base rates; beliefs must obey probability logic (complements, conjunctions); Bayes's rule combines base rate with diagnosticity (3% prior x 4:1 likelihood -> 11%).

pages.section: Ch. 14 "Tom W's Specialty" (Sins of Representativeness; How to Discipline Intuition; Speaking of Representativeness) and Ch. 15 "Linda: Less Is More" (opening)
pages.gist: Two keys to disciplined Bayesian reasoning: anchor on a plausible base rate and question the diagnosticity of evidence; 'Speaking of' examples about startups, company appearance, and weak evidence.

pages.section: Ch. 14 "Tom W's Specialty" (Sins of Representativeness; How to Discipline Intuition; Speaking of Representativeness) and Ch. 15 "Linda: Less Is More" (opening)
pages.gist: Introduces the Linda problem: a description strongly fitting a feminist activist and eight scenarios ranked by resemblance or probability.

pages.section: Ch. 14 "Tom W's Specialty" (Sins of Representativeness; How to Discipline Intuition; Speaking of Representativeness) and Ch. 15 "Linda: Less Is More" (opening)
pages.gist: Conjunction fallacy: 'feminist bank teller' judged more probable than 'bank teller' even within-subject (89% of undergrads, 85% of Stanford decision-science PhD students), a System 2 failure where representativeness beats logic.

pages.section: Part II, Chapter 15 "Linda: Less Is More" (incl. subsection "Less Is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation")
pages.gist: The short Linda question still gets 85-90% wrong. The conjunction fallacy is defined and, like a visual illusion, it stays tempting even when you know the answer. Explicit comparison helps (64% correct vs 15% in the long list), and representativeness makes coherent stories feel probable.

pages.section: Part II, Chapter 15 "Linda: Less Is More" (incl. subsection "Less Is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation")
pages.gist: Mistaking plausibility for probability hurts scenario forecasting: a detailed California-quake flood gets rated more likely than any North America flood. Detail that adds no coherence (Mark has blond hair) causes no fallacy. The Hsee dinnerware study is introduced.

pages.section: Part II, Chapter 15 "Linda: Less Is More" (incl. subsection "Less Is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation")
pages.gist: Hsee's dinnerware sets: the 40-piece set with broken items is worth more when judged side by side but less when judged alone ($23 vs $33). This 'less is more' is replicated with baseball cards, and probability is shown to be a sum-like variable just as value is.

pages.section: Part II, Chapter 15 "Linda: Less Is More" (incl. subsection "Less Is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation")
pages.gist: System 1 averages instead of adding, so less-is-more appears with probability too. Unlike pricing, side-by-side evaluation does not remove it for probability (Borg: 72% error). Then the die-sequence task with no words.

pages.section: Part II, Chapter 15 "Linda: Less Is More" (incl. subsection "Less Is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation")
pages.gist: Even with no words, two-thirds bet on the longer, more representative die sequence, yet accept the correct argument when shown it. 'How many of 100' framing cuts errors from 65% to 25% because frequencies make inclusion visible. System 2 is not very alert.

pages.section: Ch. 15 Linda: Less is More (end); Ch. 16 Causes Trump Statistics (start)
pages.gist: Conjunction fallacy reflects lazy System 2 and representativeness blocking logic; joint evaluation usually brings out logic (dinnerware) but not always (Linda); critics attacked the weakest example instead of the strongest evidence.

pages.section: Ch. 15 Linda: Less is More (end); Ch. 16 Causes Trump Statistics (start)
pages.gist: Critics focused on Linda because it was 'more interesting'; 'Speaking of Less is More' examples: plausible is not probable, a cheap add-on can lower a bundle's value, joint comparison does not always fix intuition.

pages.section: Ch. 15 Linda: Less is More (end); Ch. 16 Causes Trump Statistics (start)
pages.gist: Opens 'Causes Trump Statistics' with the hit-and-run cab problem (85% Green, 15% Blue, witness 80% reliable) as Bayesian inference, then introduces a causal variation.

pages.section: Ch. 15 Linda: Less is More (end); Ch. 16 Causes Trump Statistics (start)
pages.gist: Same math framed as Green cabs causing 85% of accidents gets the base rate used (Bayesian answer 41%); statistical base rates are underweighted while causal base rates are used because they fit a causal story.

pages.section: Ch. 15 Linda: Less is More (end); Ch. 16 Causes Trump Statistics (start)
pages.gist: Stereotypes are causal base rates; System 1 represents categories by prototypes; using valid stereotypes improves accuracy, but society rightly rejects them in hiring and profiling, and that rejection has a cost.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 16 "Causes Trump Statistics" (Causal Situations; Can Psychology be Taught?; Speaking of Causes and Statistics)
pages.gist: Ends the stereotyping point (denying the costs of ignoring valid stereotypes comes from the affect heuristic), then describes Ajzen's Yale exam study: causal base rates (test difficulty) affect judgment far more than statistically equivalent noncausal (sampling) base rates.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 16 "Causes Trump Statistics" (Causal Situations; Can Psychology be Taught?; Speaking of Causes and Statistics)
pages.gist: Nisbett-Borgida set up the 'helping experiment': only 4 of 15 participants helped a seizure victim at once, because diffusion of responsibility reduces helping when others can hear too.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 16 "Causes Trump Statistics" (Causal Situations; Can Psychology be Taught?; Speaking of Causes and Statistics)
pages.gist: Students who knew the 27% helping base rate still predicted that bland, nice interviewees had rushed to help, so their predictions matched those of students who did not know the result. A Bayesian would have stayed with the base rate.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 16 "Causes Trump Statistics" (Causal Situations; Can Psychology be Taught?; Speaking of Causes and Statistics)
pages.gist: Students 'quietly exempt themselves' from surprising statistics, yet generalize accurately from two surprising individual cases: people will not deduce the particular from the general but readily infer the general from the particular.

pages.section: Part II, Ch. 16 "Causes Trump Statistics" (Causal Situations; Can Psychology be Taught?; Speaking of Causes and Statistics)
pages.gist: 'Speaking of' examples: use representative individual cases to reach System 1, and expect causal statistics to be used to feed a stereotype.

pages.section: Part II, Chapter 17: Regression to the Mean (Talent and Luck; Understanding Regression)
pages.gist: Flight instructor claims punishment works better than praise; Kahneman sees regression to the mean and demonstrates it with a coin-throwing exercise at a floor target.

pages.section: Part II, Chapter 17: Regression to the Mean (Talent and Luck; Understanding Regression)
pages.gist: Instructors were trapped by perverse feedback (statistically punished for being nice, rewarded for being nasty); introduces success = talent + luck and the golf day-1 inference that a high scorer is both talented and lucky.

pages.section: Part II, Chapter 17: Regression to the Mean (Talent and Luck; Understanding Regression)
pages.gist: Best day-2 prediction is closer to the mean than day 1, more so for extreme scores; regression also runs backward in time, proving it is non-causal; Sports Illustrated jinx as a false causal story.

pages.section: Part II, Chapter 17: Regression to the Mean (Talent and Luck; Understanding Regression)
pages.gist: Ski-jump commentator invents causal stories for regression; regression is counterintuitive, discovered late by Galton in his studies of seeds and heredity.

pages.section: Part II, Chapter 17: Regression to the Mean (Talent and Luck; Understanding Regression)
pages.gist: Regression occurs whenever correlation between two measures is imperfect; ranks/standard scores compare different scales; correlation measures the weight of shared factors (parent-child height about .50).

pages.section: Ch. 17 Regression to the Mean (end, incl. "Speaking of Regression to Mediocrity"); start of Ch. 18 Taming Intuitive Predictions
pages.gist: Examples of correlation coefficients (range restriction lowers them); Galton's insight that imperfect correlation always implies regression; the 'intelligent women marry less intelligent men' puzzle as an algebraic restatement of imperfect correlation.

pages.section: Ch. 17 Regression to the Mean (end, incl. "Speaking of Regression to Mediocrity"); start of Ch. 18 Taming Intuitive Predictions
pages.gist: Regression has an explanation but no cause; System 1's demand for causal stories makes regression hard; the energy-drink/depressed-children example shows extreme groups improve on their own.

pages.section: Ch. 17 Regression to the Mean (end, incl. "Speaking of Regression to Mediocrity"); start of Ch. 18 Taming Intuitive Predictions
pages.gist: Control groups are needed to show a treatment beats regression; even scientists confuse correlation with causation; Bazerman's store-sales forecast shows forecasts must be regressive, not uniform +10%.

pages.section: Ch. 17 Regression to the Mean (end, incl. "Speaking of Regression to Mediocrity"); start of Ch. 18 Taming Intuitive Predictions
pages.gist: 'Speaking of' examples: praise vs criticism, a disappointing second interview, and expecting top screened candidates to underperform—all regression to the mean.

pages.section: Ch. 17 Regression to the Mean (end, incl. "Speaking of Regression to Mediocrity"); start of Ch. 18 Taming Intuitive Predictions
pages.gist: Opens 'Taming Intuitive Predictions': forecasts rely on calculation, skilled intuition (Klein), or heuristic substitution that yields confident nonregressive judgments from weak evidence; Julie GPA example introduced.

pages.section: Chapter 18: Taming Intuitive Predictions (Nonregressive Intuitions; A Correction for Intuitive Predictions; A Defense of Extreme Predictions?)
pages.gist: System 1 predicts Julie's GPA by finding a causal link, comparing the evidence to a norm, then using substitution and intensity matching, so the prediction comes out as extreme as the evidence.

pages.section: Chapter 18: Taming Intuitive Predictions (Nonregressive Intuitions; A Correction for Intuitive Predictions; A Defense of Extreme Predictions?)
pages.gist: An experiment with five-adjective counselor descriptions of freshmen: one group rates how impressive the description is, another predicts the student's GPA percentile.

pages.section: Chapter 18: Taming Intuitive Predictions (Nonregressive Intuitions; A Correction for Intuitive Predictions; A Defense of Extreme Predictions?)
pages.gist: Both groups gave identical judgments, so prediction matched evaluation; Israeli army officers likewise turned their unit ratings straight into officer-school grade forecasts, ignoring uncertainty.

pages.section: Chapter 18: Taming Intuitive Predictions (Nonregressive Intuitions; A Correction for Intuitive Predictions; A Defense of Extreme Predictions?)
pages.gist: A four-step correction: start from the average, find the intuitive matching value, estimate the correlation, and move only that fraction of the distance; it works for any quantitative prediction.

pages.section: Chapter 18: Taming Intuitive Predictions (Nonregressive Intuitions; A Correction for Intuitive Predictions; A Defense of Extreme Predictions?)
pages.gist: Nonregressive predictions are too optimistic for the best cases and too pessimistic for the worst; the scale correction mirrors the base-rate procedure for discrete outcomes, ending between the baseline and the intuition.

pages.section: Ch. 17 Regression to the Mean / Taming Intuitive Predictions (end, incl. "A Two-Systems View of Regression", "Speaking of Intuitive Predictions"); Part 3 title page; Overconfidence part opener
pages.gist: Correcting intuitive predictions takes System 2 effort that is worth it only when stakes are high; unbiased predictions never call extreme outcomes; when one error type costs far more (VC vs. banker), extreme language can be defended, but a rational actor bets knowing the odds are moderate.

pages.section: Ch. 17 Regression to the Mean / Taming Intuitive Predictions (end, incl. "A Two-Systems View of Regression", "Speaking of Intuitive Predictions"); Part 3 title page; Overconfidence part opener
pages.gist: Rational forecasters think in ranges and can invest in likely failures with large upside; the procedures make you ask how much you know: Kim (impressive, little information) vs. Jane (solid record) shows thin evidence calls for stronger regression to the mean.

pages.section: Ch. 17 Regression to the Mean / Taming Intuitive Predictions (end, incl. "A Two-Systems View of Regression", "Speaking of Intuitive Predictions"); Part 3 title page; Overconfidence part opener
pages.gist: Extreme predictions come from System 1 matching prediction extremeness to evidence extremeness and from confidence based on coherence; regression is alien to System 2, gets causal misreadings, and needs training; ends with example phrases on regressing predictions.

pages.section: Ch. 17 Regression to the Mean / Taming Intuitive Predictions (end, incl. "A Two-Systems View of Regression", "Speaking of Intuitive Predictions"); Part 3 title page; Overconfidence part opener
pages.gist: Part 3 title page only; no substantive content.

pages.section: Ch. 17 Regression to the Mean / Taming Intuitive Predictions (end, incl. "A Two-Systems View of Regression", "Speaking of Intuitive Predictions"); Part 3 title page; Overconfidence part opener
pages.gist: Part opener reading 'Overconfidence'; no substantive content.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence — Ch. 19 The Illusion of Understanding (The Social Costs of Hindsight; Recipes for Success)
pages.gist: Introduces Taleb's narrative fallacy: compelling stories are simple, concrete, over-credit talent/intent over luck, and ignore nonevents; the Google story illustrates the illusion of inevitability, and the true test of an explanation is whether it would have predicted the event in advance.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence — Ch. 19 The Illusion of Understanding (The Social Costs of Hindsight; Recipes for Success)
pages.gist: Luck matters more in the event than in its telling (rafter vs. Google founders); WYSIATI makes coherent stories easier with less information; the word 'knew' (and 'intuition', 'premonition') misused for past beliefs that proved true perpetuates the illusion that the world is knowable.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence — Ch. 19 The Illusion of Understanding (The Social Costs of Hindsight; Recipes for Success)
pages.gist: The mind cannot reconstruct past beliefs once changed (attitude-change studies); Fischhoff & Beyth's Nixon-trip study shows hindsight bias ('I-knew-it-all-along'), and hindsight leads to judging decisions by outcome rather than process.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence — Ch. 19 The Illusion of Understanding (The Social Costs of Hindsight; Recipes for Success)
pages.gist: Outcome bias: agents blamed for good decisions that turned out badly (Duluth flood monitor 24% vs 56%; 9/11 CIA memo); fear of hindsight drives bureaucratic, risk-averse defensive procedures, while lucky reckless risk-takers get undeserved credit.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence — Ch. 19 The Illusion of Understanding (The Social Costs of Hindsight; Recipes for Success)
pages.gist: System 1 sense-making makes the world seem tidy and predictable, feeding illusions of control; CEO quality-firm success correlation of ~.30 means the better CEO leads the better firm in only ~60% of pairs, 10 points above chance.

pages.section: Ch. 19 The Illusion of Understanding (end: Recipes for Success, Speaking of Hindsight); Part 3 / Ch. 20 The Illusion of Validity (opening)
pages.gist: Business books sell illusory certainty. Through the halo effect, a CEO is called methodical when the firm thrives and rigid when it fails, which reverses cause and effect. Built to Last-style comparisons of successful and unsuccessful firms are largely comparisons of luck.

pages.section: Ch. 19 The Illusion of Understanding (end: Recipes for Success, Speaking of Hindsight); Part 3 / Ch. 20 The Illusion of Validity (opening)
pages.gist: The performance gaps of 'excellent' firms shrink after study (regression to the mean, not complacency); success stories hide luck; 'Speaking of Hindsight' phrases on hindsight, narrative fallacy, outcome bias and halo.

pages.section: Ch. 19 The Illusion of Understanding (end: Recipes for Success, Speaking of Hindsight); Part 3 / Ch. 20 The Illusion of Validity (opening)
pages.gist: Near-blank page (part divider, single letter 'P'); no content.

pages.section: Ch. 19 The Illusion of Understanding (end: Recipes for Success, Speaking of Hindsight); Part 3 / Ch. 20 The Illusion of Validity (opening)
pages.gist: Ch. 20 opening: System 1 jumps to conclusions without knowing the size of its jumps. Confidence reflects how coherent the story is, not how much evidence there is or how good it is. Introduces the Israeli Army leaderless group challenge used to evaluate officer candidates.

pages.section: Ch. 19 The Illusion of Understanding (end: Recipes for Success, Speaking of Hindsight); Part 3 / Ch. 20 The Illusion of Validity (opening)
pages.gist: Evaluators felt completely confident in coherent impressions of leadership, yet feedback showed their predictions were barely better than chance. That knowledge did not change their confidence or moderate their forecasts, which is the origin of the term illusion of validity (analogy: Müller-Lyer illusion).

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence — Ch. 20 "The Illusion of Validity" (illusion of validity, illusion of stock-picking skill, what supports the illusions, start of illusions of pundits)
pages.gist: Names the illusion of validity from the army officer-selection story (substitution, representativeness, nonregressive predictions, WYSIATI), argues confidence is a feeling of coherence not a probability estimate, and opens the stock-picking skill section.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence — Ch. 20 "The Illusion of Validity" (illusion of validity, illusion of stock-picking skill, what supports the illusions, start of illusions of pundits)
pages.gist: Efficient-market puzzle: Odean's study of 163,000 trades shows stocks individual investors sold beat those they bought by 3.2 points/year, and the most active traders did worst.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence — Ch. 20 "The Illusion of Validity" (illusion of validity, illusion of stock-picking skill, what supports the illusions, start of illusions of pundits)
pages.gist: Individuals sell winners, hold losers and buy attention-grabbing news stocks; skill is diagnosed by year-to-year persistence of rankings, and mutual fund outcomes show near-zero persistence; setup of the wealth-adviser dataset.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence — Ch. 20 "The Illusion of Validity" (illusion of validity, illusion of stock-picking skill, what supports the illusions, start of illusions of pundits)
pages.gist: Average of 28 year-pair rank correlations among 25 advisers was .01, so the firm rewarded luck as skill, and executives and advisers ignored the base-rate fact in favor of personal experience.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence — Ch. 20 "The Illusion of Validity" (illusion of validity, illusion of stock-picking skill, what supports the illusions, start of illusions of pundits)
pages.gist: Unlike visual illusions, cognitive illusions persist after you know about them; illusions of skill are sustained by real high-level skill applied to the wrong question, System 1 confidence and a professional culture; hindsight narratives feed forecasting overconfidence (pundits).

pages.section: Ch. 20 The Illusion of Validity (end: Tetlock, hedgehogs/foxes, 'the world is difficult'); Ch. 21 Intuitions vs. Formulas (start: Meehl, Ashenfelter, broken-leg rule)
pages.gist: Luck shapes history (Hitler/Stalin/Mao embryo odds), yet the illusion of valid prediction persists; Tetlock's 20-year study of 284 experts and 80,000+ predictions found experts did worse than equal-probability guessing, and more knowledge brought overconfidence.

pages.section: Ch. 20 The Illusion of Validity (end: Tetlock, hedgehogs/foxes, 'the world is difficult'); Ch. 21 Intuitions vs. Formulas (start: Meehl, Ashenfelter, broken-leg rule)
pages.gist: Famous experts are more overconfident and full of excuses; hedgehogs (one big theory) forecast worse than foxes (many interacting forces plus luck); lessons: the world is unpredictable, and high subjective confidence does not show accuracy; tests with validity .20-.30 are worth using but no more should be expected.

pages.section: Ch. 20 The Illusion of Validity (end: Tetlock, hedgehogs/foxes, 'the world is difficult'); Ch. 21 Intuitions vs. Formulas (start: Meehl, Ashenfelter, broken-leg rule)
pages.gist: Short-term forecasts may be possible but long-term pundit forecasts are not; 'Speaking of Illusory Skill' phrases: illusion of validity, coherent story, smarter than the market, hedgehog, and 'is their world predictable?'

pages.section: Ch. 20 The Illusion of Validity (end: Tetlock, hedgehogs/foxes, 'the world is difficult'); Ch. 21 Intuitions vs. Formulas (start: Meehl, Ashenfelter, broken-leg rule)
pages.gist: Chapter 21 opens with Meehl's review: simple statistical rules beat or tie clinical judgment (formula beat 11 of 14 counselors); about 200 studies later, roughly 60% favor algorithms, the rest are draws, and no convincing exception exists.

pages.section: Ch. 20 The Illusion of Validity (end: Tetlock, hedgehogs/foxes, 'the world is difficult'); Ch. 21 Intuitions vs. Formulas (start: Meehl, Ashenfelter, broken-leg rule)
pages.gist: Algorithms match or beat experts in low-validity environments; Ashenfelter's 3-variable weather formula predicts Bordeaux prices (r>.90); experts lose because they try to be clever with complex combinations and override formulas; Meehl's broken-leg rule is the narrow exception.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence — Ch. 21 "Intuitions vs. Formulas" (inconsistency of judgment, Dawes improper linear models, Apgar score, The Hostility to Algorithms, Learning from Meehl)
pages.gist: Experts are inconsistent (radiologists contradict themselves 20% of the time) because System 1 is context-dependent; formulas give the same answer for the same input, so final decisions in low-validity settings should go to formulas, and interviews/tasting can lower accuracy.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence — Ch. 21 "Intuitions vs. Formulas" (inconsistency of judgment, Dawes improper linear models, Apgar score, The Hostility to Algorithms, Learning from Meehl)
pages.gist: Dawes: equal-weight 'improper' linear models of standardized valid predictors match or beat optimal regression, so back-of-envelope algorithms beat experts; the Apgar score example begins.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence — Ch. 21 "Intuitions vs. Formulas" (inconsistency of judgment, Dawes improper linear models, Apgar score, The Hostility to Algorithms, Learning from Meehl)
pages.gist: The Apgar 5-variable 0-2 score gave delivery rooms consistent standards; clinicians resist Meehl because short-term hunches with fast feedback succeed while long-term predictions without feedback fail, and they don't know the boundaries of their skill.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence — Ch. 21 "Intuitions vs. Formulas" (inconsistency of judgment, Dawes improper linear models, Apgar score, The Hostility to Algorithms, Learning from Meehl)
pages.gist: Algorithm aversion: preference for the natural, hostility to Ashenfelter's wine formula, and greater outrage at algorithm-caused errors than human errors; Kahneman starts the story of designing the Israeli army interview.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence — Ch. 21 "Intuitions vs. Formulas" (inconsistency of judgment, Dawes improper linear models, Apgar score, The Hostility to Algorithms, Learning from Meehl)
pages.gist: Kahneman's army interview redesign: six traits scored separately via factual past-behavior questions in a fixed order on 5-point scales, combined by a fixed formula to combat the halo effect, with interviewers told to provide reliable measurements, not predictions.

pages.section: Ch. 21 "Intuitions vs. Formulas" (end: Do It Yourself, Speaking of) and Ch. 22 "Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?" (opening: Marvels and Flaws, Intuition as Recognition, Acquiring Skill)
pages.gist: Israeli army interview results: summing six separately scored factual trait ratings beat global impressions, and a 'close your eyes' intuitive score given afterward was just as valid; then a do-it-yourself recipe for structured hiring begins.

pages.section: Ch. 21 "Intuitions vs. Formulas" (end: Do It Yourself, Speaking of) and Ch. 22 "Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?" (opening: Marvels and Flaws, Intuition as Recognition, Acquiring Skill)
pages.gist: Finishes the hiring recipe (score one trait at a time, add up scores, hire the top scorer and don't invent 'broken legs'), plus 'Speaking of Judges vs. Formulas' quotes.

pages.section: Ch. 21 "Intuitions vs. Formulas" (end: Do It Yourself, Speaking of) and Ch. 22 "Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?" (opening: Marvels and Flaws, Intuition as Recognition, Acquiring Skill)
pages.gist: Opens Ch. 22: hostile academic exchanges are pointless, so Kahneman did an 'adversarial collaboration' with Gary Klein (Naturalistic Decision Making) on when expert intuition can be trusted.

pages.section: Ch. 21 "Intuitions vs. Formulas" (end: Do It Yourself, Speaking of) and Ch. 22 "Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?" (opening: Marvels and Flaws, Intuition as Recognition, Acquiring Skill)
pages.gist: The kouros fake and the Harding election show intuition's successes and failures (Harding was elected because he looked the part, a substitution); Klein's fireground commanders produced a single option and mentally simulated it.

pages.section: Ch. 21 "Intuitions vs. Formulas" (end: Do It Yourself, Speaking of) and Ch. 22 "Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?" (opening: Marvels and Flaws, Intuition as Recognition, Acquiring Skill)
pages.gist: Recognition-primed decision model (System 1 suggests a plan, System 2 simulates it); Simon's line that intuition is just recognition; some intuitions like fear are learned from a single bad event.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence – Chapter 22 "Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?" (Acquiring Skill; The Environment of Skill; Feedback and Practice; Evaluating Validity)
pages.gist: Fear and hope are learned quickly, even from words, but real expertise (e.g., chess, ~10,000 hours) is slow because it is a large collection of miniskills, like learning to read patterns.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence – Chapter 22 "Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?" (Acquiring Skill; The Environment of Skill; Feedback and Practice; Evaluating Validity)
pages.gist: Kahneman and Klein agree that subjective confidence (driven by cognitive ease, coherence, WYSIATI) is not a reliable guide to an intuition's validity; skill needs a regular environment plus prolonged practice to learn it.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence – Chapter 22 "Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?" (Acquiring Skill; The Environment of Skill; Feedback and Practice; Evaluating Validity)
pages.gist: Valid intuitions rest on valid cues; zero-validity and 'wicked' environments teach wrong lessons; algorithms beat humans in noisy settings by using weak cues consistently; intuition cannot be trusted without stable regularities.

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence – Chapter 22 "Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?" (Acquiring Skill; The Environment of Skill; Feedback and Practice; Evaluating Validity)
pages.gist: Intuitive expertise depends on quality and speed of feedback and practice; expertise is task-specific, so experts overreach from short-term skills to long-term forecasts they never learned (anesthesiologist vs radiologist, therapist).

pages.section: Part III Overconfidence – Chapter 22 "Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?" (Acquiring Skill; The Environment of Skill; Feedback and Practice; Evaluating Validity)
pages.gist: Judge intuitions by provenance (regular environment + opportunity to learn) not by confidence; in low-validity settings substitution answers an easier question with high confidence; the conclusion seems obvious in hindsight.

pages.section: Ch. 22 Expert Intuition (end, 'Speaking of'); Ch. 23 The Outside View (opening, Drawn to the Inside View, The Planning Fallacy start)
pages.gist: End of Kahneman–Klein collaboration story plus 'Speaking of Expert Intuition' prompts: how much practice, regular environment, confidence is a poor index of accuracy, quality of feedback.

pages.section: Ch. 22 Expert Intuition (end, 'Speaking of'); Ch. 23 The Outside View (opening, Drawn to the Inside View, The Planning Fallacy start)
pages.gist: Opens 'The Outside View': curriculum team privately estimates ~2 years to finish; asked about similar teams, expert Seymour recalls ~40% failed and finishers took 7-10 years.

pages.section: Ch. 22 Expert Intuition (end, 'Speaking of'); Ch. 23 The Outside View (opening, Drawn to the Inside View, The Planning Fallacy start)
pages.gist: Team rated slightly below average, yet base-rate info was noted and set aside; book took 8 more years and went unused; three lessons: inside vs outside view, planning fallacy, irrational perseverance.

pages.section: Ch. 22 Expert Intuition (end, 'Speaking of'); Ch. 23 The Outside View (opening, Drawn to the Inside View, The Planning Fallacy start)
pages.gist: Inside view extrapolates from current plan (WYSIATI), missing unknown unknowns; outside view uses a reference class to form a baseline prediction that anchors case-specific adjustment.

pages.section: Ch. 22 Expert Intuition (end, 'Speaking of'); Ch. 23 The Outside View (opening, Drawn to the Inside View, The Planning Fallacy start)
pages.gist: People with case info rarely seek class statistics and discard 'pallid' statistics; 'every case is unique' resistance; planning fallacy defined as best-case forecasts improvable by consulting similar cases.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence — Ch. 23 The Outside View (Planning Fallacy, Mitigating, Decisions and Errors, Failing a Test, Speaking of) and start of Ch. 24 The Engine of Capitalism
pages.gist: Planning-fallacy horror stories (Scottish Parliament £40M→£431M, rail projects overestimating passengers by 106% with 45% cost overruns, kitchen remodels doubling), plus strategic misrepresentation to get plans approved and Flyvbjerg's call to use distributional information.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence — Ch. 23 The Outside View (Planning Fallacy, Mitigating, Decisions and Errors, Failing a Test, Speaking of) and start of Ch. 24 The Engine of Capitalism
