pages.gist: Reference class forecasting as the cure: a 3-step procedure (reference class, baseline statistics, case-specific adjustment), budget reserves becoming self-fulfilling, and organizations rewarding precise execution and penalizing failure to allow for unknown unknowns.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence — Ch. 23 The Outside View (Planning Fallacy, Mitigating, Decisions and Errors, Failing a Test, Speaking of) and start of Ch. 24 The Engine of Capitalism
pages.gist: Kahneman & Lovallo's theory that optimistic bias, not favorable odds, drives risky decisions; and Kahneman's own failure to stop the curriculum project due to sunk costs, no explicit forecast, and lethargy.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence — Ch. 23 The Outside View (Planning Fallacy, Mitigating, Decisions and Errors, Failing a Test, Speaking of) and start of Ch. 24 The Engine of Capitalism
pages.gist: 'Speaking of the Outside View' example sentences: inside view, planning fallacy as best-case assumption, baseline prediction for a legal case, and sunk-cost fallacy.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence — Ch. 23 The Outside View (Planning Fallacy, Mitigating, Decisions and Errors, Failing a Test, Speaking of) and start of Ch. 24 The Engine of Capitalism
pages.gist: Start of 'The Engine of Capitalism': optimistic bias is pervasive and perhaps the most consequential bias; optimists are healthier and happier but influential leaders are likely optimistic, overconfident, and take more risks than they realize.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence, ch. 24 "The Engine of Capitalism": Entrepreneurial Delusions, Competition Neglect, Overconfidence
pages.gist: Risk-takers voluntarily taking big bets are driven by optimistic bias; entrepreneurs estimate 60% success for 'business like yours' vs 35% real, and 47% of inventors told their idea was hopeless kept going, doubling their losses.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence, ch. 24 "The Engine of Capitalism": Entrepreneurial Delusions, Competition Neglect, Overconfidence
pages.gist: Optimism is widespread, stubborn and costly: above-average beliefs, the hubris hypothesis for mergers, overconfident CEOs (Malmendier & Tate) taking value-destroying risks, award-winning CEOs underperforming, and the motel bought after six or seven owners failed.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence, ch. 24 "The Engine of Capitalism": Entrepreneurial Delusions, Competition Neglect, Overconfidence
pages.gist: Policy dilemma of subsidizing likely-failing entrepreneurs; competition neglect is explained by WYSIATI (planning fallacy, neglect of others, illusion of control, overconfidence), and the above-average effect is introduced via driver questions.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence, ch. 24 "The Engine of Capitalism": Entrepreneurial Delusions, Competition Neglect, Overconfidence
pages.gist: The above-average effect is substitution of an easy question for a hard one; founders credit 80%+ of outcome to their own actions; Disney 'hubris' quote shows competition neglect leading to excess entry and 'optimistic martyrs'.

pages.section: Part 3 Overconfidence, ch. 24 "The Engine of Capitalism": Entrepreneurial Delusions, Competition Neglect, Overconfidence
pages.gist: Duke CFO survey: 11,600 S&P forecasts had about zero correlation with outcomes; 80% intervals produced 67% surprises, honest intervals would be over 4x wider, but admitting ignorance is socially penalized.

pages.section: Ch. 24 "The Engine of Capitalism" (end: Overconfidence, The Premortem, Speaking of Optimism); Part 4 "Choices" title pages
pages.gist: Social and market pressures reward confident experts over honest ones (TV pundits, ICU physicians 'completely certain' yet wrong 40%); risk takers are less aware of risk ('bold forecasts and timid decisions'); optimism mainly helps by giving resilience through an optimistic explanatory style.

pages.section: Ch. 24 "The Engine of Capitalism" (end: Overconfidence, The Premortem, Speaking of Optimism); Part 4 "Choices" title pages
pages.gist: Training against overconfidence works only a little; confidence tracks how coherent the story is, not how good the evidence is; Klein's premortem (imagine the plan has failed, write its history) counters groupthink and the suppression of doubt.

pages.section: Ch. 24 "The Engine of Capitalism" (end: Overconfidence, The Premortem, Speaking of Optimism); Part 4 "Choices" title pages
pages.gist: 'Speaking of Optimism' sample phrases: illusion of control, competitor neglect, overconfidence, and a call to run a premortem.

pages.section: Ch. 24 "The Engine of Capitalism" (end: Overconfidence, The Premortem, Speaking of Optimism); Part 4 "Choices" title pages
pages.gist: Title page for Part 4; no substantive content.

pages.section: Ch. 24 "The Engine of Capitalism" (end: Overconfidence, The Premortem, Speaking of Optimism); Part 4 "Choices" title pages
pages.gist: Title page reading 'Choices' (Part 4 title); no substantive content.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Chapter 25 "Bernoulli's Errors"
pages.gist: Opens Part IV: Frey's claim that economic agents are rational, selfish and stable contrasts with psychologists' Humans (System 1, WYSIATI); simple gambles introduced as the 'fruit fly' model for risky decisions.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Chapter 25 "Bernoulli's Errors"
pages.gist: Expected utility theory as normative logic of choice (von Neumann–Morgenstern axioms) vs descriptive study; Kahneman and Tversky used their own intuitive choices (coin toss $100 vs sure $46) as quick hypotheses to verify later, leading to prospect theory.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Chapter 25 "Bernoulli's Errors"
pages.gist: Prospect theory as a descriptive model of violations of rationality; framing effects defined; Fechner's psychophysics and logarithmic law; Bernoulli's idea that utility of wealth is logarithmic so changes are felt proportionally.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Chapter 25 "Bernoulli's Errors"
pages.gist: Expected value vs expected utility: people prefer $80 sure over a gamble worth $82; Bernoulli explained risk aversion via diminishing marginal utility of wealth (Table 3).

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Chapter 25 "Bernoulli's Errors"
pages.gist: Worked utility example showing sure thing beats equal-EV gamble; insurance explained by poor transferring risk to rich; Bernoulli's flaw exposed by Jack and Jill—happiness depends on change from a reference point, not wealth level.

pages.section: Part 4 Choices: ch. 25 "Bernoulli's Errors" (end, incl. Speaking of) and ch. 26 "Prospect Theory" (opening)
pages.gist: Reference dependence: Anthony (1M) and Betty (4M) face identical wealth options, but a sure 2M is a doubling gain for Anthony and a halving loss for Betty, so they will choose differently.

pages.section: Part 4 Choices: ch. 25 "Bernoulli's Errors" (end, incl. Speaking of) and ch. 26 "Prospect Theory" (opening)
pages.gist: Bernoulli's model lacks a reference point, so it cannot explain risk seeking when all options are bad; Kahneman names theory-induced blindness and closes with 'Speaking of' examples (bonus, salary, alimony).

pages.section: Part 4 Choices: ch. 25 "Bernoulli's Errors" (end, incl. Speaking of) and ch. 26 "Prospect Theory" (opening)
pages.gist: Near-blank page (single stray character), part/chapter separator; no content.

pages.section: Part 4 Choices: ch. 25 "Bernoulli's Errors" (end, incl. Speaking of) and ch. 26 "Prospect Theory" (opening)
pages.gist: Prospect Theory chapter opens: Kahneman's outsider ignorance of utility theory plus Markowitz's idea led to defining outcomes as gains and losses rather than states of wealth, escaping theory-induced blindness.

pages.section: Part 4 Choices: ch. 25 "Bernoulli's Errors" (end, incl. Speaking of) and ch. 26 "Prospect Theory" (opening)
pages.gist: Switching to losses reverses risk attitude: people take sure $900 gain but gamble to avoid a sure $900 loss; Problem 3 begins demonstrating Bernoulli's central error.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 26 Prospect Theory (reference point, value function, loss aversion, Rabin's theorem)
pages.gist: Problems 3 and 4 have the same final wealth outcomes, yet people take the sure thing when it is framed as a gain and the gamble when it is framed as a loss. This shows that choices depend on a reference point, which people largely ignore.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 26 Prospect Theory (reference point, value function, loss aversion, Rabin's theorem)
pages.gist: The reference point is the missing variable in Bernoulli's theory. Three System 1 features sit at the core of prospect theory: evaluation relative to a reference point (the three-bowls-of-water demo), diminishing sensitivity and loss aversion.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 26 Prospect Theory (reference point, value function, loss aversion, Rabin's theorem)
pages.gist: The S-shaped value function has a kink at the reference point, and the loss side is steeper. The section on loss aversion opens with mixed prospects (startups, lawsuits, offensives) and the coin-toss gamble: lose $100 or win $150.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 26 Prospect Theory (reference point, value function, loss aversion, Rabin's theorem)
pages.gist: Most people reject a positive-EV mixed gamble. The loss aversion ratio is about 1.5–2.5, it rises with stakes and is infinite when a loss could be ruinous. Being told to 'think like a trader' reduces it.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 26 Prospect Theory (reference point, value function, loss aversion, Rabin's theorem)
pages.gist: Loss aversion drives risk aversion in mixed gambles, while diminishing sensitivity drives risk seeking when all choices are bad. Rabin's theorem shows that utility of wealth cannot explain aversion to small risks, a case of theory-induced blindness that lasted 250 years.

pages.section: Part 4 Choices: ch. 26 Prospect Theory (end: Blind Spots of Prospect Theory, Speaking of Prospect Theory); ch. 27 The Endowment Effect (start)
pages.gist: Ends the Rabin-Thaler 'ex-hypothesis' critique, then opens 'Blind Spots of Prospect Theory': theory-induced blindness also applies to prospect theory, whose assumption that the reference point (status quo) is worth zero gives absurd results.

pages.section: Part 4 Choices: ch. 26 Prospect Theory (end: Blind Spots of Prospect Theory, Speaking of Prospect Theory); ch. 27 The Endowment Effect (start)
pages.gist: Prospect theory cannot handle disappointment, because a highly likely big win sets a new reference point and missing it feels like a loss, or regret, where an outcome is judged against the option not chosen ($1M gamble vs sure $50 or sure $150,000).

pages.section: Part 4 Choices: ch. 26 Prospect Theory (end: Blind Spots of Prospect Theory, Speaking of Prospect Theory); ch. 27 The Endowment Effect (start)
pages.gist: Theories get adopted when their extra concepts give new predictions that turn out true, not merely because they are more realistic; then 'Speaking of Prospect Theory' examples (losses weighted about twice gains).

pages.section: Part 4 Choices: ch. 26 Prospect Theory (end: Blind Spots of Prospect Theory, Speaking of Prospect Theory); ch. 27 The Endowment Effect (start)
pages.gist: Opens 'The Endowment Effect' with the economics indifference map (income vs vacation days), whose convex curves show diminishing marginal utility, and the claim that points on one curve are equally attractive.

pages.section: Part 4 Choices: ch. 26 Prospect Theory (end: Blind Spots of Prospect Theory, Speaking of Prospect Theory); ch. 27 The Endowment Effect (start)
pages.gist: The indifference map leaves out the current reference point (theory-induced blindness again). Reference points and loss aversion drive labor negotiations, job changes and unemployed workers' wage floors, and the Albert/Ben hedonic twins example shows status-quo preference.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 27 The Endowment Effect (status quo bias, endowment effect, Thinking Like a Trader)
pages.gist: Albert/Ben hedonic twins: once a position becomes the reference point, switching is coded as a loss, so tastes depend on the reference point and loss aversion biases toward the status quo and small changes; the endowment effect section opens with Thaler.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 27 The Endowment Effect (status quo bias, endowment effect, Thinking Like a Trader)
pages.gist: Professor R's wine (won't sell under $100, won't buy over $35) and concert-ticket examples define the endowment effect, explained by prospect theory's loss-averse value function depending on ownership as reference point.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 27 The Endowment Effect (status quo bias, endowment effect, Thinking Like a Trader)
pages.gist: Endowment effect is not universal: goods held 'for exchange' (money, merchant's shoes) show no loss aversion, unlike goods held 'for use'; Vernon Smith token markets trade exactly as theory predicts.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 27 The Endowment Effect (status quo bias, endowment effect, Thinking Like a Trader)
pages.gist: Mug experiments: sellers ask about twice what buyers pay, trades are under half the predicted volume, and Sellers ($7.12) vs Choosers ($3.12) differ despite facing the same choice; brain imaging links selling owned goods to pain.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 27 The Endowment Effect (status quo bias, endowment effect, Thinking Like a Trader)
pages.gist: Loss-to-gain ratio of ~2:1 recurs (price increases hit purchases twice as hard as decreases); Knetsch pen/chocolate swap only ~10%; Boston condo owners anchored on purchase price; trading experience and an exchange mindset eliminate the endowment effect.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — end of ch. 27 "The Endowment Effect" (incl. Speaking Of) and start of ch. 28 "Bad Events" (Negativity Dominance; Goals are Reference Points)
pages.gist: List's trading experiment: experienced traders show no endowment effect (48% trade vs 18% of novices); physical possession is required for the effect; veteran traders ask the opportunity-cost question; the poor live in the losses, so for them every cost is a loss.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — end of ch. 27 "The Endowment Effect" (incl. Speaking Of) and start of ch. 28 "Bad Events" (Negativity Dominance; Goals are Reference Points)
pages.gist: 'Speaking of the endowment effect' phrases: reluctance to trade an office once assigned, stuck negotiations because losses loom larger, refusing to sell a house below purchase price, a miser treating spending as loss.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — end of ch. 27 "The Endowment Effect" (incl. Speaking Of) and start of ch. 28 "Bad Events" (Negativity Dominance; Goals are Reference Points)
pages.gist: Opens 'Bad Events': loss aversion as psychology's main gift to behavioral economics, framed within negativity dominance; masked fearful eyes trigger the amygdala without conscious awareness.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — end of ch. 27 "The Endowment Effect" (incl. Speaking Of) and start of ch. 28 "Bad Events" (Negativity Dominance; Goals are Reference Points)
pages.gist: Brain prioritizes bad news (angry faces pop out, bad words grab attention, disagreeable opinions register as threats in under 0.25 s); 'bad is stronger than good' evidence, Rozin's cockroach, Gottman's 5:1 ratio; good/bad boundary is a shifting reference point.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — end of ch. 27 "The Endowment Effect" (incl. Speaking Of) and start of ch. 28 "Bad Events" (Negativity Dominance; Goals are Reference Points)
pages.gist: Goals act as reference points: missing a goal is a loss weighted more than exceeding it; NY cabdrivers with daily targets quit early on rainy days; golfers' par as reference point sets up the bogey vs birdie putt comparison.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, ch. 28 "Bad Events": Goals are Reference Points (end), Defending the Status Quo, Loss Aversion in the Law, Speaking of Losses
pages.gist: Golfers putt 3.6% better for par than for birdie (2.5M putts), showing goals as reference points; loss aversion makes renegotiations hard, concessions are valued asymmetrically, and negotiators signal reference points/anchors.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, ch. 28 "Bad Events": Goals are Reference Points (end), Defending the Status Quo, Loss Aversion in the Law, Speaking of Losses
pages.gist: Defenders win because loss aversion makes potential losers fight harder, so reforms get diluted with grandfather clauses; start of the Thaler-Knetsch-Kahneman fairness surveys with the snow-shovel price example.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, ch. 28 "Bad Events": Goals are Reference Points (end), Defending the Status Quo, Loss Aversion in the Law, Speaking of Losses
pages.gist: 82% call the post-blizzard price rise unfair; cutting a current worker's wage is unfair (83%) but paying a replacement less is acceptable (73%); dual entitlements: firms may pass on losses but need not share gains.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, ch. 28 "Bad Events": Goals are Reference Points (end), Defending the Status Quo, Loss Aversion in the Law, Speaking of Losses
pages.gist: Fairness concerns have economic teeth (customers cut purchases 15% after seeing a lower price), altruistic punishment is rewarding, and the law distinguishes actual losses from foregone gains.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, ch. 28 "Bad Events": Goals are Reference Points (end), Defending the Status Quo, Loss Aversion in the Law, Speaking of Losses
pages.gist: 'Speaking of Losses' summary quotes on reform resistance, concession asymmetry, expanding vs shrinking pie, and tenant entitlement.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 29 The Fourfold Pattern (Changing Chances; Allais's Paradox; Decision Weights)
pages.gist: System 1 automatically assigns weights to features of complex objects; the expectation principle (probability-weighted outcomes) is introduced and challenged with four equal 5% improvements in chance.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 29 The Fourfold Pattern (Changing Chances; Allais's Paradox; Decision Weights)
pages.gist: Defines the possibility effect (0→5% overweighted) and certainty effect (95→100% looms large), illustrated by lottery tickets, a $910,000 offer for a 95% lawsuit, surgery risks; notes von Neumann–Morgenstern showed non-proportional weights are irrational.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 29 The Fourfold Pattern (Changing Chances; Allais's Paradox; Decision Weights)
pages.gist: Allais's paradox: people prefer 61%/$520k over 63%/$500k but 100%/$500k over 98%/$520k, explained via an urn of 100 marbles showing the inconsistency.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 29 The Fourfold Pattern (Changing Chances; Allais's Paradox; Decision Weights)
pages.gist: The inconsistency stems from the certainty effect; economists ignored the anomaly, theorists rationalized it, while Kahneman and Tversky built prospect theory with decision weights differing from probabilities; Table 4 introduced.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 29 The Fourfold Pattern (Changing Chances; Allais's Paradox; Decision Weights)
pages.gist: Decision weights: 2% weighted 8.1, 98% weighted 87.1; certainty effect stronger than possibility effect; 5–95% compressed into 13.2–79.3; very rare events either ignored or overweighted; insensitivity among small probabilities; worry requires zero risk.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, Ch. 29 "The Fourfold Pattern" (certainty premium, fourfold pattern, Gambling in the Shadow of the Law, Speaking of the Fourfold Pattern)
pages.gist: Insect-spray study: parents pay $2.38 to cut a risk from 15 to 5 per 10,000 but $8.09 to eliminate it, showing a certainty premium; the fourfold pattern (Figure 13) is introduced.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, Ch. 29 "The Fourfold Pattern" (certainty premium, fourfold pattern, Gambling in the Shadow of the Law, Speaking of the Fourfold Pattern)
pages.gist: Explains the fourfold pattern cells: risk aversion for likely gains, lotteries from the possibility effect, insurance for unlikely losses, and the surprising risk seeking for likely losses.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, Ch. 29 "The Fourfold Pattern" (certainty premium, fourfold pattern, Gambling in the Shadow of the Law, Speaking of the Fourfold Pattern)
pages.gist: Risk seeking in losses comes from diminishing sensitivity plus underweighting of high probabilities; desperate gambles turn failures into disasters; a strong-case plaintiff is risk averse.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, Ch. 29 "The Fourfold Pattern" (certainty premium, fourfold pattern, Gambling in the Shadow of the Law, Speaking of the Fourfold Pattern)
pages.gist: A weak-case defendant is risk seeking and has the stronger bargaining hand; frivolous suits flip the roles; the NYC example shows that settling 200 suits costs $20M against $10M for litigating.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, Ch. 29 "The Fourfold Pattern" (certainty premium, fourfold pattern, Gambling in the Shadow of the Law, Speaking of the Fourfold Pattern)
pages.gist: Systematic deviations from expected value add up to losses over many decisions; 'Speaking of' examples cover frivolous claims, paying for certainty, refusing to cut losses, and the possibility effect.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 30 "Rare Events" (opening, Overestimation and Overweighting, Vivid Outcomes)
pages.gist: Israeli bus bombings: a tiny real risk still drives avoidance because vivid images create an availability cascade; System 1 emotion cannot be turned off, doesn't respond to how big the probability is, and lotteries work the same way.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 30 "Rare Events" (opening, Overestimation and Overweighting, Vivid Outcomes)
pages.gist: Only possibility matters for vivid rare events; emotion and vividness drive overweighting; overestimation (judging probability) differs from overweighting (deciding), but both come from focused attention, confirmation bias and cognitive ease.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 30 "Rare Events" (opening, Overestimation and Overweighting, Vivid Outcomes)
pages.gist: Probability judgments follow how easily a plausible scenario comes to mind; the mind focuses on the unusual alternative, and Fox's NBA study shows probabilities for eight focal teams summing to 240% when the alternative is left vague, versus 100% for East/West.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 30 "Rare Events" (opening, Overestimation and Overweighting, Vivid Outcomes)
pages.gist: Fans' cash equivalents for the eight team bets add up to $287 for a $160 payoff, which ties to the planning fallacy (success is specific, failure is diffuse); in prospect theory decision weights are flat compared with probability (71.2 vs 18.6 for 90%/10%), and emotional outcomes are even less sensitive to probability.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 30 "Rare Events" (opening, Overestimation and Overweighting, Vivid Outcomes)
pages.gist: Princeton work: insensitivity to probability comes from the lack of an expected-value anchor for non-money outcomes, not from emotional intensity; giving an explicit dollar value still did not restore sensitivity.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, Ch. 30 "Rare Events" (vividness of outcomes, Vivid Probabilities, Decisions from Global Impressions, Speaking of Rare Events)
pages.gist: A rich, vivid picture of an outcome (roses, a blue envelope of cash) reduces sensitivity to probability by boosting both possibility and certainty effects; the urn experiment shows many choose 8/100 over 1/10.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, Ch. 30 "Rare Events" (vividness of outcomes, Vivid Probabilities, Decisions from Global Impressions, Speaking of Rare Events)
pages.gist: Denominator neglect: attention to the count of winners ignores the total; frequency formats (1 in 100,000; 1,286 of 10,000) make risks seem bigger than percentages, even for forensic professionals.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, Ch. 30 "Rare Events" (vividness of outcomes, Vivid Probabilities, Decisions from Global Impressions, Speaking of Rare Events)
pages.gist: Frequency format nearly doubled refusals to discharge a patient (41% vs 21%); advocates and lawyers exploit format; salience from mention, vividness and format drives overestimation and overweighting; choice from experience is introduced.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, Ch. 30 "Rare Events" (vividness of outcomes, Vivid Probabilities, Decisions from Global Impressions, Speaking of Rare Events)
pages.gist: In choice from experience rare events are underweighted, often because people never experienced them (earthquakes, financial crises); Adele vs Brian example of choosing between colleagues.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, Ch. 30 "Rare Events" (vividness of outcomes, Vivid Probabilities, Decisions from Global Impressions, Speaking of Rare Events)
pages.gist: System 1 decides from pooled global impressions biased to typical and recent instances; rare events are overweighted only if they get explicit attention, otherwise neglected; closing phrases on the disaster cycle and making alternatives add to 100%.

pages.section: Ch. 30 Rare Events (closing "Speaking of" line); Ch. 31 Risk Policies (Broad or Narrow?; Samuelson's Problem)
pages.gist: The last 'Speaking of Rare Events' quote, about expressing a risk as 1 death per 1,000 to exploit denominator neglect; the chapter ends here.

pages.section: Ch. 30 Rare Events (closing "Speaking of" line); Ch. 31 Risk Policies (Broad or Narrow?; Samuelson's Problem)
pages.gist: Opens 'Risk Policies' with two concurrent choices (sure $240 gain vs. gamble; sure $750 loss vs. gamble). 73% choose A and D, a combination that only 3% reverse, which shows risk aversion for gains and risk seeking for losses.

pages.section: Ch. 30 Rare Events (closing "Speaking of" line); Ch. 31 Risk Policies (Broad or Narrow?; Samuelson's Problem)
pages.gist: Combining the two choices shows the popular A+D pick is dominated by B+C. This introduces narrow framing (separate decisions) versus broad framing (one comprehensive choice), with broad never worse.

pages.section: Ch. 30 Rare Events (closing "Speaking of" line); Ch. 31 Risk Policies (Broad or Narrow?; Samuelson's Problem)
pages.gist: Humans are natural narrow framers because of WYSIATI and aversion to effort. Samuelson's friend rejects one favorable coin bet but would accept 100 of them, and Rabin and Thaler show that bundle is overwhelmingly favorable.

pages.section: Ch. 30 Rare Events (closing "Speaking of" line); Ch. 31 Risk Policies (Broad or Narrow?; Samuelson's Problem)
pages.gist: Sam weights losses twice as heavily, so one toss is worth 0 to him, but bundled tosses gain value fast (5 tosses: 18.75% chance of loss, cash equivalent $203). Kahneman's 'sermon' says to treat each small favorable gamble as part of a bundle.

pages.section: Part IV Choices: Risk Policies (end of chapter); Keeping Score (start: mental accounts, sunk cost, disposition effect)
pages.gist: Qualifications for the 'you win a few, you lose a few' mantra (independence, small stakes relative to wealth, no long shots), and an experiment showing 'think like a trader' broad framing blunts emotional reaction to losses and increases risk taking.

pages.section: Part IV Choices: Risk Policies (end of chapter); Keeping Score (start: mental accounts, sunk cost, disposition effect)
pages.gist: Checking investments less often reduces loss-aversion-driven churn; risk policies (e.g., max deductible, no extended warranties) are broad frames analogous to the outside view; outside view counters optimism while risk policy counters loss aversion; Thaler's 25-division executive gamble begins.

pages.section: Part IV Choices: Risk Policies (end of chapter); Keeping Score (start: mental accounts, sunk cost, disposition effect)
pages.gist: The CEO wants all 25 division heads to accept their risks because he sees the aggregate; 'Speaking of Risk Policies' summary quotes.

pages.section: Part IV Choices: Risk Policies (end of chapter); Keeping Score (start: mental accounts, sunk cost, disposition effect)
pages.gist: Keeping Score: money as emotional scorekeeping leads to refusal to cut losses, regret aversion, omission/commission asymmetry and agent conflicts; Thaler's mental accounts as narrow framing; blizzard ticket example begins.

pages.section: Part IV Choices: Risk Policies (end of chapter); Keeping Score (start: mental accounts, sunk cost, disposition effect)
pages.gist: Paid-ticket fan braves blizzard (sunk cost via mental accounting) and the counterfactual question System 2 must ask; investors prefer selling winners over losers — the disposition effect, an instance of narrow framing.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 32 "Keeping Score" (disposition effect, sunk costs, regret, responsibility)
pages.gist: The disposition effect costs money (selling winners is worse on taxes and momentum, about 3.4% after tax). The sunk-cost fallacy is shown by a $50M project that wants $60M more, and escalation can come from the executive's own interest.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 32 "Keeping Score" (disposition effect, sunk costs, regret, responsibility)
pages.gist: Agency problem: boards replace CEOs who are tied to sunk costs, and teaching the fallacy helps people walk away. Regret is a counterfactual emotion set off by abnormal events (plane-crash stories, the Brown/Smith hitchhiker case).

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 32 "Keeping Score" (disposition effect, sunk costs, regret, responsibility)
pages.gist: Regret and blame use different norms (Brown 88% regret vs Smith 77% blame). In the Paul/George stock example, 92% expect more regret when a bad outcome came from acting rather than from not acting.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 32 "Keeping Score" (disposition effect, sunk costs, regret, responsibility)
pages.gist: Leaving the default, not commission itself, causes regret (blackjack hit/stand, the coach). Fear of regret pushes people toward conventional, risk-averse choices (brands, fund managers, physicians). Loss aversion grows when you are responsible.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Ch. 32 "Keeping Score" (disposition effect, sunk costs, regret, responsibility)
pages.gist: Thaler's disease example: people ask about 50 times more to accept a 1/1000 risk than they will pay to remove it. Parents refuse any discount for a 15→16 per 10,000 insecticide risk, a stance that is incoherent and can do harm.

pages.section: Part IV ch. 32 "Keeping Score" (end: taboo tradeoff, precautionary principle, regret inoculation, Speaking of) and ch. 33 "Reversals" (single vs joint evaluation, preference reversals, Challenging Economics)
pages.gist: The taboo against trading any added risk wastes a limited safety budget and may come from fear of regret. Kahneman extends this to the precautionary principle, then advises naming the possibility of regret explicitly before deciding.

pages.section: Part IV ch. 32 "Keeping Score" (end: taboo tradeoff, precautionary principle, regret inoculation, Speaking of) and ch. 33 "Reversals" (single vs joint evaluation, preference reversals, Challenging Economics)
pages.gist: Regret comes with hindsight bias, so Kahneman decides either very thoroughly or casually. Gilbert's 'psychological immune system' means people expect more regret than they feel. Ends with 'Speaking of Keeping Score' quotes on mental accounts, the disposition effect and taboo tradeoffs.

pages.section: Part IV ch. 32 "Keeping Score" (end: taboo tradeoff, precautionary principle, regret inoculation, Speaking of) and ch. 33 "Reversals" (single vs joint evaluation, preference reversals, Challenging Economics)
pages.gist: Opens chapter 'Reversals' with the crime-victim compensation case: judged side by side (joint evaluation), the store where he was shot is seen as irrelevant.

pages.section: Part IV ch. 32 "Keeping Score" (end: taboo tradeoff, precautionary principle, regret inoculation, Speaking of) and ch. 33 "Reversals" (single vs joint evaluation, preference reversals, Challenging Economics)
pages.gist: Judged alone (single evaluation), the victim shot in an unusual store gets more because of poignancy, via substitution and intensity matching. Moral principles apply only in joint mode, and life is mostly lived one option at a time (WYSIATI). The Lichtenstein–Slovic bets show people choose the safe bet B but put a higher selling price on bet A, anchored on its prize.

pages.section: Part IV ch. 32 "Keeping Score" (end: taboo tradeoff, precautionary principle, regret inoculation, Speaking of) and ch. 33 "Reversals" (single vs joint evaluation, preference reversals, Challenging Economics)
pages.gist: Joint evaluation brings out features (safety) that single evaluation hides, while single evaluation is driven by System 1 emotion and anchors. A within-subject test confirms the reversal, Grether and Plott failed to refute it, and established theories resist one awkward finding.

pages.section: Part IV, Ch. 33 "Reversals": Categories; Unjust Reversals; Speaking of Reversals
pages.gist: Economists barely changed their views after the preference-reversal findings; the 'Categories' section explains that System 1 judges objects against norms of their own category (John's height), so judgments are coherent within categories but can clash across them.

pages.section: Part IV, Ch. 33 "Reversals": Categories; Unjust Reversals; Speaking of Reversals
pages.gist: Apples vs steak have no stable comparison; the dolphin donation appeal shows that the dollar amount comes from substitution plus intensity matching against the dolphin's rank among endangered species.

pages.section: Part IV, Ch. 33 "Reversals": Categories; Unjust Reversals; Speaking of Reversals
pages.gist: The farmworker skin-cancer appeal ranks low among public-health issues, so it gets less in single evaluation, but joint evaluation makes 'human vs animal' stand out and reverses the preference; Hsee's dictionary example illustrates the evaluability hypothesis.

pages.section: Part IV, Ch. 33 "Reversals": Categories; Unjust Reversals; Speaking of Reversals
pages.gist: Mock jurors gave a defrauded bank more than a burned child in single evaluation (anchored on the dollar loss) but more than doubled personal-injury awards in joint evaluation; broader frames usually help rationality unless someone who controls the context is manipulating it.

pages.section: Part IV, Ch. 33 "Reversals": Categories; Unjust Reversals; Speaking of Reversals
pages.gist: The legal system bars juries from comparing cases, which favors single evaluation; agency fines make sense within each agency but not across agencies (worker safety $7,000 vs Wild Bird $25,000); closing quotes urge broadening the frame.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Chapter 34 "Frames and Reality" (opening: Emotional Framing)
pages.gist: Essentially blank page (single stray character), a chapter separator; no content.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Chapter 34 "Frames and Reality" (opening: Emotional Framing)
pages.gist: Opens 'Frames and Reality': 'Italy won' vs 'France lost' are logically equivalent but evoke different System 1 associations; framing effects defined as unjustified influence of wording, with the gamble-vs-lottery-ticket example.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Chapter 34 "Frames and Reality" (opening: Emotional Framing)
pages.gist: The lottery-ticket framing wins more acceptance because costs feel less bad than losses; Thaler's 'cash discount not credit surcharge'; introduces the UCL brain-imaging KEEP £20 vs LOSE £30 experiment.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Chapter 34 "Frames and Reality" (opening: Emotional Framing)
pages.gist: Frame-conforming choices engaged the amygdala (emotional System 1), resisting the frame engaged the anterior cingulate (conflict), and the least framing-prone subjects showed frontal activity integrating emotion and reasoning.

pages.section: Part IV Choices — Chapter 34 "Frames and Reality" (opening: Emotional Framing)
pages.gist: Rational subjects were reality-bound with little conflict; physicians chose surgery 84% under '90% survival' vs 50% favoring radiation under '10% mortality'; expertise doesn't protect; reframing to a common frame is effortful and lazy System 2 accepts problems as framed.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, ch. 34 "Frames and Reality": Empty Intuitions; Good Frames
pages.gist: Asian disease problem: logically identical lives-saved vs lives-lost framings flip majority preference from the sure option to the gamble, matching prospect theory's risk aversion for gains and risk seeking for losses.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, ch. 34 "Frames and Reality": Empty Intuitions; Good Frames
pages.gist: Public-health professionals are equally framing-susceptible; confronted with their inconsistency people fall silent because System 2 has no independent moral intuitions; Schelling's child-exemption tax example begins.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, ch. 34 "Frames and Reality": Empty Intuitions; Good Frames
pages.gist: Schelling's bonus vs surcharge formulations show moral intuitions attach to an arbitrary reference point, so there is no underlying preference behind frames; 'Good Frames' introduces the lost-tickets vs lost-cash problem.

pages.section: Part IV Choices, ch. 34 "Frames and Reality": Empty Intuitions; Good Frames
pages.gist: Lost tickets vs lost cash is explained by mental accounting and sunk cost, the broader cash frame is better; the MPG illusion shows miles-per-gallon misleads intuitions (Adam's 12→14 saves more than Beth's 30→40).

pages.section: Part IV Choices, ch. 34 "Frames and Reality": Empty Intuitions; Good Frames
pages.gist: Gallons-per-mile should replace mpg; organ donation rates (Austria ~100% vs Germany 12%) are driven by opt-out vs opt-in defaults, a System 2 laziness effect, so choice of formulation is itself a policy decision.

pages.section: Ch. 34 Frames and Reality (end, incl. Speaking of); Part 5 title page; Ch. 35 Two Selves (opening: experienced vs decision utility, Experience and Memory)
pages.gist: Concludes framing chapter: trivial features of how a choice is put (e.g., organ-donation default) control important choices, which counts against the rational-agent model; 'Speaking of' lines on reframing via reference point, mental accounts and opt-in vs opt-out.

pages.section: Ch. 34 Frames and Reality (end, incl. Speaking of); Part 5 title page; Ch. 35 Two Selves (opening: experienced vs decision utility, Experience and Memory)
pages.gist: Part divider page reading 'Part 5'; no substantive content.

pages.section: Ch. 34 Frames and Reality (end, incl. Speaking of); Part 5 title page; Ch. 35 Two Selves (opening: experienced vs decision utility, Experience and Memory)
pages.gist: Title page for 'Two Selves'; no substantive content.

pages.section: Ch. 34 Frames and Reality (end, incl. Speaking of); Part 5 title page; Ch. 35 Two Selves (opening: experienced vs decision utility, Experience and Memory)
pages.gist: Distinguishes experienced utility (Bentham's pleasure/pain) from decision utility (wantability); injection puzzle shows people pay more to cut 6→4 than 20→18 injections despite identical pain saved.

pages.section: Ch. 34 Frames and Reality (end, incl. Speaking of); Part 5 title page; Ch. 35 Two Selves (opening: experienced vs decision utility, Experience and Memory)
pages.gist: Measuring experienced utility: Edgeworth's hedonimeter and 'area under the curve'; colonoscopy study with pain rated every 60s shows patient B (longer procedure) suffered more by hedonimeter totals.

pages.section: Part V: Two Selves — Ch. 35 "Two Selves" (Experience and Memory; Which Self Should Count?; Biology vs. Rationality; Speaking of Two Selves)
pages.gist: Colonoscopy study: retrospective pain ratings follow the peak-end rule and show duration neglect; patient A (bad ending) remembers worse than patient B despite less total pain; hedonimeter totals are duration-weighted.

pages.section: Part V: Two Selves — Ch. 35 "Two Selves" (Experience and Memory; Which Self Should Count?; Biology vs. Rationality; Speaking of Two Selves)
pages.gist: Medical choice depends on objective (reduce remembered vs experienced pain); introduces experiencing self vs remembering self, the scratched-symphony example, and the 'tyranny of the remembering self'.

pages.section: Part V: Two Selves — Ch. 35 "Two Selves" (Experience and Memory; Which Self Should Count?; Biology vs. Rationality; Speaking of Two Selves)
pages.gist: Cold-hand experiment: a 60s episode vs a 90s episode with a slightly milder 30s tail; 80% of those who noticed relief chose to repeat the longer, objectively worse episode.

pages.section: Part V: Two Selves — Ch. 35 "Two Selves" (Experience and Memory; Which Self Should Count?; Biology vs. Rationality; Speaking of Two Selves)
pages.gist: Subjects chose by memory, not known duration; less-is-more effect explained by System 1 representing sets by averages/prototypes not sums; rats also show duration neglect.

pages.section: Part V: Two Selves — Ch. 35 "Two Selves" (Experience and Memory; Which Self Should Count?; Biology vs. Rationality; Speaking of Two Selves)
pages.gist: Decision utility diverges from experienced utility (via diminishing sensitivity or peak-end/duration neglect), so preferences built from memory cannot be fully trusted; 'Speaking of' examples on divorce and duration neglect.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves: ch. 36 "Life as a Story" (incl. Amnesic Vacations, Speaking of Life as a Story); start of ch. 37 "Experienced Well-Being"
pages.gist: La Traviata example: we care about the last 10 minutes, not the length of a life; stories are about significant moments and endings, and we care about the quality of people's life stories, even after death.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves: ch. 36 "Life as a Story" (incl. Amnesic Vacations, Speaking of Life as a Story); start of ch. 37 "Experienced Well-Being"
pages.gist: Diener's 'Jen' study: doubling a happy life's length has no effect on judged desirability, and adding 5 mildly happy years lowers it (less-is-more), even when the same people judge both versions; labor and vacation length seem to matter only because they change how the episode ends.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves: ch. 36 "Life as a Story" (incl. Amnesic Vacations, Speaking of Life as a Story); start of ch. 37 "Experienced Well-Being"
pages.gist: Amnesic Vacations: tourism is about building memories; Diener's spring-break diary study shows plans to repeat a vacation depend wholly on the final global rating, not the diary record; thought experiment about a vacation whose memories are erased.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves: ch. 36 "Life as a Story" (incl. Amnesic Vacations, Speaking of Life as a Story); start of ch. 37 "Experienced Well-Being"
pages.gist: Many people value amnesic experiences little and are indifferent to pain they will not remember; 'I am my remembering self'; Speaking of Life as a Story examples.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves: ch. 36 "Life as a Story" (incl. Amnesic Vacations, Speaking of Life as a Story); start of ch. 37 "Experienced Well-Being"
pages.gist: Experienced Well-Being opens: life-satisfaction surveys ask the remembering self; Kahneman proposes measuring the experiencing self by time spent in activities one would rather continue than stop (flow, resistance to interruption), following Edgeworth's hedonimeter.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves — Chapter 37: Experienced Well-Being
pages.gist: Describes experience sampling and the Day Reconstruction Method (DRM), which reconstructs the previous day as episodes rated for feelings and weighted by how long each lasted.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves — Chapter 37: Experienced Well-Being
pages.gist: Introduces the U-index (share of time in an unpleasant state), shows suffering is unequally distributed, gives U-index values by activity, and argues that mood depends mainly on the current situation and on attention.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves — Chapter 37: Experienced Well-Being
pages.gist: Shows that attending to an activity (focal eating) increases pleasure, discusses ways for individuals and policy to lower the U-index, describes Gallup's large-scale experience measures, and contrasts experienced well-being with life evaluation (Cantril ladder).

pages.section: Part V Two Selves — Chapter 37: Experienced Well-Being
pages.gist: Some factors (education, money) raise life evaluation but not experience, while others (illness, children) hurt experience more; poverty amplifies misfortunes; experienced well-being stops rising at about $75k income.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves — Chapter 37: Experienced Well-Being
pages.gist: Concludes that life satisfaction and experienced well-being are different things, not one being a flawed measure of the other; 'Speaking of' examples on the U-index, using time, and income satiation.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves — ch. 38 "Thinking About Life" (incl. The Focusing Illusion)
pages.gist: Figure 16 shows life satisfaction rising and then dropping steeply around marriage; Kahneman calls getting married an affective-forecasting error, since couples think divorce statistics don't apply to them, and offers a reading based on judgment heuristics.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves — ch. 38 "Thinking About Life" (incl. The Focusing Illusion)
pages.gist: Life-satisfaction answers are made by substitution: a mood heuristic (the planted-dime and dating studies) plus a small sample of easily recalled ideas. On this reading, Figure 16 tracks how likely people are to think of their marriage, not how happy they are.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves — ch. 38 "Thinking About Life" (incl. The Focusing Illusion)
pages.gist: DRM data show marriage has no net effect on experienced well-being because its good and bad changes balance out; well-being is heritable. In a study of 12,000 elite-college students, the money goals they set as teenagers predicted their later income.

pages.section: Part V Two Selves — ch. 38 "Thinking About Life" (incl. The Focusing Illusion)
pages.gist: Goals shape satisfaction: those who wanted money and got it are more satisfied, while goals that are very hard to reach lead to dissatisfaction. This leads to a hybrid view of well-being and to the focusing illusion: 'Nothing in life is as important as you think it is when you are thinking about it.'

pages.section: Part V Two Selves — ch. 38 "Thinking About Life" (incl. The Focusing Illusion)
pages.gist: In the California vs Midwest study, Californians liked their climate more, yet life satisfaction was the same in both regions; students in both regions wrongly believed Californians were happier. The car-pleasure question shows how substitution plus duration neglect creates a focusing illusion.

pages.section: Part IV/V – Thinking About Life (focusing illusion, adaptation, miswanting); 'Time and Time Again'; Speaking of Thinking About Life
pages.gist: Focusing illusion continues: long-term Californians rarely think of climate while recent movers do, and paraplegics adapt because attention is gradually withdrawn from their condition (exceptions: chronic pain, noise, depression).

pages.section: Part IV/V – Thinking About Life (focusing illusion, adaptation, miswanting); 'Time and Time Again'; Speaking of Thinking About Life
pages.gist: Cohn's survey shows people who know a paraplegic predict adaptation (41% bad mood at a year vs 68% from others); colostomy patients' life evaluations clash with their experienced well-being; Gilbert & Wilson's 'miswanting'; a new car loses attention while a weekly club keeps it.

pages.section: Part IV/V – Thinking About Life (focusing illusion, adaptation, miswanting); 'Time and Time Again'; Speaking of Thinking About Life
pages.gist: 'Time and Time Again': the remembering self represents episodes by beginning, peak and end, and states by the transition to them, so it neglects duration and adaptation; chapter ends with 'Speaking of' examples on affective forecasting and miswanting.

pages.section: Part IV/V – Thinking About Life (focusing illusion, adaptation, miswanting); 'Time and Time Again'; Speaking of Thinking About Life
pages.gist: Near-empty page containing only a stray letter 'P' (likely a part-opener or conversion artifact); no substantive content.

pages.section: Conclusions (Two Selves; Econs and Humans)
pages.gist: Conclusions open by recapping the three distinctions (System 1/2, Econs/Humans, two selves) and argue that cold-hand choices driven by duration neglect and the peak-end rule are mistakes, since time is the ultimate finite resource.

pages.section: Conclusions (Two Selves; Econs and Humans)
pages.gist: Duration neglect distorts fear of pain and anticipated regret; a duration-weighted view counts all moments, treats 'I will always remember' as a fallible prediction, and well-being policy must weigh both selves.

pages.section: Conclusions (Two Selves; Econs and Humans)
pages.gist: Well-being indices for policy; rationality in economics means internal coherence only, which Humans cannot meet (priming, WYSIATI, narrow framing, inside view), but that makes them not irrational, just in need of help; Chicago-school libertarianism.

pages.section: Conclusions (Two Selves; Econs and Humans)
pages.gist: Look for good reasons before psychological explanations (Becker); behavioral economists' dilemma over freedom's cost; Nudge, libertarian paternalism, defaults and choice architecture, and protection from exploiters of System 1.

pages.section: Conclusions: Econs and Humans (libertarian paternalism / Nudge); Two Systems
pages.gist: Humans need simple, readable contracts rather than mere disclosure; Save More Tomorrow uses defaults, foregone gains and automaticity to raise savings; nudge units spread to governments.

pages.section: Conclusions: Econs and Humans (libertarian paternalism / Nudge); Two Systems
pages.gist: Examples of framing-aware regulation (90% fat-free must show 10% fat, Food Plate); recap that the two systems are fictions, that System 2 often rationalizes System 1's feelings, and that System 1 drives most correct actions too.

pages.section: Conclusions: Econs and Humans (libertarian paternalism / Nudge); Two Systems
pages.gist: Skill needs a regular environment, practice and rapid feedback; System 1 substitutes more accessible answers and gives no warning when unreliable; System 1 is hardly educable, but one can learn to recognize error-prone situations.

pages.section: Conclusions: Econs and Humans (libertarian paternalism / Nudge); Two Systems
pages.gist: Debiasing: recognize cognitive minefields, slow down, call System 2; organizations do better via checklists, reference-class forecasting, premortems, quality control at framing/information/review stages, precise vocabulary, and judging decisions by process not outcome.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Tversky & Kahneman) — intro and Representativeness
pages.gist: Blank or divider page (only a stray letter 'P'), with no substantive content.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Tversky & Kahneman) — intro and Representativeness
pages.gist: Opens Appendix A: people use a few heuristics to simplify probability judgments; like judging distance by clarity, these heuristics are useful but cause systematic biases. Introduces representativeness, which judges probability by how much A resembles B.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Tversky & Kahneman) — intro and Representativeness
pages.gist: The 'Steve the librarian' example shows people rank occupations by probability exactly as they rank them by similarity. The engineer/lawyer experiment (70/30 vs 30/70) shows base rates are ignored once a personality description is given, although Bayes' rule requires a 5.44 odds ratio between the two conditions.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Tversky & Kahneman) — intro and Representativeness
pages.gist: The uninformative 'Dick' description makes people answer .5 whatever the base rate, so worthless evidence wipes out the priors. Insensitivity to sample size: people judge sample outcomes as if sample size did not matter (heights of 10, 100 or 1,000 men), and the hospital problem begins: most answer 'about the same'.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Tversky & Kahneman 1974) — Representativeness (sample size, chance, predictability, validity, regression) and start of Availability
pages.gist: Hospital problem and urn problem show people ignore sample size and are conservative about posterior odds; misconceptions of chance (local representativeness) begin.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Tversky & Kahneman 1974) — Representativeness (sample size, chance, predictability, validity, regression) and start of Availability
pages.gist: Gambler's fallacy, the 'law of small numbers' among research psychologists, and insensitivity to predictability: predictions as extreme as evaluations regardless of evidence reliability (student-teacher study).

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Tversky & Kahneman 1974) — Representativeness (sample size, chance, predictability, validity, regression) and start of Availability
pages.gist: Illusion of validity (confidence from good fit and consistent/redundant inputs) and introduction of regression toward the mean.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Tversky & Kahneman 1974) — Representativeness (sample size, chance, predictability, validity, regression) and start of Availability
pages.gist: Regression is not expected and gets spurious causal stories (flight instructors praise/punishment); availability heuristic introduced as judging frequency by ease of recall.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Availability; Adjustment and Anchoring)
pages.gist: Availability biases: easily retrieved (famous, salient, recent) instances seem more numerous; search-set effects (words starting with r vs. r third; abstract vs. concrete words); start of imaginability bias with committee example.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Availability; Adjustment and Anchoring)
pages.gist: Imaginability bias: small committees judged more numerous than large ones (median 70 vs 20, truth 45 for both); vividly imagined risks inflate/deflate perceived danger; illusory correlation (Chapman draw-a-person) explained by associative strength.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Availability; Adjustment and Anchoring)
pages.gist: Summary of availability heuristic as estimation by ease of retrieval/construction/association; introduction of anchoring with insufficient adjustment (wheel of fortune, UN African countries 25 vs 45) and the 8x7x...x1 vs 1x2x...x8 product task.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Availability; Adjustment and Anchoring)
pages.gist: Product estimates (512 vs 2,250, truth 40,320) show anchoring on partial computation; conjunctive events overestimated and disjunctive underestimated (Bar-Hillel marbles), causing planning optimism and risk underestimation in complex systems.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Tversky & Kahneman 1974) — anchoring in compound events and probability distributions, Discussion, Summary
pages.gist: Conjunctive (chain) events are overestimated and disjunctive (funnel) risks underestimated due to anchoring; subjective probability distributions are miscalibrated, with ~30% of true values falling outside stated 98% intervals because people anchor on their best estimate and adjust insufficiently.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Tversky & Kahneman 1974) — anchoring in compound events and probability distributions, Discussion, Summary
pages.gist: Elicitation procedure changes calibration: asking for percentiles yields too-narrow intervals, asking for odds on given values anchors toward 50-50 and yields too-conservative judgments; Discussion notes biases are cognitive not motivational and affect trained experts thinking intuitively.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Tversky & Kahneman 1974) — anchoring in compound events and probability distributions, Discussion, Summary
pages.gist: People fail to learn statistical rules (regression, sample size) from experience because instances are not coded appropriately; calibration could be learned by tallying outcomes grouped by stated probability; subjective probability theory demands only coherence.

pages.section: Appendix A: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Tversky & Kahneman 1974) — anchoring in compound events and probability distributions, Discussion, Summary
pages.gist: Internal consistency is not enough for rational probability (gambler's-fallacy example); judgments must fit the whole web of beliefs; Summary restates three heuristics—representativeness, availability, anchoring-and-adjustment—as economical but systematically biased.

pages.section: Appendix A notes (Judgment Under Uncertainty references); start of Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames
pages.gist: Notes/references 1-12 for Appendix A (Tversky & Kahneman 1974), citing papers on prediction, representativeness, conservatism and law of small numbers; no substantive content.

pages.section: Appendix A notes (Judgment Under Uncertainty references); start of Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames
pages.gist: Notes/references 13-24 for Appendix A, citing availability, illusory correlation (Chapman & Chapman), compound-event probability and calibration work; no substantive content.

pages.section: Appendix A notes (Judgment Under Uncertainty references); start of Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames
pages.gist: Final notes 24-25 (Savage, de Finetti on subjective probability); references only.

pages.section: Appendix A notes (Judgment Under Uncertainty references); start of Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames
pages.gist: Opening of Appendix B 'Choices, Values, and Frames': abstract states risk aversion for gains, risk seeking for losses, overweighting of sure and improbable events, framing violating invariance, and mental accounting (cost vs uncompensated loss); introduces normative vs descriptive analysis and risky choice.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky) — Risky Choice; Framing of Outcomes
pages.gist: Risky choice is treated as choosing gambles; the 85%-to-win-$1,000 vs sure $800 example defines risk aversion; Bernoulli's concave utility explains it, and the authors argue people evaluate gains and losses (changes), not total wealth, which is the basis of prospect theory.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky) — Risky Choice; Framing of Outcomes
pages.gist: The S-shaped value function: defined on gains/losses, concave for gains, convex for losses, steeper for losses (loss aversion; people refuse a $10 coin bet unless they could win ~$30); risk seeking with losses (prefer 85% chance to lose $1,000 over sure loss of $800).

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky) — Risky Choice; Framing of Outcomes
pages.gist: Risk seeking in losses also holds for pain and lives; normative axioms (transitivity, substitution) and the two core principles dominance and invariance are introduced; the Asian disease problem's 'lives saved' version shows 72% choose the sure option.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky) — Risky Choice; Framing of Outcomes
pages.gist: The 'lives lost' version flips preferences to 78% for the gamble, showing invariance fails pervasively even for experts and persists after reflection, like a perceptual illusion; Problem 3 sets up a dominance violation (E vs F).

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky) — framing/invariance, dominance violations, psychophysics of chances
pages.gist: Concurrent decisions (sure gain vs gamble; sure loss vs gamble) lead 73% to choose a combination that is dominated by the rejected one, showing framing plus S-shaped value violates dominance.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky) — framing/invariance, dominance violations, psychophysics of chances
pages.gist: Invariance is normatively essential but psychologically unfeasible; canonical representation and actuarial evaluation are hard, so test preferences by reframing; introduces nonlinear probability weighting and the category-boundary effect.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky) — framing/invariance, dominance violations, psychophysics of chances
pages.gist: Decision weights are regressive: moderate/high probabilities underweighted, low probabilities overweighted or neglected, explaining both lotteries and insurance; sets up the two-stage game problem.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky) — framing/invariance, dominance violations, psychophysics of chances
pages.gist: Two-stage game vs equivalent single-stage gamble yields reversed preferences: people ignore the shared first stage and treat a conditional sure thing as certain (pseudo-certainty effect).

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky): probabilistic insurance, Formulation Effects, Transactions and Trades / mental accounting
pages.gist: People reject probabilistic insurance because cutting a risk by half feels worth far less than removing it entirely, so protection framed as eliminating a risk sells better than protection framed as reducing it (the vaccine example). The page then introduces formulation effects: 'lives saved' vs 'lives lost' and survival vs mortality statistics for surgery.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky): probabilistic insurance, Formulation Effects, Transactions and Trades / mental accounting
pages.gist: Framing can be used deliberately, as with the 'cash discount' vs 'credit surcharge' label. Formulation effects come from a reference point implied by the wording, and the mind cannot recode equivalent frames into one form. The page then introduces mental accounts for multiattribute trades and the jacket/calculator problem.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky): probabilistic insurance, Formulation Effects, Transactions and Trades / mental accounting
pages.gist: Accounts can be minimal, topical or comprehensive, and people default to topical ones. So 68% would drive 20 minutes to save $5 on a $15 calculator but only 29% to save it on a $125 one. Store price spread grows with the price, which shows savings are judged in relative terms.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky): probabilistic insurance, Formulation Effects, Transactions and Trades / mental accounting
pages.gist: Lost-ticket vs lost-cash: 46% would buy another ticket after losing one, but 88% would still buy after losing $10 cash, because the ticket loss is posted to the play's account. Showing both problems side by side made people more willing to replace the lost ticket. Mental-accounting effects may partly reflect real secondary consequences such as regret.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky 1984): Losses and Costs; Concluding Remarks; start of References
pages.gist: Looking at a choice under several framings helps a decision maker weigh primary against secondary consequences. Loss aversion relative to the status quo produces the endowment effect: buying and selling prices differ, people won't trade jobs in either direction, and the 'twins' example shows that adapting to a reference point favours stability.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky 1984): Losses and Costs; Concluding Remarks; start of References
pages.gist: Routine exchanges treat money as a cost rather than a loss. The same $50 is rejected when framed as a sure loss but paid when framed as insurance. Of 132 subjects, 42 rejected a gamble but accepted the identical lottery when the $5 was framed as a payment.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky 1984): Losses and Costs; Concluding Remarks; start of References
pages.gist: The dead-loss effect: a man plays tennis in pain so the fee stays a 'cost'. Decision value differs from experience value. Hedonic reference points move with expectations and social comparison, the hedonic treadmill makes gains short-lived, and framing can create decision values that have no counterpart in experience.

pages.section: Appendix B: Choices, Values, and Frames (Kahneman & Tversky 1984): Losses and Costs; Concluding Remarks; start of References
pages.gist: A closing note that framing can shape the experience itself, not only the decision. The rest of the page is the start of the appendix's reference list.

pages.section: Back matter: end of references for Appendix B "Choices, Values, and Frames", "Also by Daniel Kahneman", Acknowledgments, and the start of Notes (Introduction)
pages.gist: References: the rest of the bibliography for the reprinted 'Choices, Values, and Frames' article (McNeil et al., Thaler on mental accounting, Tversky & Kahneman 1981 on framing, von Neumann & Morgenstern). No substantive text.

pages.section: Back matter: end of references for Appendix B "Choices, Values, and Frames", "Also by Daniel Kahneman", Acknowledgments, and the start of Notes (Introduction)

pages.gist: Notes/references for Ch.5 on fluency: repetition breeds belief, needless long words lower credibility, rhyme as reason, fluent names given more weight and doing better on the stock market, hard-to-read material triggering analytic thinking, mere exposure, and remote-association triads.

insights.claim: An attractive, confident presenter leads audiences to rate the content more favorably than it deserves; a general positive impression spills over to judgments of unrelated qualities.
insights.evidence: Handsome, confident speaker bounding onto the stage is judged too favorably.

insights.claim: Biases are systematic and recur predictably in particular circumstances, so having precise labels for them, like a physician's disease labels, makes errors easier to anticipate, recognize and fix.
insights.evidence: Analogy to medical diagnosis: labels bind symptoms, causes, consequences and interventions.

insights.claim: It is easier to spot others' errors than our own; we are often confident when wrong, and an objective observer detects our mistakes better, so anticipating informed critique motivates self-criticism.
insights.evidence: Watercooler gossip framing; anticipated evaluations by colleagues as a motive for serious self-criticism.

insights.concept: unconscious origin of impressions (System 1 silent work)
insights.claim: Most impressions, intuitions and many decisions are produced silently without awareness of how they arose; confidence in them is usually justified but not always.
insights.evidence: Cannot trace how you knew a lamp is on the desk, sensed irritation in a voice, or avoided a road threat.

insights.concept: law of small numbers / belief in small samples
insights.claim: Even trained researchers and statisticians lack intuition for the unreliability of small samples: they over-believe findings from little evidence, overestimate replication, and collect too few observations.
insights.evidence: Survey of Society of Mathematical Psychology experts, incl. textbook authors, exaggerated replication odds and advised too-small samples.

insights.claim: Identify the first answer that comes to mind, the one tempting even when known to be wrong, and analyze it separately from the correct answer; intuitions shared by two people are likely widely shared.
insights.evidence: Kahneman and Tversky's conversational mini-experiments examining their own intuitive answers.

insights.claim: Intuitive predictions are governed by how closely a case resembles a stereotype, producing appealing but absurd forecasts.
insights.evidence: Predicting toddlers' professions (argumentative child as lawyer, nerdy one as professor); Steve, randomly drawn, described as shy.

insights.claim: People estimate how big or frequent a category is by how easily examples come to mind, so whatever is easy to retrieve, including media-covered items, gets overestimated.
insights.evidence: Letter K is judged more common in first position than third; politicians' adultery seems more common because it is reported more; media coverage drives which public issues seem important.

insights.claim: People judge probability by how much a case resembles a stereotype and ignore relevant statistical facts such as base rates, which produces predictable errors.
insights.evidence: Steve, 'meek and tidy', is judged a librarian even though male farmers outnumber male librarians more than 20 to 1 in the US.

insights.concept: availability bias in one's own examples (self-check)
insights.claim: Even the choice of examples is driven by availability; trying a problem on yourself first exposes your own bias, which is more convincing than reports about others.
insights.evidence: Kahneman notes his 'little-covered' examples were themselves frequently mentioned; demonstration questions let readers see their own thinking fail.

insights.concept: role of luck in success stories
insights.claim: Luck plays a large role in every success story; a small change in the story can usually turn a remarkable achievement into a mediocre one.
insights.evidence: Kahneman credits luck for the choice of demonstration method and the impact of their work.

insights.concept: expert intuition as recognition (validity of intuition)
insights.claim: Accurate intuition comes from prolonged practice: a cue triggers memory and the stored information gives the answer. Professional intuitions are not all real expertise, so trust a gut call only when there was practice in a recognizable domain.
insights.evidence: Klein's firefighter commander who sensed the floor would collapse; Simon's chess masters; the investment officer who bought Ford stock because he liked the cars.

insights.claim: Judgments and decisions are often driven directly by feelings of liking or disliking, with little deliberation.
insights.evidence: Executive invested tens of millions in Ford because he liked the cars at an auto show, never asking whether the stock was underpriced.

insights.claim: Faced with a hard question, intuition often quietly answers an easier related one instead, and we usually don't notice the swap.
insights.evidence: 'Should I invest in Ford stock?' was replaced by 'Do I like Ford cars?'

insights.concept: System 1 and System 2 (fast vs slow thinking)
insights.claim: Fast thinking (expert and heuristic intuition, plus automatic perception and memory) is System 1; when no intuitive answer comes, we shift to slow, effortful System 2. System 1 is more influential than we feel.
insights.evidence: Chess master's first moves are strong; when no answer comes to mind we switch to deliberate thinking.

insights.claim: System 1 thinks by association, metaphor and cause, but statistics needs many things held in mind at once, which System 1 cannot do. So intuitive judgments neglect statistical structure.
insights.evidence: Introduces the theme of Part 2: why thinking statistically is so hard for people.

insights.claim: Memory follows its own rules, so a worse (longer) painful episode can leave a better memory. People then choose by memory and expose their experiencing self to needless pain.
insights.evidence: Two painful experiences: the strictly worse, longer one is remembered more favorably and chosen for repeat.

insights.claim: Choices shift because of unimportant features of how a problem is presented, even when the real options are the same.
insights.evidence: Part 4 preview; the 1984 appendix article sums up the framing studies.

insights.claim: Looking back makes the past seem more certain than it was, and this false certainty feeds overconfidence. Lessons from the past should be drawn without falling for it.
insights.evidence: Overconfidence is described as fed by the illusory certainty of hindsight.

insights.claim: People tend to judge each decision on its own instead of as part of a wider set of related choices, which breaks the rules of rationality.
insights.evidence: Part 4 previews the tendency to treat problems in isolation.

insights.claim: People overrate how much they understand, fail to see how much they don't know, and give chance too little role in how events turn out.
insights.evidence: Part 3 theme, influenced by Taleb's The Black Swan.

insights.claim: System 1 reads situations instantly and on its own, and even predicts what comes next, without intention or a sense of doing anything. Problems like 17 × 24 are seen as needing effortful System 2 work.
insights.evidence: An angry woman's face (Figure 1) gives an instant reading of her mood and a premonition of harsh words; 17 × 24 does not.

insights.claim: System 1 can quickly rule out absurd answers and give a rough range, but it cannot tell close wrong answers from the right one. Only working the problem through settles it.
insights.evidence: For 17×24, 12,609 and 123 feel implausible right away, but you cannot rule out 568 without computing (the answer is 408).

insights.claim: Thinking has two modes. System 1 is automatic, fast and effortless and gives impressions. System 2 is slow, effortful and deliberate, and it is the only one that can build reasoning in ordered steps.
insights.evidence: Seeing an angry woman's face (instant reading) versus computing 17×24 (stepwise, effortful, pupils dilate).

insights.concept: Expert intuition is learned through prolonged practice
insights.claim: Some fast, automatic skills, such as finding strong chess moves, come only from long, specialized practice. Other associations, like matching a stereotype, rest on knowledge most people share.
insights.evidence: A chess master's quick strong move; recognizing that a 'meek and tidy soul' matches an occupational stereotype.

insights.concept: Limited attention budget / effortful tasks interfere
insights.claim: Attention is a limited budget. Effortful activities compete for it and break down when run in parallel, while easy tasks can run together.
insights.evidence: You cannot compute 17×24 while turning left into dense traffic; passengers stop talking while the driver overtakes a truck.

insights.concept: System 2 programming System 1 (setting a search set)
insights.claim: System 2 can deliberately set automatic attention and memory to look for specific cues, which makes them more likely to be detected. Holding the set takes ongoing effort.
insights.evidence: Setting yourself to look for a white-haired woman at a train station; the Heathrow attendant reminding renters that 'we drive on the left'.

insights.concept: Inattentional blindness (invisible gorilla) and blindness to blindness
insights.claim: Focusing hard on a narrow task, especially with an instruction to ignore something, can make people miss obvious events. They are also confident that nothing was missed.
insights.evidence: Chabris and Simons: viewers counting the white team's passes, about half miss a gorilla that is on screen for 9 seconds and are sure it was not there.

insights.concept: System 2 endorsement default and surprise as a trigger
insights.claim: System 2 usually accepts System 1's suggestions with little change. Deliberate processing kicks in only when System 1 has no answer, something violates the world-model and causes surprise, or an error is about to happen.
insights.evidence: Plot synopsis: impressions become beliefs once endorsed; surprise (lamps that jump, gorillas on courts) makes you stare and search memory for an explanation.

insights.concept: System 1 biases: question substitution, weak logic and statistics, cannot be turned off
insights.claim: System 1 makes systematic errors in specific circumstances. It sometimes answers an easier question than the one asked, it understands little logic or statistics, and it cannot be switched off.
insights.evidence: You cannot help reading a word shown in a language you know unless your attention is fully elsewhere.

insights.concept: conflict between automatic response and intention (System 2 self-control)
insights.claim: When a task needs a response that cuts against an automatic one, System 2 must actively suppress the System 1 impulse. This takes strain and slows performance, and System 2 is in charge of self-control.
insights.evidence: Saying 'upper/lower' or 'left/right' for words that are themselves those words; steering into a skid on ice; not staring at an oddly dressed couple.

insights.concept: Müller-Lyer illusion / cognitive illusion: mistrust impressions in recognized patterns
insights.claim: Knowing the truth does not remove a System 1 impression. The only defense is to learn which patterns produce illusions, spot them when they appear, and refuse to act on the impression. Kahneman says this applies to cognitive illusions as well as visual ones.
insights.evidence: The Müller-Lyer lines are equal when measured but still look unequal; a therapist was taught that strong sympathy for a patient with many failed prior treatments is a danger sign of psychopathic charm.

insights.concept: danger sign: attraction to a case with a repeated history of others' failure
insights.claim: A strong feeling that you are uniquely able to succeed where many others have failed is itself a warning cue. It should not be read as evidence that you will succeed.
insights.evidence: The psychotherapy teacher's advice: a patient who says all previous clinicians failed him, but that you are different, is most likely a psychopath, so do not take him on.

insights.concept: compromise vigilance: recognize error-prone situations and try harder when stakes are high
insights.claim: System 1 cannot be switched off, and questioning everything all the time is impractical and too slow. The workable compromise is to learn which situations invite mistakes and to apply effortful System 2 checking mainly when the stakes are high. Spotting other people's errors is easier than spotting your own.
insights.evidence: Kahneman's argument that biases can't always be avoided, because System 2 may have no clue that an error exists.

insights.concept: working-memory load and mental effort (Add-1 task, pupil dilation)
insights.claim: Anything that occupies working memory reduces the capacity to think. Effortful tasks like Add-1 quickly hit cognitive limits, and pupil size gives an objective record of effort. Short labels save working memory, and agent-style descriptions are easier to grasp and remember.
insights.evidence: In the Add-1/Add-3 tasks, few people can handle more than four digits; Hess's work on pupils; 'System 1' is used instead of 'automatic system' because it takes less space in working memory.

insights.claim: System 2 is effortful and reluctant to invest more effort than strictly necessary. As a result, choices it believes it made are often actually guided by System 1.
insights.evidence: The film metaphor: System 2 is a supporting character who believes herself to be the hero.

insights.claim: When System 2 is near capacity, it protects the priority task and does not register other stimuli, even ones in plain view.
