insights.evidence: During Add-1, subjects missed a flashed letter K almost half the time at peak effort, but almost never at the start or end.

insights.claim: When several routes reach the same goal, people eventually drift to the least demanding one. Effort is treated as a cost, so the mind is lazy by default.
insights.evidence: Skill and intelligence reduce pupil and brain effort; people gravitate to the easier course of action.

insights.concept: System 2 exclusive capabilities (rules, multi-attribute comparison, base-rate integration)
insights.claim: Only deliberate System 2 can follow rules, compare options on several attributes and combine an intuition with statistical information. System 1 handles one thing at a time and ignores statistics.
insights.evidence: A 'meek and tidy' person looks like a librarian, but combining that impression with how few librarians there are takes System 2; so does weighting a surprising survey result by its small sample.

insights.concept: task switching cost and time pressure
insights.claim: Switching between task sets is effortful, especially under time pressure. Holding several ideas at once while hurrying is the most demanding kind of thinking.
insights.evidence: Counting the letter f, then switching to counting commas; Add-3 needs rapid switching and is paced by a metronome; attention-control efficiency predicted how well pilots and air traffic controllers performed.

insights.concept: first intuition is System 1, so restart deliberately
insights.claim: Something that comes to mind quickly is a System 1 intuition. Tasks that need effort call for a deliberate restart and a memory search, and they should not be attempted while another demanding task is running.
insights.evidence: Speaking-of examples: 'I won't try to solve this while driving'; 'What came quickly to my mind was an intuition from System 1.'

insights.concept: offload working memory (divide into easy steps)
insights.claim: People avoid mental overload by breaking a task into several easy steps and storing intermediate results on paper or in long-term memory instead of in working memory.
insights.evidence: Even knowledge workers rarely face Add-3-level demands, because they split tasks up and write things down.

insights.concept: limited budget of effort (self-control and deliberate thought share resources)
insights.claim: Effortful thinking, self-control and keeping up a demanding pace all draw on one limited System 2 budget. When several run at once, coherent reasoning gets worse.
insights.evidence: A friend asked to compute 23×78 while walking stops in his tracks. At a fast walking pace Kahneman cannot think at all.

insights.claim: When System 2 is busy, System 1 has more influence on behavior. People under load pick the tempting option, choose more selfishly and judge more superficially. Alcohol, lack of sleep, off-peak hours and anxious self-monitoring have the same effect.
insights.evidence: People holding seven digits in memory were more likely to choose chocolate cake over fruit salad.

insights.claim: In flow, deep concentration on the task needs no effortful control of attention. That separates task effort from self-control effort and frees resources for the task.
insights.evidence: Csikszentmihalyi's 'optimal experience': chess, motorcycle racing, painting, writing.

insights.concept: law of least effort / task switching aversion
insights.claim: Frequent task switching and speeded-up mental work are unpleasant, so people avoid them. Even without time pressure, keeping a coherent train of thought takes discipline, and minds drift toward easy escapes.
insights.evidence: Kahneman notices how often he checks e-mail or the refrigerator during an hour of writing.

insights.claim: Effort of will in one task lowers self-control and persistence in the next task, partly through loss of motivation. Depleting tasks involve suppressing a natural tendency. Signs of depletion include impulsive choices, quitting early and poor logical decisions. Strong incentives (and, in Baumeister's studies, glucose) can counter it.
insights.evidence: Suppressing emotion during a film shortened later handgrip persistence. Resisting cookies led to quitting sooner on hard puzzles. Glucose lemonade, unlike Splenda, prevented intuitive errors.

insights.claim: Tired, hungry or depleted decision makers fall back on the easier default option. Outcomes then track the time since the last break rather than the merits of the case.
insights.evidence: Israeli parole judges approved about 65% of requests right after meals, dropping to about zero just before the next break. The default is denial, and the overall approval rate is 35%.

insights.concept: lazy System 2 / failure to check intuitive answers (bat-and-ball)
insights.claim: System 2 often endorses an intuitive answer from System 1 that a few seconds of checking would reject. Many people are overconfident in their intuitions and avoid even cheap verification. A suspiciously easy question is a cue to check.
insights.evidence: Bat-and-ball puzzle: the intuitive answer is 10¢ and the correct one is 5¢. More than 50% of Harvard, MIT and Princeton students, and more than 80% at less selective schools, gave 10¢.

insights.claim: When a conclusion seems true, people accept arguments that appear to support it even when the logic is invalid; with System 1 the conclusion comes first and the arguments follow.
insights.evidence: Most college students judged valid the syllogism 'All roses are flowers; some flowers fade quickly; therefore some roses fade quickly'.

insights.claim: Knowing a fact does not mean it comes to mind when it is needed. Automatic retrieval by System 1 is patchy, so System 2 has to slow down and search actively for every relevant fact before estimating.
insights.evidence: People asked about murders in Michigan guessed lower on average than people asked about Detroit, because most did not think of Detroit.

insights.claim: Weak self-control and reliance on intuition go with choosing a smaller immediate reward over a larger delayed one, even when the implied discount rate is unreasonable. Resisting depends on redirecting attention away from the temptation.
insights.evidence: In Mischel's experiment, 4-year-olds who waited 15 minutes for two cookies later showed higher executive control and intelligence; CRT low scorers chose $3,400 now over $3,800 in a month.

insights.claim: Capable people fail easy checks because they are satisfied with a plausible answer that comes readily and stop thinking, not because they lack ability. 'Engaged' thinkers are more skeptical of their intuitions.
insights.evidence: Students at good universities fail the bat-and-ball, flowers syllogism and Michigan problems; the 'Speaking of Control' lines describe someone who didn't check whether what he said made sense.

insights.concept: Cognitive Reflection Test (intuitive vs reflective responding)
insights.claim: Questions built to invite a compelling but wrong intuitive answer measure how weak someone's System 2 supervision is. Low scorers are also impulsive and impatient, and CRT-type items predict bias better than IQ.
insights.evidence: 63% of intuitive responders preferred $3,400 this month to $3,800 next month, against 37% of perfect scorers; low scorers would pay twice as much for overnight delivery.

insights.concept: rationality vs intelligence (reflective vs algorithmic mind)
insights.claim: Stanovich splits System 2 into an algorithmic mind (computational brainpower, measured by IQ) and a reflective mind (rationality, the willingness to check intuitions). High intelligence does not protect against bias.
insights.evidence: Stanovich and West's research on individual differences; bat-and-ball-type questions predict cognitive errors better than IQ tests.

insights.concept: ego depletion leading to default procedures
insights.claim: After sustained effort, a depleted System 2 falls back on standard operating procedures instead of thinking problems through.
insights.evidence: 'Speaking of Control': after a long day of meetings he turned to standard procedures instead of thinking.

insights.claim: One evoked idea automatically triggers a spreading, coherent cascade of related ideas, emotions and bodily responses. It even invents a causal story linking items that are merely placed side by side.
insights.evidence: Reading 'Bananas Vomit' produces disgust, a sketchy causal scenario, a temporary aversion to bananas, priming of related words and mild surprise.

insights.claim: Given an unexpected input, System 1 quickly and automatically builds a self-reinforcing causal story. Ideas, emotions and bodily reactions all line up behind it and get ready for related events. It treats a mere conjunction of words as if it were reality.
insights.evidence: Reading 'Bananas Vomit' triggers disgust, a recoil and a causal story within about a second.

insights.claim: Ideas are nodes in a huge network, linked as cause to effect, thing to property and thing to category. Activating one node spreads silently to many others, and only a few of them ever reach consciousness, so we know less about our own minds than we feel we do.
insights.evidence: Hume's three principles (resemblance, contiguity, causality), links such as virus→cold, and the DAY word-association task.

insights.concept: illusion of conscious control (limited introspective access)
insights.claim: System 2 believes it is in charge and knows why it chose what it did, yet priming happens in System 1 with no conscious access. Disbelief is therefore no defence, and the effects apply to you as well.
insights.evidence: Audiences disbelieve priming results, and students insisted the words had not influenced them. The honesty box with eye vs. flower posters is introduced as a demonstration.

insights.claim: Ideas can prime actions, and actions or bodily states can prime ideas and attitudes in return. The two together produce a coherent reaction that feeds itself.
insights.evidence: Florida effect (old-age words → slower walking), walking slowly → faster recognition of old-age words, pencil smile → funnier cartoons, nodding → agreeing with editorials.

insights.claim: Recent exposure to a word, image or setting makes related ideas easier to retrieve and shifts later judgments and choices, without awareness. The effects are robust but usually small, though they can tip close decisions.
insights.evidence: EAT primes SOUP over SOAP. Schools as polling stations raised support for school funding, and pictures of classrooms had a larger effect than being a parent.

insights.concept: money priming / environmental primes (Florida, Lady Macbeth effects)
insights.claim: Background reminders change values and behaviour without awareness. Money cues push toward individualism and less helping, mortality cues toward authoritarian ideas, and guilt toward a wish to cleanse.
insights.evidence: In Vohs's studies, money-primed people persisted about twice as long before asking for help, picked up fewer pencils and set chairs 118 vs 80 cm apart. People who lied by phone preferred mouthwash, and those who lied by email preferred soap.

insights.claim: Small background cues that people don't notice can change behavior a lot. A poster of watching eyes made people pay more for what they used, and nobody was aware of the effect.
insights.evidence: In an office kitchen honesty box, people paid about 70p per liter in an eyes week and about 15p in a flowers week, close to 3x more during eye weeks overall.

insights.concept: System 1 constructs a story, System 2 believes it
insights.claim: System 1 produces impressions and impulses that turn into beliefs and choices, and it makes things look more coherent than the world really is. System 2 tends to accept the story without checking it, and this is where many systematic errors start.
insights.evidence: Chapter summary ('Strangers to Ourselves') and the 'Speaking of Priming' sentences.

insights.claim: People who have been primed to look for a certain thing, such as flaws, tend to find exactly that. What they expected decides what they find.
insights.evidence: 'Speaking of Priming' example: reviewers primed to find flaws found them.

insights.claim: Clarity, repetition, priming and good mood all produce the same feeling of ease. Under ease people are trusting, casual and superficial. Under strain they are vigilant, put in more effort and make fewer errors, but they are less creative.
insights.evidence: Figure 5, causes and consequences of cognitive ease: clear vs. poor fonts, repetition, a pencil held in the mouth to force a 'smile', frowning.

insights.claim: Something that has been seen before is easier to perceive, and that ease feels like familiarity, or 'pastness'. So a name seen once can later seem to belong to a famous person, even though no real knowledge stands behind it.
insights.evidence: Jacoby's 'Becoming Famous Overnight': made-up names such as David Stenbill were later judged famous. Words that are primed or shown in sharper contrast are judged familiar.

insights.claim: People confuse familiarity with truth, so repeating a statement makes it more believable. Repeating only part of it, a single phrase, is enough. When the source is forgotten, cognitive ease is all people have to judge truth by.
insights.evidence: People repeatedly exposed to the phrase 'the body temperature of a chicken' were more likely to accept an arbitrary value such as 144° as true. Kahneman also judged driving-test answers by whether they felt familiar.

insights.concept: processing fluency as a false truth signal (illusion of truth / persuasion)
insights.claim: Statements that are easier to process (legible, high-contrast, simple, rhyming, from an easy-to-pronounce source) are judged more true, insightful and credible, whether or not they are. Fluency adds no evidence.
insights.evidence: 'Hitler born 1892' is believed more than '1887'. Rhyming aphorisms ('Woes unite foes') are rated more insightful than non-rhyming versions. Oppenheimer found that needless long words lower perceived intelligence.

insights.claim: Some problems are built to trigger an immediate wrong answer. Proportional-sounding problems (5 machines → 100 minutes) and exponential-growth problems (half the lake → 24 days) catch people who don't check the first idea.
insights.evidence: CRT items: 100 machines make 100 widgets in 5 minutes, not 100. The lily pad patch covers half the lake on day 47, not day 24.

insights.claim: Strain from any source, even a hard-to-read font, moves people from a casual intuitive mode to an analytic one and makes them more likely to reject wrong intuitive answers.
insights.evidence: 40 Princeton students took the Cognitive Reflection Test (bat-and-ball, 5 machines/5 widgets, lily pads doubling over 48 days). At least one error: 90% with a normal font vs 35% with a faint gray small font.

insights.claim: When sources disagree, people give extra weight to the one that is easier to process, such as an easy-to-pronounce name, when they should average them. System 2 avoids anything that feels like effort.
insights.evidence: Fictitious Turkish stock reports: the Artan report got much more weight than the Taahhut report, even though the best procedure was to average the two.

insights.claim: Repeated exposure to a neutral stimulus makes people like it more, even without conscious awareness. The effect is stronger when exposure is subliminal, because a repeated stimulus followed by nothing bad becomes a safety signal.
insights.evidence: Zajonc's newspaper ads with Turkish-like words (kadirga, saricik...) shown 1 to 25 times: frequent words were rated much more 'good'. Fluent stock names and tickers outperform early. Chicks exposed to a tone in the egg made fewer distress calls.

insights.concept: intuitive coherence sensing (cognitive ease as a faint valid signal)
insights.claim: System 1 can sense that things are coherent before it finds the reason. That feeling is better than chance, but anything that increases ease (priming, a clear font, pre-exposure) inflates it.
insights.evidence: Remote Association Test: in 2 seconds, people guessed better than chance whether triads (dive/light/rocket → sky) were linked. Priming, a clear font and pre-exposure all increased 'linked' judgments.

insights.concept: mood modulates System 1 vs System 2 reliance
insights.claim: A good mood improves intuitive accuracy but loosens System 2 control, bringing more gullibility and reliance on System 1. A sad mood goes with vigilance, suspicion and analytic effort, and with losing touch with intuition.
insights.evidence: In the RAT, happy-mood induction more than doubled the intuition index. Sad participants guessed at chance level.

insights.concept: cognitive ease debiasing (font, repetition, mere exposure)
insights.claim: Surface fluency, such as a readable font, repetition or familiarity, shifts belief and liking regardless of merit. Judgment should not rest on presentation or on how often something has been heard.
insights.evidence: The 'Speaking of Cognitive Ease' quotes: don't dismiss a plan because its font is hard to read; repeated claims feel true; familiarity breeds liking (mere exposure).

insights.concept: misattribution of feeling (affect as the basis of coherence judgments)
insights.claim: The feeling that something is coherent or right comes from a brief pleasant emotion. When people are given another explanation for that feeling, the sense of coherence disappears, which shows the feeling is the signal being judged.
insights.evidence: Remote Association Test triads (salt deep foam → sea) produce a slight smile. Telling subjects their earphone music affects emotions eliminated their intuition of coherence.

insights.concept: mood and System 2 vigilance (good mood loosens control)
insights.claim: A good mood signals safety, so System 2 relaxes: people become more intuitive and creative but also less vigilant and more prone to logical errors. A bad mood brings suspicion and analytic effort.
insights.evidence: Good mood, intuition, creativity and gullibility cluster together, while sadness goes with vigilance and analysis. The book's advice: 'I'm in a very good mood… I should be extra careful.'

insights.concept: norm theory: a single incident makes a recurrence feel normal
insights.claim: System 1 keeps a model of what is normal, and one striking event changes it. A repeat then feels less surprising even when it is objectively less likely, and passive expectations can turn active.
insights.evidence: Meeting Jon twice, on the Great Barrier Reef and then in a London theater, was less surprising the second time. Burning cars at the same spot of road on two Sundays created a lasting expectation.

insights.claim: When a wrong element fits the activated context, System 1 detects coherence and accepts the statement, so the error goes unnoticed. Only an element that breaks the context triggers detection of the anomaly.
insights.evidence: 'How many animals of each kind did Moses take into the ark?' Few notice that it was Noah. Swap in George W. Bush and the error is obvious.

insights.concept: norm theory: retroactive linking of surprises into a causal story
insights.claim: A second abnormal event pulls the first from memory, and the two are read together as one pattern or cause. Which explanation forms depends on which surprise came next, not on advance expectations.
insights.evidence: A guest winces at the soup. If the guest then startles at a waiter's touch, they seem a tense person. If another guest rejects the soup, the soup gets blamed.

insights.concept: category norms (typical value plus range) and fast anomaly detection
insights.claim: System 1 holds norms for categories, giving both a typical value and a plausible range. It detects violations within about 0.2 seconds, using a great deal of world knowledge, and shared norms let people communicate without spelling everything out.
insights.evidence: The brain responds to 'Earth revolves around the trouble' within 0.2 s, and responds the same way to a man saying he is pregnant or an upper-class voice mentioning a tattoo. 'Large mouse' and 'small elephant' are read on their own scales.

insights.claim: System 1 automatically links available fragments into a coherent causal story, so a salient event gets credited as the cause of whatever happens; an explanation that fits contradictory outcomes explains nothing.
insights.evidence: Bloomberg headlines credited Saddam Hussein's capture for Treasuries rising, then for them falling, within half an hour.

insights.claim: People apply causal thinking where situations need statistical reasoning about categories and ensembles; System 1 cannot reason statistically, and only trained System 2 can. Bad luck gets turned into a story of intent or sabotage.
insights.evidence: Michotte's launching squares and the Heider-Simmel triangle film: causality and intention are seen directly, even by infants; the 'she was just unlucky' example.

insights.concept: consider the full range of norms, not just the average
insights.claim: Little repetition makes new experiences feel normal, and evaluations focus on averages; one should look at the whole range of normal reactions.
insights.evidence: 'Speaking of' examples: a second old-friend applicant feels unsurprising; surveying product reactions beyond the average.

insights.concept: jumping to conclusions (when it is safe vs risky)
insights.claim: Jumping to conclusions is efficient when conclusions are likely right, occasional errors are cheap, and it saves effort; it is risky when the situation is unfamiliar, stakes are high and there's no time to gather information, where System 2 should intervene.
insights.evidence: Danny Kaye's 'favorite sport is jumping to conclusions' line, used to describe System 1.

insights.concept: neglect of ambiguity and suppression of doubt
insights.claim: System 1 resolves ambiguity silently using context and recent experience, keeps no record of rejected alternatives, and doubt (holding incompatible interpretations) requires System 2 effort.
insights.evidence: Same shape read as B among letters and 13 among numbers; 'Ann approached the bank' read as a money bank unless a river was just mentioned.

insights.claim: Understanding a statement starts with automatically believing it; unbelieving is effortful System 2 work, so when System 2 is busy or tired, false claims get accepted.
insights.evidence: Gilbert: nonsense statements ('a dinca is a flame') labeled true/false; participants holding digits in memory later recalled many false ones as true.

insights.concept: confirmation bias (positive test via associative memory)
insights.claim: How a question is framed determines which instances come to mind; asking 'Is Sam friendly?' retrieves friendly evidence, so searches drift toward confirming the hypothesis.
insights.evidence: 'Is Sam friendly?' vs 'Is Sam unfriendly?' evokes different instances of Sam's behavior.

insights.claim: Both memory and deliberate testing look for evidence that fits the current hypothesis instead of trying to refute it. This leads to accepting suggestions without criticism and to overestimating extreme, vivid events.
insights.evidence: 'Is Sam friendly?' brings up different memories than 'Is Sam unfriendly?'; asked about a California tsunami, people picture tsunamis and overestimate the risk.

insights.claim: Liking or disliking one trait spreads to traits we have never observed, and the first traits we see change how later, ambiguous ones are read. The result is a picture that is more coherent than reality.
insights.evidence: Joan is pleasant at a party, so people assume she is generous; Asch's Alan (intelligent first) is rated better than Ben (envious first), though both lists have the same traits.

insights.concept: evaluate item-by-item across candidates (halo-taming grading procedure)
insights.claim: To keep one early dimension from coloring the rest, score one dimension across all candidates before moving to the next, and hide earlier scores. Feeling less confident afterward is a sign the method is working, because the old consistency was false.
insights.evidence: Kahneman graded exam booklets one at a time and his grades came out uniform. When he graded question by question with earlier scores hidden, the grades varied more and were more accurate.

insights.claim: Averaging many judgments reduces error only when the sources are independent; shared bias or influence between sources lowers their real number. Keep sources separate and collect individual positions before any discussion.
insights.evidence: Averaged estimates of pennies in a jar come out accurate; police keep witnesses apart before testimony; meeting members write a short position before discussion so early, assertive speakers don't dominate.

insights.concept: WYSIATI (what you see is all there is)
insights.claim: System 1 builds the most coherent story it can from the information currently active and ignores what is missing. It is insensitive to how much evidence there is and how good it is, so it jumps to conclusions.
insights.evidence: 'Will Mindik be a good leader? She is intelligent and strong…' brings an instant yes, without asking what one would need to know; the next adjectives could be corrupt and cruel.

insights.claim: The same information described in different ways triggers different emotions and judgments, as when the same risk is stated as survival or as mortality.
insights.evidence: '90% survival after one month' is more reassuring than '10% mortality within one month'; '90% fat-free' cold cuts.

insights.claim: Confidence follows how coherent the story is, not how complete it is. People who hear only one side are more confident, even when they know the other side exists and could easily imagine its argument.
insights.evidence: Thornton v. Thrifty Drug false-arrest scenario: participants who heard only one lawyer were swayed more and were more confident than those who heard both sides.

insights.claim: Collecting separate judgments before any group discussion yields more information because errors stay independent rather than being herded.
insights.evidence: Speaking-of line: obtain separate judgments on the issue before discussion.

insights.concept: Halo effect from a single impression
insights.claim: A good impression on one dimension (e.g., a strong presentation) is extended to unrelated, unobserved qualities like management skill.
insights.evidence: Judging a person's management skills solely from a good presentation.

insights.concept: WYSIATI (what you see is all there is) — insufficient-evidence decisions
insights.claim: People make big decisions from a single available source and fail to notice how little information they have, even avoiding information that could spoil their story.
insights.evidence: Speaking-of examples: a big decision based on one consultant's good report; not wanting more information that might spoil the story.

insights.claim: System 1 can map intensity from one dimension onto another scale, which enables easy but unjustified substitutions.
insights.evidence: 'If Sam were as tall as he is intelligent, how tall would he be?'; political future scaled from losing primary to presidency.

insights.claim: Intending to answer one specific question automatically triggers other computations beyond what was needed, which can contaminate the answer.
insights.evidence: System 2 evaluating one attribute triggers basic assessments automatically.

insights.concept: Substitution of basic assessments for hard questions (judgment heuristic)
insights.claim: System 1 continuously produces easy assessments (safety, similarity, mood, facial competence) that silently replace the harder question System 2 was asked.
insights.evidence: Todorov: competence ratings from 0.1-second face exposures predicted ~70% of election winners, though facial features don't predict performance in office.

insights.claim: The less informed the judge, the more automatic System 1 cues drive the choice; the facial-competence effect was about three times larger for uninformed, TV-heavy voters.
insights.evidence: Political scientists' follow-up to Todorov's voting studies.

insights.concept: Averages not sums (prototype representation) / scope neglect
insights.claim: System 1 represents sets by prototypes, judging averages well but ignoring set size in sum-like quantities, so magnitude barely affects valuations.
insights.evidence: Exxon Valdez study: willingness to pay $80, $78, $88 to save 2,000, 20,000, 200,000 birds; total line length needs System 2.

insights.concept: Counting requires System 2 (limits of glance assessment)
insights.claim: Not every attribute is assessed automatically; equal counts across differently arranged sets are invisible at a glance and require deliberate counting, and number is only precise up to about four.
insights.evidence: Figure 7: towers vs blocks on floor; numerosity precise only for four or fewer objects.

insights.claim: System 1 can put intensities on very different dimensions onto one shared scale: how severe a crime is, how loud a sound is, how precocious a child is, how tall a man is. The matches are easy to make and quite consistent across people.
insights.evidence: People set the loudness of a sound to match the severity of crimes or punishments. Julie read fluently at four: how tall is a man who is as tall as Julie was precocious?

insights.claim: When people predict an outcome such as GPA from an early indicator such as reading age, they pick the outcome as extreme as the indicator. This feels right to System 1 and is accepted by System 2, but it is statistically wrong.
insights.evidence: Predicting Julie's college GPA from the age she learned to read by picking the GPA that matches her precocity.

insights.claim: We cannot aim System 1 precisely. Asking it one question sets off extra computations that were never asked for, and these can slow down or bias the intended judgment.
insights.evidence: Rhyme detection is slower for VOTE–GOAT than for VOTE–NOTE because spelling gets compared too. Literal-falsity judgments are slower for 'Some jobs are jails' because the metaphor is processed. An analyst's liking of a company's product leaks into a judgment of its financial soundness.

insights.claim: Intuitive feelings and opinions come to mind about almost everything, including things we know little about. They rest on evidence we can neither explain nor defend, so having an answer ready is not a sign of knowing.
insights.evidence: We like or dislike people, trust strangers, or feel a venture will succeed before analyzing anything. Only something like 17 × 24 leaves us dumbfounded.

insights.claim: When a hard target question has no quick answer, System 1 answers a related, easier heuristic question and believes it has answered the target. This is why we are rarely stumped and why intuitive opinions on complex matters can be seriously wrong.
insights.evidence: Judging probability by judging something else. Table 1: how much to give to save a species becomes how much emotion dying dolphins evoke; life happiness becomes current mood; punishment for predatory advisers becomes how much anger I feel; a candidate's political future becomes whether she looks like a winner.

insights.claim: Swapping in an easier problem can be a valid strategy when System 2 chooses it on purpose and knowingly, as Pólya advised. The danger lies in substitutions that are not chosen and go unnoticed.
insights.evidence: Pólya, How to Solve It: if you can't solve a problem, find an easier problem you can solve.

insights.claim: Context cues that don't matter to the task can force an automatic substitution you can't switch off by will. The resulting bias is predictable, so it has to be checked with an outside measurement.
insights.evidence: Corridor drawing: the figure on the right looks larger, but a ruler shows equal size, because 3-D distance cues override 2-D judgment.

insights.claim: System 1 maps how strongly something is felt onto any other scale, such as dollars or how far a career will go, so a feeling turns straight into a number.
insights.evidence: Feelings about dolphins become a donation amount; impression of political skill maps onto 'defeated in primary' to 'president'.

insights.claim: When a target question is hard, System 1 answers a related easy heuristic question and a lazy System 2 endorses it, often without noticing that a swap happened or that the original was hard.
insights.evidence: Table 1 pairs: dolphin donation vs. feelings about dying dolphins; candidate's political future vs. whether she looks like a winner.

insights.claim: A global judgment like overall happiness gets replaced by whatever emotionally relevant topic was just brought to mind, so question order can create a strong correlation that wasn't there before.
insights.evidence: German students: dates-then-happiness order gave a very high correlation; happiness-first gave about zero. Parents or finances questions had the same effect.

insights.claim: Likes and dislikes set beliefs about benefits and risks, and the two move together: liking something makes its benefits seem high and its risks low. News about lower risk also raises perceived benefit.
insights.evidence: Slovic: attitudes to health policy, nuclear power, red meat, motorcycles; hawks vs. doves judging another nation's strength; 'He likes the project, so he thinks costs low, benefits high.'

insights.claim: When attitudes and emotions are involved, System 2 mostly looks for arguments that fit existing beliefs and defends System 1's conclusions instead of testing them; conclusions come before arguments.
insights.evidence: Political preference determines which arguments seem compelling; System 2's search is limited to belief-consistent information.

insights.claim: When you use an easy proxy such as last year's performance or interview skill, say so out loud and ask whether it is good enough and what other information you need.
insights.evidence: 'The question we face is whether this candidate can succeed... whether she interviews well. Let's not substitute.' and last year's performance used to value a firm years ahead.

insights.claim: System 1 frames decision problems narrowly, treating each in isolation from related decisions.
insights.evidence: Listed as a System 1 characteristic (developed later in the book).

insights.claim: System 1 generates impressions that become beliefs when System 2 endorses them; it seeks coherence, believes and confirms, suppresses doubt, ignores absent evidence, substitutes easier questions, and frames problems narrowly.
insights.evidence: Summary table of System 1 traits closing Part 1 (halo, WYSIATI, mental shotgun, substitution, loss aversion, narrow framing).

insights.concept: causal over-interpretation of statistical facts (System 1 causal bias)
insights.claim: System 1 automatically builds causal stories for patterns, even spurious ones, and is inept with merely statistical facts that change probabilities without causing outcomes.
insights.evidence: Readers explain low rural cancer by clean living and high rural cancer by poverty; the same feature cannot explain both.

insights.concept: law of small numbers / sample-size neglect
insights.claim: Extreme outcomes, both high and low, appear far more often in small samples, yet people read them as real differences needing explanation rather than sampling noise.
insights.evidence: Lowest and highest kidney-cancer rates both found in sparsely populated rural counties; Jack (4 marbles) sees all-same samples 8x more than Jill (7 marbles): 12.5% vs 1.56%.

insights.claim: Differences produced by the research method (e.g., sample size) are artifacts; the extreme groups will shift on repeat measurement, so there may be nothing to explain.
insights.evidence: Repeat the county analysis next year: small counties still show extremes, but not the same counties.

insights.claim: People, including expert researchers, believe small samples closely resemble the population, so they pick samples too small and trust results from few observations; small samples produce extreme results more often.
insights.evidence: Researchers' typical sample sizes gave ~50% risk of failing to confirm true hypotheses; Tversky's questionnaire of sophisticated researchers (incl. textbook authors) showed same errors.

insights.claim: Statistical intuitions should be treated with suspicion; sample size and risk of failure should be computed rather than chosen by tradition or feel.
insights.evidence: Kahneman taught statistics yet never computed sample sizes, getting nonsensical results that were artifacts of small samples.

insights.concept: insensitivity to sample size / source reliability
insights.claim: People attend to the story of a message and largely ignore its source and reliability (sample size, method), and System 1 cannot distinguish degrees of belief unless the message is plainly discredited.
insights.evidence: 'Telephone poll of 300 seniors, 60% support president' summarized as 'elderly support president'; 150 vs 3,000 feels the same; NYT vs watercooler.

insights.claim: System 1 suppresses ambiguity and builds maximally coherent stories, so we slide into certainty; holding incompatible possibilities requires effortful System 2, and we exaggerate the coherence of what we see (linked to halo and WYSIATI).
insights.evidence: Researchers' faith in few observations; halo effect of feeling we know a person from scraps.

insights.concept: misperception of randomness / seeing causes in chance
insights.claim: The associative machinery seeks causes, so we see patterns and clusters in random processes and misclassify random variation as systematic; the statistical view asks what else could have happened instead.
insights.evidence: BBBGGG/GGGGGG/BGBBGB equally likely; London V-bomb hit gaps blamed on spies; hot hand in basketball refuted by thousands of shot sequences.

insights.concept: accept luck; stop the search for nonobvious causes
insights.claim: When there's no prior reason to expect a difference and no operational differences are found, the outcome gap is most likely luck, and a random search for hidden causes is hopeless and can harm people.
insights.evidence: Yom Kippur War: one squadron lost four planes, another none; Kahneman advised stopping the inquiry.

insights.concept: law of small numbers / variability of small samples
insights.claim: Small samples produce extreme results at both ends, so 'the best performers are small' usually means small units are more variable, not better. Look at both tails before drawing a conclusion.
insights.evidence: Gates Foundation small-schools investment: the worst schools were also small; large schools, if anything, did better.

insights.claim: Small units dominate both the best and worst extremes because of variance; studying only top performers yields a false causal story, so also examine the bottom performers.
insights.evidence: Gates Foundation's $1.7B small-schools push: 6 of top 50 Pennsylvania schools were small, but bad schools also tend to be small.

insights.claim: Intuition infers skill too quickly from a few successes; one should ask how many successes are needed before ruling out luck.
insights.evidence: How many good years before an investment adviser is judged skilled; how many acquisitions before a CEO is credited with flair.

insights.claim: Many statistical patterns come from chance, including sampling accidents, yet they invite causal stories. Causal explanations of chance events are inevitably wrong.
insights.evidence: A causal story about personal attention in small schools; a hot-hand CEO after three hit films; a trader's streak.

insights.claim: People attend to what a message says more than to how reliable its source or sample is. The result is a world view simpler and more coherent than the data justify.
insights.evidence: The exaggerated faith in small samples, offered as an example of this more general illusion.

insights.concept: premature conclusion pressure (withhold results until sample is sufficient)
insights.claim: Keep experiment results private until the sample is large enough, so that no one is pushed to conclude early.
insights.evidence: 'Speaking of' example: keeping experimental results secret until the sample is sufficient.

insights.claim: If you consider a specific value for an unknown quantity before estimating it, your estimate stays close to that value. This holds even when the value is obviously uninformative and even when you try to resist it.
insights.evidence: A rigged wheel stopping at 10 or 65 shifted estimates of African UN members to 25% vs 45%; Gandhi died before or after 114 vs 35; the listing price of a house.

insights.claim: System 2 starts from an anchor and moves away from it, but stops at the near edge of its range of uncertainty, the point where it is no longer sure it should move further. The adjustment is effortful, so it shrinks when mental resources are depleted.
insights.evidence: A 2.5-inch line drawn from the bottom vs from the top; speeding off the highway; a teen turning loud music down 'enough'; Washington's presidency (after 1776); Everest boiling point (<100°C); less adjustment under digit load or mild drunkenness.

insights.claim: Most anchoring involves no conscious adjustment. An anchor works as suggestion: it automatically primes compatible evidence in System 1, so even an absurd anchor that nobody believes still pulls the estimate.
insights.evidence: 'Was Gandhi more or less than 144?' raises age estimates without anyone adjusting down from 144; the numb-left-leg suggestion example.

insights.claim: Adjustment is a deliberate search for reasons to move away from the anchor. Actively rejecting the anchor leads to more adjustment, and accepting it increases anchoring.
insights.evidence: Epley and Gilovich: people told to shake their heads at the anchor moved further from it, and nodding people showed more anchoring.

insights.claim: An anchor primes memories compatible with it, so estimates draw on a biased sample of ideas; System 1 tries to construct a world where the anchor is true, and System 2 then reasons over that biased retrieval without knowing it.
insights.evidence: Mussweiler & Strack: 20°C vs 5°C anchors sped recognition of summer vs winter words; high/low car-price anchors primed luxury vs mass-market brands.

insights.claim: Anchoring can be quantified as the ratio of the difference in mean estimates to the difference between anchors; typical values are around 30-55%, not small.
insights.evidence: Redwood: anchors 1,200 vs 180 ft produced means 844 vs 282 ft, index 562/1,020 = 55%; seabird donations $20 vs $143 for $5 vs $400 anchors (>30%).

insights.claim: Anchors that are obviously random or uninformative are as powerful as plausible hints, and experts are nearly as susceptible as novices while confidently denying any influence.
insights.evidence: Wheel of fortune for UN African nations (44%); SSN digits; German judges rolling loaded dice gave 8 vs 5 months (50%); real-estate agents 41% vs students 48%, agents denied effect.

insights.concept: strategic anchors: first move, rationing, caps
insights.claim: Anchors are exploitable: moving first sets the reference in single-issue negotiations, arbitrary purchase limits raise quantity, and a cap can pull many smaller values upward toward it. Do not counter an outrageous anchor with an equally outrageous one; reject it outright.
insights.evidence: Sioux City soup: 'limit 12' led to 7 cans, double the no-limit purchases; list price in home sales; $1M damages cap would raise smaller awards.

insights.claim: Deliberately searching memory for arguments against the anchor negates the biased recruitment of thoughts; in negotiation, focusing on the opponent's minimal acceptable offer or their cost of no deal reduces or eliminates anchoring. Assume every number on the table has anchored you and engage System 2 when stakes are high.
insights.evidence: Galinsky & Mussweiler negotiation instructions; Epley & Gilovich-style adjustment; 'Speaking of Anchors' advice to set aside a target firm's revenue plan.

insights.claim: Business plans and stated expectations are best-case scenarios; forecasting actual outcomes should not anchor on them, and imagining how the plan could go wrong counters the pull.
insights.evidence: 'Speaking of Anchors': acquisition target's expected revenue should be set aside; plans are best-case scenarios.

insights.claim: People estimate how frequent or large a category is by how easily instances come to mind; this substitutes an easier question (ease of recall) for the target one (frequency), producing systematic errors.
insights.evidence: Letter sets XUZONLCJM vs TAPCERHOB: you instantly sense one yields far more words without generating any; frequency of countries in the news.

insights.claim: Each collaborator recalls their own efforts more easily than others', so self-estimated shares add to more than 100%; simply noting that total credit usually exceeds 100% can defuse tension—a rare case where personal debiasing works.
insights.evidence: Spouses' self-rated contributions to tidying, garbage, social plans summed above 100%; they also overclaimed causing quarrels, so it's not purely self-serving.

insights.concept: listing non-frequency factors that ease retrieval (availability bias audit)
insights.claim: To find where availability misleads, list factors other than true frequency that make instances easy to recall—salience, dramatic recent events, personal experience, vivid pictures—each is a potential bias source; then ask whether a belief rests on a few recent or vivid cases.
insights.evidence: Celebrity divorces and political scandals overestimated; a publicized plane crash alters felt flight safety; a judicial error affecting you hurts faith in justice more than one read about; 'is teen theft a problem due to a few recent local cases?'

insights.concept: ease of retrieval vs. amount retrieved (Schwarz fluency effect)
insights.claim: Judgments are dominated by how fluently instances come to mind, not how many are retrieved: struggling to generate many examples lowers belief in the trait or option, so asking for more supporting reasons can reduce confidence.
insights.evidence: Listing 12 assertive acts led to lower self-rated assertiveness than listing 6; listing 12 non-assertive acts made people feel assertive; frowners (more strain) rated themselves less assertive; fewer bike-use beliefs after recalling many instances; more arguments → less confidence in a choice; more car advantages → less impressed; UCLA students listing more course improvements rated the course higher.

insights.claim: The fluency paradox is not universal—people sometimes judge by retrieved content rather than ease; understanding a bias means knowing the conditions that reverse it.
insights.evidence: Schwarz and colleagues set out to find conditions under which people rely on content instead of retrieval ease.

insights.claim: People infer something from how hard examples are to recall only when the difficulty is unexpected; once the difficulty gets an explanation, even a fake one, it stops affecting the judgment.
insights.evidence: Schwarz: subjects told background music would hinder recall rated themselves equally assertive after listing 12 or 6 instances.

insights.concept: availability bias from recent/vivid events and success streaks
insights.claim: Recent salient events, media coverage, or a run of personal successes make some outcomes come to mind easily and others hardly at all, distorting risk estimates and breeding overconfidence.
insights.evidence: Two plane crashes make someone switch to trains; indoor pollution risks underestimated for lack of stories; CEO after successes can't imagine failure.

insights.concept: content vs. fluency: System 2 engagement reduces availability bias
insights.claim: When people are personally involved and vigilant, they judge by the number and content of retrieved instances instead of by ease of retrieval; reliance on fluency rises under cognitive load, good mood, novice knowledge, faith in intuition and feeling powerful.
insights.evidence: Students with family cardiac history felt safer after recalling many safe behaviors, while uninvolved students followed ease of retrieval.

insights.claim: Protective effort spikes right after a disaster and decays as memories fade, and protections are sized to the worst event actually experienced because worse scenarios don't come to mind.
insights.evidence: Californians insure after earthquakes then lapse; societies since pharaonic Egypt prepared only for the recorded high-water mark.

insights.claim: Frequency judgments track how often and how emotionally events are reported, so novel, dramatic causes are overestimated and common quiet ones underestimated.
insights.evidence: Slovic/Lichtenstein/Fischhoff: accidents judged likelier than strokes (which cause ~2x more deaths); tornadoes over asthma (20x more deaths); accidents vs diabetes judged 300:1, true 1:4.

insights.claim: People judge and decide by consulting feelings of liking or disliking, substituting the easy question 'how do I feel about it?' for the hard 'what do I think about it?'; fluent, vivid danger thoughts amplify fear, though appropriate emotion is also needed for good decisions.
insights.evidence: Slovic's technology survey (fluoridation, chemical plants, preservatives, cars) on benefits and risks; Damasio's patients lacking emotions decide poorly.

insights.claim: Liking an option makes people judge its risks low and benefits high together; information that changes only benefits also shifts perceived risks, producing an unrealistically tidy world with no tradeoffs.
insights.evidence: Slovic: respondents reading only benefit arguments for a technology also rated it less risky; those told only that risks were mild rated benefits higher.

insights.concept: combine expert analysis with stakeholder emotions
insights.claim: Neither pure expert cost-benefit analysis nor public sentiment suffices: fears, even unreasonable ones, have real costs and affect acceptance, so good policy combines expert knowledge with people's emotions and values.
insights.evidence: Kahneman sides with both Sunstein (insulate priorities from irrational fear) and Slovic (policies ignoring public fear get rejected; fear itself is painful).

insights.concept: risk measure choice (defining risk is an exercise in power)
insights.claim: There is no single objective risk; the metric chosen (deaths per million people vs. per dollar of product, lives vs. life-years) changes the evaluation and may be chosen to favor an outcome. Counted statistics also miss distinctions people legitimately care about (voluntary vs. involuntary, good vs. bad deaths).
insights.evidence: Slovic lists nine ways to define mortality risk of a toxic release; experts count lives while the public distinguishes voluntary deaths like skiing.

insights.claim: A self-reinforcing loop where media coverage of a minor risk arouses worry, the worry itself becomes news, availability entrepreneurs feed it, dissenters are dismissed, and priorities get reset toward that risk while others fade.
insights.evidence: Kuran & Sunstein: Love Canal (1979) leading to Superfund, and the 1989 Alar apple scare where a tiny risk led to a ban and fewer apples eaten; terrorism vs. traffic deaths.

insights.claim: Concern about small risks is insensitive to probability: we either ignore them or overweight them, imagining the vivid numerator story and not the denominator.
insights.evidence: A parent waiting up for a late teenager; terror casualties far below traffic deaths yet dominating fear (Sunstein's term).

insights.claim: When you know nothing specific about a case, the best prediction comes from the proportion of each category in the population: the base rate.
insights.evidence: Tom W chosen at random from graduate students, like a marble drawn from an urn. Humanities and education is more likely than library science because it has more students.

insights.claim: People treat a description as fully diagnostic even when they are told it comes from a source of uncertain validity. A sound probability judgment should discount weak evidence.
insights.evidence: The Tom W sketch came from psychological tests 'of uncertain validity', and participants still ranked fields purely by stereotype fit.

insights.concept: expert knowledge does not prevent base-rate neglect
insights.claim: Knowing statistics does not lead experts to use base rates on their own initiative. They recognise the error only when someone mentions 'base rate', so the check has to be an explicit step.
insights.evidence: Robyn Dawes, an expert statistician who was skeptical of intuition, guessed 'computer scientist' and saw his mistake only once base rates were mentioned.

insights.claim: People judge how probable an outcome is by how closely the case resembles its stereotype. They ignore the base rates and the reliability of the description, even when they know both.
insights.evidence: 114 psychology graduate students trained in statistics ranked Tom W's fields by probability the same way they ranked them by similarity. Computer science, a small field, came out as most likely.

insights.concept: substitution of similarity for probability (mental shotgun)
insights.claim: A hard question about probability fires a mental shotgun. System 1 answers an easier similarity question instead. Similarity does not follow the logic of probability, so the result contains errors.
insights.evidence: The probability rankings matched the similarity rankings exactly. The Elvis-as-dentist joke works because a mismatch in similarity is detected automatically.

insights.claim: Selecting by statistics of past performance beats forecasting by how candidates 'look the part'. Representativeness-based selection also leaves undervalued options for others to pick up.
insights.evidence: Billy Beane overruled his scouts and chose players by past statistics. The Oakland A's got excellent results at low cost.

insights.concept: sin of representativeness: overpredicting low-base-rate events
insights.claim: Representativeness is usually better than chance. Relied on alone, it makes people too willing to predict rare outcomes, because a common category can produce the matching cue more often in absolute numbers.
insights.evidence: A woman reads the NYT on the New York subway. Representativeness says she has a PhD, but many more nongraduates ride the subway.

insights.claim: When a vivid individual description is available, people bet on the category it resembles and ignore that a much larger category contains more matching cases; individual-case info is almost always overweighted versus statistics.
insights.evidence: Shy poetry lover: Chinese literature vs business administration; Tom W base-rate concern disappears once personality is described; NYT reader on subway PhD vs no degree.

insights.concept: insensitivity to the quality of evidence (WYSIATI)
insights.claim: System 1 processes available information as if true, so unreliable evidence moves judgments as much as solid evidence; worthless information should be treated like no information, keeping estimates near the base rate.
insights.evidence: Tom W description that readers were told not to trust still convinced them he wasn't in social science; correct answer stays close to priors.

insights.concept: think like a statistician / System 2 activation
insights.claim: Base-rate neglect is largely System 2 laziness, not ignorance: prompting a statistician frame or increasing effort/vigilance (frowning) restores sensitivity to base rates, while a 'clinician' frame worsens it.
insights.evidence: Schwarz et al. statistician vs clinician instruction; Harvard students frowning vs puffing cheeks on Tom W problem.

insights.claim: Subjective beliefs must obey probability logic: complements sum to 100%, a sub-event can't be likelier than its containing event, and sequential probabilities multiply.
insights.evidence: 40% rain implies 60% no rain and not 50% rain in the morning; 30% elected x 80% reelected = 24% two terms.

insights.concept: disciplined Bayesian reasoning (anchor on base rate, question diagnosticity)
insights.claim: Combine a plausible base rate with the diagnosticity of the evidence (how much more likely it is under the hypothesis than alternatives); intuitive diagnosticity is usually exaggerated by WYSIATI and associative coherence.
insights.evidence: 3% CS base rate with description 4x more likely in CS yields 11%; with 80% prior yields 94.1%. Startup that 'could not fail' vs low industry success base rate.

insights.claim: Judging quality or outcome by how much surface features resemble the stereotype (tidy lawn, competent receptionist) substitutes resemblance for probability.
insights.evidence: Speaking-of example: attractive offices do not mean a well-managed company; board should not go by representativeness.

insights.claim: Adding detail makes a scenario more coherent and representative but can only lower its probability; people (even trained statisticians) rank the more detailed conjunction as more probable, a System 2 failure.
insights.evidence: Linda as 'feminist bank teller' ranked more probable than 'bank teller': 89% of undergrads, 85% of Stanford decision-science doctoral students.

insights.claim: People rate a conjunction of two events (A and B) as more probable than one of its parts (A) when the conjunction fits a stereotype or story better. This breaks the rule that adding conditions can only lower probability.
insights.evidence: Linda problem: 85-90% of undergraduates said 'bank teller and feminist' was more likely than 'bank teller'. Borg: 72% ranked 'lose first set but win match' above 'lose first set'.

insights.claim: Judging options side by side can bring in System 2 and logical rules that single evaluation misses. It removed the less-is-more error for prices, and the short direct Linda comparison raised accuracy among sophisticated students. But when the sum-like rule is not obvious, as with probability, side-by-side comparison may still fail.
insights.evidence: Short direct Linda version: 64% correct vs 15% in the 8-item list. Dinnerware joint evaluation: $32 vs $30, the logical order. Borg and Linda errors survived joint evaluation.

insights.concept: plausibility substituted for probability (scenario detail trap)
insights.claim: Adding detail to a scenario makes it more coherent and persuasive but less likely to come true. System 1 answers 'how plausible is this story' when asked 'how probable is it'.
insights.evidence: A flood in North America killing 1,000+ was rated less probable than a California earthquake causing such a flood. Detail that adds no coherence ('Mark has blond hair') does not trigger the error.

insights.concept: System 2 is not impressively alert (knowing a rule is not applying it)
insights.claim: People who know the rule, even statistics doctoral students, often fail to apply it when the information is right in front of them. When shown the arguments, though, most recognize the correct one. So prompting an explicit check works better than trusting what people know.
insights.evidence: In the die task, two-thirds bet on the representative longer sequence GRGRRR, yet most found the correct argument for RGRRR more convincing. Gould's 'homunculus' kept insisting even though he knew the answer.

insights.concept: less is more (System 1 averages instead of adding)
insights.claim: For sum-like quantities such as total value or probability, System 1 judges a set by its average or prototype. So removing weaker items can raise the judged value of the set, even though adding positive items can only increase the true total.
insights.evidence: Hsee's dinnerware: judged alone, a 24-piece intact set was priced at $33 vs $23 for a 40-piece set that had broken items. List found the same effect with baseball cards.

insights.claim: Asking 'how many out of 100 people' instead of 'what percentage' makes subset relations visible, like groups sorting into corners of a room. It sharply reduces the conjunction fallacy.
insights.evidence: In the medical-survey problem, errors were 65% with the percentage wording and 25% with the 'how many of the 100 participants' wording.

insights.concept: attack the strongest argument, not the weakest (scientific vs political critique)
insights.claim: Lawyers and debaters discredit a position by going after its weakest point, but a fair scientific evaluation should deal with the strongest evidence. If one salient example can be explained away, the rest of the body of evidence still stands.
insights.evidence: Critics focused on the Linda problem and ignored the stronger between-subjects evidence for heuristics; Hertwig said Linda 'was more interesting'.

insights.claim: Judging options separately lets intuition decide, while a direct side-by-side comparison usually makes people more careful and logical. It is not a guarantee, though: in the Linda problem intuition often won even in joint evaluation.
insights.evidence: Dinnerware: logic won when both sets were shown together; Linda: the conjunction fallacy often persisted even in joint evaluation.

insights.concept: lazy System 2 / plausibility substitutes for probability (conjunction fallacy)
insights.claim: People who know probability logic still back a detailed conjunction because it seems plausible, and System 2 does not check it when little is at stake. A rich scenario is a plausible story, not a probable one.
insights.evidence: Linda problem; students who knew Venn diagrams still ranked the conjunction as more likely; 'a very complicated scenario... only a plausible story'.

insights.concept: less is more (adding a low-value item dilutes the whole)
insights.claim: When people judge a bundle on its own, they judge it by its average or prototype, so adding a cheap or damaged item lowers its value even though more can only add value. Seeing the options side by side usually brings back the logical rule.
insights.evidence: Hsee's dinnerware study: in separate evaluation, the set that also had broken dishes got a lower price; a cheap gift added to an expensive product made the deal less attractive.

insights.concept: Bayesian combination of base rate and witness reliability
insights.claim: Estimating the probability of a case takes two inputs: the base rate (the prior), adjusted by how reliable the specific evidence is. When the base rate is uninformative (50/50), only reliability matters. When the base rate is more extreme than the evidence's reliability, it pulls the answer toward itself.
insights.evidence: Prior of 15% Blue plus an 80% reliable witness gives 41% Blue, not the intuitive 80%.

insights.concept: causes trump statistics: statistical vs causal base rates
insights.claim: Purely statistical base rates (how common something is in a population) get underweighted or ignored once there is specific information about the case. The same numbers framed causally, as a propensity that explains the case, get used readily.
insights.evidence: Cab problem: 85% of cabs are Green and a witness who is 80% reliable says Blue, so the Bayesian answer is 41% Blue. People ignore the base rate in the 'share of cabs' version but use it when told Green cabs cause 85% of accidents.

insights.concept: stereotypes as causal base rates (System 1 represents categories by prototypes)
insights.claim: System 1 holds categories as 'normal' prototype members, and group statistics get read as propensities in each member. That can make judgments more accurate, but in sensitive contexts like hiring or profiling society rightly rejects it, and doing so has a real accuracy cost.
insights.evidence: 'Green drivers are dangerous'; graduates of an inner-city school going to college; cycling interest in France; the norm against profiling.

insights.concept: affect heuristic in charged arguments (costless positions)
insights.claim: In emotionally or politically charged debates, people believe that the positions they favor have no costs and the ones they oppose have no benefits, so they deny real trade-offs.
insights.evidence: Opposition to stereotyping and profiling is morally laudable, but it is wrong to deny that ignoring valid stereotypes has costs.

insights.claim: Base rates that suggest a cause (the test was hard, the cab company is reckless) are folded into judgment. Purely statistical base rates (how a sample was built) are mostly neglected, even though a Bayesian treats both the same.
insights.evidence: Ajzen's Yale exam study: '75% failed' as a class fact vs '75% failed' as a sampling choice of the investigator; the causal version had a much larger effect.

insights.claim: When people know that others also heard a request, each feels less personally responsible and is less likely to act.
insights.evidence: Seizure helping experiment: only 4 of 15 responded immediately; 6 never left their booth.

insights.claim: People can recite a surprising statistical finding and its official explanation, yet they 'quietly exempt' themselves and the people they know from it, so their predictions do not change.
insights.evidence: Students who knew the helping results predicted the same as students who did not; the same happened when teaching a social-pressure shock study.

insights.concept: stay with the base rate when individual information is uninformative
insights.claim: Begin from the prior that the base rate gives. Move away from it only when the case information is actually diagnostic. Bland, nondiagnostic detail should leave the estimate at the base rate.
insights.evidence: Only 4 of 15 helped (27%), so the prior for any participant is 'did not rush to help'. The bland interviews carried no information, yet students predicted quick helping.

insights.concept: infer the general from the particular (surprising individual cases teach)
insights.claim: People resist deducing the particular from the general but readily infer the general from surprising particular cases. Concrete surprising cases, especially ones about oneself, change beliefs more than statistics do.
insights.evidence: Students told that two nice interviewees did not help then guessed the overall low helping rate very accurately.

insights.claim: People make up causal stories, such as praise backfiring, punishment working, or pressure and tension, to explain changes that are really just regression. This creates perverse feedback: being nasty seems to pay off and being nice seems to be punished.
insights.evidence: Flight instructor's claim that screaming improves cadets; ski-jump commentator saying a leader 'will be tense' and a laggard 'relaxed'.

insights.claim: When outcomes depend partly on luck, extreme results tend to be followed by results closer to the average, whatever anyone does. Regression happens whenever two measures are imperfectly correlated.
insights.evidence: Coin-throwing at a chalk target: the best first throwers mostly did worse on the second throw, and the worst mostly improved, with no feedback given.

insights.claim: An outstanding result is evidence of both above-average skill and above-average luck. Since luck does not persist, the larger and rarer the success, the bigger the share luck probably had.
insights.evidence: Golfer who shot 66 against a par-72 average on day 1 is probably talented and also lucky that day. Great success = a little more talent + a lot of luck.

insights.claim: Regression also shows up when you predict the earlier event from the later one. Because a cause cannot run backward in time, this shows that regression needs no causal explanation.
insights.evidence: Golfers ranked by day-2 scores also did less well on day 1. Sports Illustrated cover jinx explained by a lucky prior season.

insights.claim: Predict a future result by keeping the stable (skill) part and assuming average luck. The forecast should sit closer to the mean than the evidence, and should be pulled in more the more extreme the evidence is.
insights.evidence: Day-2 golf forecasts: the leader stays above average but by less, the trailer improves, and the gap between them shrinks.

insights.concept: correlation as shared factors / imperfect correlation implies regression
insights.claim: The correlation between two measures reflects the relative weight of the factors they share. Whenever it is below 1, predicting one from the other must regress, and variables on different scales can be compared through ranks or standard scores.
insights.evidence: Weight = age + ice cream and piano = age + practice; predicting one from the other regresses. Parent-child height correlation is about .50.

insights.claim: A predictor's correlation with outcomes drops in a pre-selected group because the predictor varies little there, so its weak validity inside the group says little about its value overall.
insights.evidence: SAT–GPA correlation about .60 but aptitude tests predict graduate success much less, since graduate students have similar aptitude; height–weight r=.41 among men, higher with women and children.

insights.concept: regression to the mean (imperfect correlation implies regression)
insights.claim: Whenever two measures are imperfectly correlated, extreme scores on one are followed by less extreme scores on the other; the regression is no more interesting or explainable than the imperfect correlation itself.
insights.evidence: Highly intelligent women marry less intelligent men on average—algebraically equivalent to spouses' IQ correlation being below 1; golfers who excelled on day 1 deteriorate on day 2.

insights.claim: System 1 automatically searches memory for causes when an event draws attention, so regression effects get wrong causal stories; regression has an explanation (luck) but no cause.
insights.evidence: Business commentator saying a firm did better because it did poorly last year would lose his job; instructor believing criticism beats praise; eminent researchers listed by Howard Wainer making the same error.

insights.concept: control group to separate treatment from regression
insights.claim: To claim a treatment works on an extreme group, compare it to an untreated or placebo control that will also improve by regression; only the excess improvement counts.
insights.evidence: Depressed children given an energy drink, standing on their heads, or hugging a cat all improve over three months.

insights.claim: When outcomes are partly random, forecasts should shrink toward the mean: low performers should be forecast to grow more than average and high performers less, rather than applying a uniform change.
insights.evidence: Bazerman's department-store forecast: adding 10% to every store's 2011 sales is wrong; the screening line 'very best candidates often fail to meet expectations'.

insights.concept: skilled intuition vs heuristic substitution in prediction
insights.claim: Intuitive forecasts come either from expertise recognizing familiar cues or from heuristics substituting an easy question; the two can feel identical, and the latter yields high confidence from nonregressive use of weak evidence.
insights.evidence: Klein's chess masters and fireground commanders vs Julie read fluently at four, so people guess her GPA as 3.7–3.8.

insights.concept: insensitivity to predictive quality of evidence (dichotomous relevance)
insights.claim: System 1 either throws evidence out as irrelevant or accepts it in full. It cannot discount evidence for being only weakly predictive. Once a causal link is found, WYSIATI builds the best possible story.
insights.evidence: Fly-fishing wins would be rejected as irrelevant, but early reading is accepted at full weight as a GPA signal.

insights.claim: System 1 maps the strength of the evidence onto the outcome scale at the same percentile. The prediction ends up as extreme as the evidence and ignores regression to the mean.
insights.evidence: Reading fluently at age four gets mapped to a GPA of about 3.7-3.8. Officers' predicted grade distribution matched the school's actual grade distribution.

insights.claim: When asked to predict a future outcome, people answer an easier question: how impressive is the current evidence. They do not notice the swap, and they leave out everything uncertain that happens between now and the outcome.
insights.evidence: Counselor-description study: percentile ratings of how impressive the description was matched GPA predictions exactly. Army officers translated their own ratings into officer-school grades.

insights.concept: correcting intuitive predictions (regress toward the mean)
insights.claim: To make an unbiased quantitative prediction, start at the average, find the value your intuition matches to the evidence, estimate the correlation between evidence and outcome, and move only that fraction of the distance from the average toward the intuition. With no useful evidence you stay at the baseline. You keep the full intuition only if the correlation is near perfect after critical review.
insights.evidence: Julie's GPA with an optimistic correlation of about .30: move 30% of the way from the average GPA toward the matching GPA. The method also applies to investment profit and company growth.

insights.concept: regression to the mean in successive performance
insights.claim: Predicting that extreme performers will repeat their results is biased. Top performers tend to do worse next time and the worst tend to improve. Corrected predictions err equally often in both directions and make smaller errors.
insights.evidence: Predicting each golfer's day-2 score as equal to day 1. Early readers usually disappoint in college grades, while late readers pleasantly surprise.

insights.claim: Probability predictions and scale predictions use the same correction. Anchor on the base rate or category average, form the intuitive answer, and settle in between based on how much you trust the evidence.
insights.evidence: Tom W uses base rates for field-of-study probabilities. GPA and firm revenue use the category average as the baseline.

insights.concept: asymmetric error costs justify departing from unbiased prediction
insights.claim: Unbiased, moderate prediction is best when all errors cost the same. When one direction of error is far worse, the decision can lean that way, but the probability estimate itself should stay honest and you should know you are indulging yourself.
insights.evidence: A VC fears missing the next Google more than a modest failed bet; a conservative banker fears one big default more than turning away good clients.

insights.claim: Correcting intuition is costly System 2 work: you have to find the reference class, estimate the baseline, and judge the evidence. It is worth doing when the stakes are high and mistakes are costly.
insights.evidence: The text describes the steps needed for an unbiased prediction and when their effort pays off.

insights.claim: System 1 makes a prediction as extreme as the evidence looks, through substitution, and feels too sure of it because confidence comes from how coherent the story is. The result is predictions that are too extreme.
insights.evidence: Two-Systems View of Regression; the 'outstanding proof of concept' start-up should not be expected to do as well in the future.

insights.concept: rational betting on likely failures / think in ranges
insights.claim: A rational actor can back a venture that will most likely fail if the payoff from success is big enough. She gives a range of outcomes instead of one number and does not inflate the odds to justify the bet.
insights.evidence: The rational VC picks the most promising of the available bets; 'Let's not say we really believe it is the next Google.'

insights.concept: regress more for smaller samples of information (Kim vs. Jane)
insights.claim: A candidate who makes a striking impression on little evidence is a small sample, and small samples produce extreme results by luck. Their predicted performance should be pulled harder toward the mean than that of a candidate with a long track record.
insights.evidence: Hiring committee: Kim has brilliant interviews and no track record; Jane has 3 productive postdoc years and less sparkling talks. Kahneman would vote for Jane.

insights.claim: Regression to the mean feels foreign even to System 2, and experience will not teach it. When people do notice a regression, they almost always give it a cause, and the cause is usually wrong.
insights.evidence: Galton struggled to understand it; statistics teachers dread the topic; the flight instructors read regression as an effect of praise and punishment.

insights.concept: prefer large-sample evidence over a single glowing data point
insights.claim: One excellent review could be a fluke. Compare only options with many data points, then pick the best of those.
insights.evidence: A 'Speaking of' line: read one excellent brand review, so consider only brands with many reviews.

insights.claim: We build simple, concrete causal stories of the past that over-credit talent, stupidity and intentions, under-credit luck, and ignore the many events that failed to happen; these flimsy stories then shape our expectations.
insights.evidence: The Google success story, including the near-sale for under $1M; competitors portrayed as blind and slow.

insights.concept: test of an explanation (predictable in advance)
insights.claim: An explanation only earns trust if it would have made the event predictable beforehand; post-hoc stories of unlikely successes fail this test.
insights.evidence: No story of Google's unlikely success could have predicted it in advance.

insights.claim: Saying people 'knew' a crisis was coming, or had an 'intuition/premonition', reserves those words for beliefs that happened to come true, implying the world is more knowable than it is; clean up the language for past beliefs.
insights.evidence: Claims that people 'knew' the 2008 financial crisis was inevitable, while many informed people did not foresee it.

insights.concept: luck-skill learnability (the rafter vs. the founder)
insights.claim: Learning is possible where an agent gets many repeated trials with feedback; the more luck drove an outcome, the less there is to learn from it.
insights.evidence: Skilled rafter has run rapids hundreds of times; young founders have few chances to learn to build a giant company.

insights.claim: We treat the information we have as all there is; coherent stories are easier to build when we know little, and our conviction rests on ignoring our ignorance.
insights.evidence: Author's discussion of the Google narrative and the comfort of a sense-making world.

insights.claim: Once beliefs change we cannot reconstruct what we used to believe, substituting current beliefs, so we underestimate how surprised we were and overstate the accuracy of past predictions.
insights.evidence: Fischhoff & Beyth: before Nixon's 1972 China/USSR trip people rated 15 outcomes; afterward they inflated recalled probabilities for events that occurred and lowered them for ones that did not. Attitude-change studies show people recall their current view as their past one.

insights.claim: Observers judge a decision by whether its outcome was good or bad rather than by whether the process and the beliefs reasonable at the time were sound; worse consequences magnify this.
insights.evidence: Duluth bridge-monitor case: 24% (foresight info only) vs 56% (told of flood) said city should hire monitor despite instructions to ignore hindsight; low-risk surgery death; 9/11 CIA July 10 memo.

insights.concept: hindsight-driven defensive risk aversion / rewarding lucky gamblers
