insights.claim: Fear of hindsight scrutiny pushes decision makers to bureaucratic procedures and excessive risk aversion, while lucky reckless risk-takers receive an undeserved halo of foresight.
insights.evidence: Physicians under malpractice threat ordering more tests and referrals that protect them more than patients; a general or entrepreneur whose crazy gamble won.

insights.concept: illusion of understanding feeds illusion of control
insights.claim: System 1's sense-making makes the world look tidier and more predictable than it is; believing we understand the past feeds the belief we can predict and control the future, which business 'recipes' exploit.
insights.evidence: Business books tailor-made to the need that success rewards wisdom and courage.

insights.claim: Even a generous .30 correlation between CEO quality and firm success means the stronger CEO leads the more successful firm only about 60% of the time, 10 points above chance; expecting more signals overestimating the world's predictability.
insights.evidence: Pairs-of-similar-firms thought question; perfect correlation gives 100%, no correlation 50%, .30 gives ~60%.

insights.claim: Knowing that an outcome was good or bad colours how we judge the actor's traits. We then read those traits as the cause of the outcome, when the outcome actually produced the description of the traits.
insights.evidence: The same CEO is described as flexible, methodical and decisive while the firm thrives, and as confused, rigid and authoritarian a year later when it falters.

insights.claim: Comparing successful firms with less successful ones largely compares lucky firms with unlucky ones. If very consistent patterns show up in such a comparison, treat them with suspicion, because where randomness is strong, regular patterns are likely mirages.
insights.evidence: Built to Last analysed 18 pairs of rival companies, and its 'best practices' message is overstated because luck plays a large part in which firm succeeds.

insights.claim: Stories of rise and fall attract us because they give a simple message with clear causes. They leave out the large role of luck and the certainty of regression, which creates an illusion of understanding with lessons of little lasting value.
insights.evidence: Business success stories, and the comment: 'He's learning too much from this success story, which is too tidy.'

insights.claim: People judge a decision by how it turned out rather than by how good it was when it was made. Something bad that happened was not necessarily foreseeable, and a reckless decision that worked out was still a bad decision.
insights.evidence: Speaking of Hindsight example: 'This was a stupid decision even though it worked out well.' Another example concludes the firm is badly managed only because its stock fell.

insights.concept: regression to the mean in performance gaps
insights.claim: Part of any extreme performance gap comes from luck, so on average the gap has to shrink later on. Causal stories such as complacency or trying harder are not needed to explain the shrinking.
insights.evidence: The profitability gap between Built to Last firms and their comparison firms almost disappeared after the study. Profits of In Search of Excellence firms fell soon after. Over 20 years, the least admired companies on Fortune's list earned higher stock returns than the most admired.

insights.claim: How confident we feel tracks how coherent the story is, not how much evidence there is or how good it is. Weak evidence can still make a very good story, and System 1 cannot sense how big its jumps to conclusions are.
insights.evidence: Opening argument of ch. 20: under WYSIATI, only the evidence at hand counts, and some important beliefs rest on nothing more than the fact that trusted people hold them.

insights.claim: General feedback that a forecasting method has failed does not carry over to confidence in each new specific judgment. People keep acting as though each individual prediction is valid.
insights.evidence: Every few months the evaluators learned their predictions were negligible, felt downcast, and then the next day judged new candidates 'as clearly as before'.

insights.claim: A coherent, vivid impression gives a feeling that a prediction is valid. This feeling persists even when the person knows, as a statistical fact, that such predictions are nearly useless, much like the Müller-Lyer lines still look unequal after you know they are equal.
insights.evidence: Officer-candidate evaluators in the leaderless group challenge were completely confident about each soldier. Feedback sessions showed their predictions were barely better than chance, yet their confidence and the way they judged the next batch stayed the same.

insights.concept: confidence as a feeling of coherence
insights.claim: Subjective confidence is a System 1 feeling produced by coherent information and cognitive ease, not a reasoned probability that the judgment is correct; high confidence mainly shows someone built a coherent story.
insights.evidence: Officer-candidate evaluators and stock traders both felt sure; Kahneman locates confidence in System 1 via cognitive ease and associative coherence.

insights.concept: illusion of skill (rewarding luck as skill)
insights.claim: Whole industries can rest on an illusion of skill: practitioners exercise real expertise on a sub-question (firm quality) while lacking skill on the decisive question (is it already priced in), and are ignorant of that ignorance.
insights.evidence: Stock pickers analyze balance sheets and management, yet cannot tell whether information is already in the price; the firm paid bonuses on luck.

insights.claim: People keep high confidence in their individual predictions even when they know the evidence shows those predictions are barely better than chance; knowing the general rule does not change confidence about specific cases.
insights.evidence: Israeli army leaderless-group test: evaluators knew their forecasts failed but still felt each new forecast was valid, like the Müller-Lyer lines.

insights.concept: resistance to statistical base rates (failure to infer particular from general)
insights.claim: People accept statistical facts intellectually but do not let them change judgments about individual cases, especially when the facts threaten livelihood or self-esteem and clash with personal experience; cognitive illusions outlast visual ones.
insights.evidence: Nisbett and Borgida's helping-study students; executives calmly heard the zero-correlation finding and changed nothing; adviser said no one can take his success away.

insights.concept: overtrading / acting on ideas (doing nothing as baseline)
insights.claim: Acting on the ideas that come to mind often performs worse than doing nothing; the most active traders earned the least, and individuals sell winners, hold losers and buy attention-grabbing stocks.
insights.evidence: Odean: 10,000 accounts, ~163,000 trades; stocks sold beat stocks bought by 3.2 points/year after costs; 'Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth'; men traded more and did worse.

insights.concept: persistence test for skill (luck vs. skill diagnostic)
insights.claim: Skill exists only if individual differences in results are consistent over time; if year-to-year correlation of rankings is near zero, outcomes are luck, however skilled the work feels.
insights.evidence: 25 wealth advisers over 8 years: average of 28 year-pair rank correlations was .01; mutual funds show barely-above-zero year-to-year correlation and two of three underperform the market yearly.

insights.concept: hindsight narratives fuel forecasting overconfidence (illusions of pundits)
insights.claim: Because the past is easily explained in coherent stories, we feel what makes sense now was predictable then, which inflates confidence in predicting the future; professional culture and like-minded communities sustain such beliefs.
insights.evidence: Taleb's Black Swan; financial pundits nightly explaining the day's market; the 'march of history' image implying order.

insights.concept: illusion of valid prediction (expert political judgment)
insights.claim: Expert forecasters of long-range political and economic events did worse than assigning equal probabilities to the outcomes. Above a modest level, more knowledge adds little accuracy and raises overconfidence. More famous experts are more overconfident.
insights.evidence: Tetlock: 284 pundits and 80,000+ predictions rated as status quo / more / less; experts lost to 'dart-throwing monkeys' and did no better than nonspecialists, even in their own regions.

insights.concept: excuses for forecast error (resisting admission of error)
insights.claim: Experts rarely admit they were wrong. They say they were only off on timing, that an unforeseeable event intervened, or that they were wrong for the right reasons.
insights.evidence: Tetlock's interviews on how experts reacted when proved wrong.

insights.claim: Hedgehogs explain everything through one big theory, are confident, and dismiss failures as timing errors. Foxes see outcomes as interactions of many agents plus luck, and they forecast better, though still poorly.
insights.evidence: Tetlock using Isaiah Berlin's essay; foxes scored best; hedgehogs say 'off only on timing' and are favored by TV.

insights.claim: Situation-specific factors limit how well tests or past behavior predict future performance. A predictor with validity .20-.30 should still be used, but expectations should be capped accordingly. Short-term trends are more forecastable than long-term ones.
insights.evidence: Obstacle-field test vs. officer combat performance; stock pickers; pundits' long-term forecasts.

insights.concept: subjective confidence is not accuracy; world unpredictability
insights.claim: Prediction errors are unavoidable because the world is unpredictable, and high subjective confidence does not show accuracy; low confidence may tell you more. Before trusting experts, ask whether their environment is predictable, not whether they are well trained.
insights.evidence: Chapter lessons, the sniper bullet and assertive group member examples, and the phrase 'Is their world predictable?'

insights.claim: In low-validity environments, simple rules that combine a few scores match or beat trained experts' holistic judgments. They are also cheaper, so a tie counts as a win for the rule.
insights.evidence: Meehl's 20 studies (formula using HS grades plus 1 test beat 11 of 14 counselors); about 200 studies later, about 60% favor algorithms and the rest are draws; Ashenfelter's 3-weather-variable Bordeaux price formula, r>.90.

insights.concept: complexity reduces validity / overriding the formula; broken-leg rule
insights.claim: Experts lose to formulas partly because they try to be clever and weigh complex feature combinations. They also override the formula's score with 'extra information' and are usually wrong when they do. Override only for decisive, rare information (the broken-leg rule).
insights.evidence: Decision makers given the formula's score still did worse when they overrode it; Meehl's thought experiment of a moviegoer who broke a leg today.

insights.claim: Overriding a formula is justified only by information that is both very rare and decisive; ordinary 'extra information about the case' does not qualify.
insights.evidence: Meehl's thought experiment: a formula predicting moviegoing should be ignored if the person broke a leg today.

insights.claim: Humans give different summary judgments of the same information on different occasions because System 1 is swayed by fleeting context; unreliable judgments cannot be valid, while formulas always return the same answer for the same input.
insights.evidence: Radiologists contradict themselves on the same X-ray 20% of the time; 101 auditors and a review of 41 studies show similar inconsistency; parole decisions shift with time since judges' food breaks.

insights.concept: let the formula make the final decision (clinical vs statistical)
insights.claim: To maximize accuracy, especially in low-validity environments, final decisions should be computed by a formula; letting interviewers or tasters override with global impressions usually lowers validity because they overweight personal impressions.
insights.evidence: Medical school interviews that also make the final admission decision likely reduce accuracy; wine experts who taste the wine do worse than weather formula; army interview final score computed with no further interviewer input.

insights.concept: Apgar score / checklists and simple rules
insights.claim: A simple standardized checklist of a few signs, each scored 0-2, gives all practitioners consistent standards where varied clinical judgment focused on different cues and missed danger signs.
insights.evidence: Virginia Apgar's five variables (heart rate, respiration, reflex, muscle tone, color) scored at one minute; 8+ good, 4 or below needs intervention; credited with reducing infant mortality; Gawande's Checklist Manifesto.

insights.claim: Combining a few valid predictors, standardized to comparable scales and weighted equally, predicts new cases as well as or better than optimal regression weights and beats expert judgment; useful algorithms need no prior statistical research.
insights.evidence: Dawes's 'Robust Beauty of Improper Linear Models'; marital stability predicted by lovemaking frequency minus quarrel frequency.

insights.claim: People reject algorithms out of preference for the natural and human, and judge errors caused by an algorithm more harshly than equal errors by humans, even when the algorithm makes fewer mistakes.
insights.evidence: Clinicians' derogatory adjectives for statistical method; organic apple preference despite identical properties; French wine circles' 'violent and hysterical' response to Ashenfelter's formula; child-death story poignancy.

insights.concept: illusion of skill / boundaries of expertise (feedback delay)
insights.claim: Experts correctly trust short-term hunches validated by immediate feedback but wrongly extend that confidence to long-term predictions they never had feedback to learn, and they don't know where their skill ends.
insights.evidence: Therapists' in-session hunches are often confirmed, yet they fail at long-term patient-outcome predictions and rejected Meehl's findings.

insights.concept: structured interview to combat halo effect
insights.claim: Replace global impressions with several relevant traits each scored separately from factual questions about past behavior, rated in a fixed sequence before moving on, then combined by a standard formula; assessors provide reliable measurements, not predictions.
insights.evidence: Kahneman's 1955 Israeli army interview: six traits (e.g., responsibility, sociability), factual questions (number of jobs, punctuality), 5-point scale each, fixed order.

insights.concept: Do It Yourself: formula-based selection (six independent traits, pre-committed rule)
insights.claim: Pick about six traits that are prerequisites for success and as independent of each other as possible. For each, write factual questions and score anchors on a 1–5 scale, add the scores, and commit beforehand to choosing the highest total even when you like another candidate more.
insights.evidence: Hiring a sales representative takes about half an hour of preparation. Research shows this beats unprepared interviews judged on 'I looked into his eyes and liked what I saw'.

insights.concept: halo effect control: one trait at a time
insights.claim: To keep first impressions from coloring later judgments, gather evidence and score one independent dimension at a time, in a fixed order, before moving to the next. Do not skip around.
insights.evidence: Interviewers rated six traits in a fixed order on a 5-point scale. The sales-rep hiring recipe repeats this rule.

insights.concept: structured interview / disciplined intuition (close your eyes after scoring)
insights.claim: Intuition does add value, but only after information is collected in a disciplined, objective way and separate traits are scored on their own. The intuitive global score given after that structured step predicted as well as the summed trait scores.
insights.evidence: Several hundred Israeli army recruit interviews: the sum of six factual trait ratings went from 'useless' to 'moderately useful', and a 'close your eyes' 1–5 score given afterward matched it. The two were then weighted equally.

insights.claim: Decision makers are tempted to make up special-case reasons to override a formula's ranking in favor of the option they personally like better. This usually lowers accuracy.
insights.evidence: In the hiring recipe: 'resist your wish to invent broken legs to change the ranking'.

insights.concept: pre-specified weights for evidence (judges vs. formulas)
insights.claim: Whenever a formula can replace human judgment, consider it. Decide in advance how much weight past-performance data gets, or the vivid interview impression will be overweighted.
insights.evidence: 'Speaking of Judges vs. Formulas' quotes: a simple combination of scores probably beats judgments that feel 'complex and subtle'.

insights.claim: Instead of a critique, reply and rejoinder where nobody concedes, people who disagree jointly write down their differences and the principles that would settle them, sometimes with an arbiter. This produced a shared map of when intuition can be trusted.
insights.evidence: Kahneman (heuristics and biases) and Gary Klein (NDM) spent 7–8 years writing 'Conditions for Intuitive Expertise: A Failure to Disagree'.

insights.claim: Intuition is cue-triggered retrieval of stored information. Knowing without knowing how is normal mental life, not magic, so the cue behind an expert's intuition can in principle be found by systematic inquiry.
insights.evidence: Simon's definition. Firefighters who sense danger, and instantly recognizing a friend. Klein and Kahneman think a proper search for the kouros cue would probably have succeeded.

insights.concept: looking the part (Harding): intuition by substitution
insights.claim: A confident intuitive prediction can come from answering an easier question, such as whether someone looks strong and decisive, instead of the real one, whether they will perform well. The confidence does not show that the intuition is valid.
insights.evidence: President Harding was elected mainly because he looked like a leader: square jawed and tall. The kouros contrasts with this, since the experts' gut sense of a fake was probably traceable to real cues.

insights.claim: Experts often generate a single plausible option through pattern recognition (System 1) and then mentally simulate it (System 2). They implement it if it works, modify it if it has flaws, and move to the next option only if it can't be fixed.
insights.evidence: Klein's fireground commanders usually considered one option, not a pair, drawing on more than a decade of patterns. The same process appears in chess.

insights.claim: Some intuitions, especially fear and aversion, form from a single experience and keep firing even when there is no reason to expect a repeat. Unease without any conscious memory of its source is labeled an 'intuition' only in hindsight, if something bad follows.
insights.evidence: A single dubious dish leaves a lasting reluctance to return to the restaurant. Kahneman still recalls a road-rage incident at the San Francisco airport ramp.

insights.concept: confidence is not a guide to validity
insights.claim: How confident someone feels in an intuition (including oneself) says little about whether it is right, because confidence comes from ease and coherence of the story, not accuracy.
insights.evidence: Pseudo-experts (stock pickers, pundits) are highly confident; WYSIATI produces confidence by ignoring unknowns; substituted judgments also feel confident.

insights.concept: two conditions for skilled intuition (environment regularity + opportunity to learn)
insights.claim: An intuition can be trusted only if the environment is regular enough to be predictable and the judge has had prolonged practice with feedback to learn those regularities; assess provenance, not the judgment itself.
insights.evidence: Chess, firefighters, nurses (valid) vs stock pickers, long-term political forecasters (zero-validity); art authentication analogy: check provenance.

insights.concept: algorithms beat humans in noisy environments
insights.claim: In low-validity settings statistical rules outperform humans because they detect weakly valid cues and apply them consistently, though neither is very accurate.
insights.evidence: Meehl's clinicians: best algorithms beat clinicians but were never highly accurate; no 'smoking gun' missed strong cue.

insights.concept: feedback quality and speed determine learnability
insights.claim: Intuitive skill develops only when feedback is quick and unambiguous and practice is ample; delayed, sparse or ambiguous feedback prevents learning even in regular environments.
insights.evidence: Braking on curves (immediate feedback) vs harbor pilot (delayed); anesthesiologists (fast feedback) vs radiologists (little feedback); therapists' long-term outcomes.

insights.claim: In unpredictable domains intuitive hits come from luck, and in 'wicked' environments experience teaches the wrong lessons, producing false feelings of infallibility.
insights.evidence: Hogarth/Lewis Thomas: physician predicted typhoid by palpating tongues with unwashed hands, spreading the disease and confirming his hunch.

insights.claim: Expertise is a collection of task-specific skills; experts overextend from tasks they learned (short-term anticipation) to tasks they never could learn (long-term forecasting), causing overconfidence.
insights.evidence: Therapist good at predicting next utterance but not patient outcome next year; financial expert not good at stock picking; Middle East expert doesn't know the future.

insights.claim: Trust an intuition only if the environment is regular enough and the expert had extensive practice with quick, clear feedback; subjective confidence is a poor index of accuracy.
insights.evidence: 'Speaking of Expert Intuition' prompts, e.g. start-up environment regularity vs base rates.

insights.claim: To extract a group's knowledge, collect each person's judgment confidentially before any open discussion, which uses available knowledge better than open discussion.
insights.evidence: Kahneman had team members write estimates privately on slips before tallying on the blackboard.

insights.claim: Forecast a project by first identifying a class of similar past cases and their outcome distribution (success rate, durations), rather than reasoning only from the specifics of your own plan.
insights.evidence: Seymour, asked about comparable curriculum teams, recalled ~40% never finished and finishers took 7-10 years, vs the team's own 1.5-2.5 year estimates.

insights.claim: The spontaneous inside view extrapolates from the plan in hand and early progress (WYSIATI), ignoring that early parts may be easier, motivation peaks early, and many improbable disruptions collectively make something going wrong likely.
insights.evidence: Team extrapolated from two written chapters; divorces, illnesses, bureaucratic crises caused long stalls nobody could foresee.

insights.claim: Faced with clear evidence that a project is likely to fail or take far longer, people carry on anyway, giving up rationality rather than the enterprise, because the warning lacks an immediately compelling reason to quit.
insights.evidence: After hearing 40% failure and 7+ years, the team debated briefly and continued as if nothing happened; nobody would have started under those odds.

insights.claim: Plans and forecasts tend to be unrealistically close to best-case scenarios and could be improved by consulting statistics of similar cases.
insights.evidence: Team's ~2-year estimate vs actual 8 years; book delivered after enthusiasm waned and never used.

insights.concept: base-rate neglect for one's own case ('every case is unique')
insights.claim: People holding case-specific information rarely feel the need for class statistics, and even when available, 'pallid' statistics are discarded when they clash with impressions; a knower may possess the base rate yet never apply it.
insights.evidence: Seymour knew other teams' history but did not use it until prompted; Nisbett & Borgida students ignored learned results; lawyer cousin: 'every case is unique'.

insights.concept: baseline prediction as anchor, then adjust
insights.claim: The baseline prediction (what you'd predict knowing only the category) should be the starting anchor; case-specific information then adjusts away from it in the appropriate direction, not replace it.
insights.evidence: Height of a NYC woman: start at average female height, adjust upward if her son is a starting basketball center; Seymour rated team slightly below average, so forecast should be slightly worse than the grim baseline.

insights.claim: Plans and forecasts cluster near best-case scenarios and ignore statistics of similar cases, producing large cost and schedule overruns that do not improve even as evidence accumulates.
insights.evidence: Scottish Parliament budget grew from £40M to ~£431M; rail projects (1969-1998) overestimated ridership by 106% in 90%+ of cases with 45% cost overruns; kitchen remodels expected $18,658, cost $38,769.

insights.claim: The cure for the planning fallacy is to use distributional information from similar ventures: pick a reference class, get its statistics for a baseline, then adjust only for specific reasons the case differs.
insights.evidence: Flyvbjerg's database of hundreds of transport projects' plans and outcomes, used to predict likely cost/time overruns.

insights.claim: Unrealistic budgets are often deliberately optimistic to win approval, knowing projects are rarely abandoned for overruns; customers also fail to foresee how their wishes will escalate, so the approver must demand an outside view.
insights.evidence: Contractors of kitchens and weapon systems profit mainly on additions to the original plan; executives competing for resources present rosy plans.

insights.concept: unknown unknowns / accountability for unanticipated difficulties
insights.claim: Well-run organizations reward precise execution and penalize failing to allow for difficulties, including ones that could not be specifically foreseen; there are too many ways a plan can fail to foresee them all. Budget reserves, though, can become self-fulfilling.
insights.evidence: Official: a budget reserve is to contractors as red meat to lions; 'she cannot foresee them all' quote.

insights.concept: optimistic bias as driver of risk taking
insights.claim: People often take on risky projects not because odds are favorable but because delusional optimism makes them overestimate benefits, underestimate costs, and imagine success while ignoring possible errors; influential leaders are likely optimistic and overconfident.
insights.evidence: Kahneman & Lovallo's decision theory; explains litigation, wars, small business openings; founders more sanguine than midlevel managers.

insights.concept: sunk-cost fallacy and lethargy (failure to re-plan)
insights.claim: Once effort is invested, teams continue without an explicit forecast, avoiding the embarrassment of quitting; outside-view facts are easier to ignore than in-project bad news, and absent a crisis no one reconsiders.
insights.evidence: Kahneman's curriculum team learned similar teams took 7-10 years or failed, yet carried on without discussion or a new forecast.

insights.claim: People who voluntarily take on big risks overestimate their odds of success, rarely research the true odds, and believe they are prudent when they are not.
insights.evidence: US small businesses survive 5 years at about 35%; entrepreneurs estimated 60% for similar businesses, 81% rated their own odds at 7/10 or higher, and 33% said zero chance of failure.

insights.concept: persistence after discouraging advice (sunk-cost escalation by optimists)
insights.claim: Optimists often ignore accurate negative evaluations and keep investing, which raises their losses.
insights.evidence: Inventor's Assistance Program: only 5 of 411 lowest-grade projects reached market, none successful; 47% of inventors told their project was hopeless kept going and doubled their losses.

insights.claim: Executives overrate their ability to run others' assets better; optimistic CEOs overpay in mergers, take on debt, and do more damage when they have more personal stake or have been celebrated.
insights.evidence: Malmendier & Tate: optimistic CEOs (measured by personal stock holdings) made value-destroying mergers; award-winning CEOs' firms later underperformed. Motel bought cheaply because six or seven owners had failed.

insights.claim: When asked whether they are better than average, people answer the easier question 'am I good at this?' without thinking about the average, so they rate themselves too high on tasks they do moderately well and too low on hard ones.
insights.evidence: 90% of drivers say they are better than average; people rate themselves below average at difficult tasks such as starting conversations with strangers.

insights.claim: Planners focus on their own plans and skills and leave out what competitors will do, which leads to excess entry where the average entrant loses money.
insights.evidence: Camerer & Lovallo; Disney chairman explaining that many big films open on the same holiday weekends because of 'hubris'. Founders say 80%+ of their outcome depends on their own actions.

insights.concept: WYSIATI as root of optimism (planning fallacy, illusion of control, overconfidence)
insights.claim: System 1 focuses on what is known and wanted: the goal, our plan and our skill. It leaves out base rates, others' plans, luck, and unknowns, which produces the planning fallacy, illusion of control and overconfidence.
insights.evidence: Kahneman's four-part list of focus/neglect pairs in the Competition Neglect section.

insights.claim: Experts give confidence intervals that are far too narrow because estimates are built from what comes to mind; honest intervals look embarrassingly wide and are socially penalized.
insights.evidence: Duke CFO survey: 11,600 S&P forecasts with near-zero correlation to outcomes; 80% intervals produced 67% surprises instead of 20%; calibrated intervals (-10% to +30%) would be more than 4x wider.

insights.claim: Organizations reward confident experts and punish honest admissions of ignorance, which pushes overconfident forecasts and riskier decisions.
insights.evidence: A CFO giving an honest -10% to +30% range would be laughed out of the room; Truman's wish for a 'one-armed economist'; the most confident CFOs' firms took more risk.

insights.concept: bold forecasts and timid decisions (risk unawareness)
insights.claim: Risk takers usually do not enjoy big gambles more than others. They simply notice the risks less. Optimism, cognitive limits and social pressure combine to produce risks people would avoid if they knew the odds.
insights.evidence: Phrase coined by Kahneman and Lovallo; competition among experts before the financial crisis encouraged collective blindness to risk.

insights.claim: Optimism may hurt decisions but helps execution by giving resilience: taking credit for successes and little blame for failures. Separate the optimism used for deciding from the optimism used for persisting.
insights.evidence: Seligman's training in an optimistic explanatory style for jobs with frequent failure, such as cold-call insurance sales; scientists need a 'delusional sense of significance'.

insights.claim: Clients, markets and media reward experts who sound sure and punish those who admit uncertainty, so overconfidence spreads. People who were 'completely certain' can still be wrong often.
insights.evidence: ICU physicians who were 'completely certain' of a diagnosis were wrong 40% of the time when checked against autopsies; Tetlock found the most overconfident experts got the most TV appearances.

insights.concept: confidence reflects story coherence, not evidence quality
insights.claim: How confident we feel depends on how well our story hangs together, not on how much good information backs it. Training only reduces overconfidence a little. Practice on past cases with known outcomes and weighing competing explanations help somewhat.
insights.evidence: Royal Dutch Shell geologists grew less overconfident after training on past drilling cases with known outcomes; considering competing hypotheses reduced overconfidence but did not remove it.

insights.claim: As a team moves toward a decision, especially once the leader shows her preference, people stop voicing doubts and start treating them as disloyal. Only supporters speak, so the group grows more confident.
insights.evidence: Kahneman's description of team dynamics, used to explain why the premortem helps.

insights.claim: Just before the group formally commits to a plan, knowledgeable people imagine it is a year later and the plan has failed badly, then take 5-10 minutes each to write how it failed. This frees them to voice doubts and points their imagination toward threats.
insights.evidence: Gary Klein's procedure; a CEO at Davos said it was worth the trip just to hear it.

insights.concept: illusion of control and competitor neglect
insights.claim: Overconfident planners believe they control more than they do, underestimate obstacles, and ignore what competitors will do.
insights.evidence: 'Speaking of Optimism' phrases on illusion of control, competitor neglect and overconfidence.

insights.claim: Economic theory models agents as rational, selfish and with stable tastes; real people have System 1, see only available information (WYSIATI), are sometimes generous, and mispredict their own future preferences.
insights.evidence: Bruno Frey's essay opening line; Thaler's Econs/Humans label.

insights.claim: Kahneman and Tversky used their own immediate intuitive choices on simple problems to generate fast hypotheses about how most people choose, explicitly treating these as hunches requiring later verification.
insights.evidence: Coin toss for $100 vs $46 sure: both picked the sure thing and assumed others would too, then tested.

insights.claim: Expected utility theory prescribes how choices should be made from axioms of rationality; prospect theory instead describes how people actually choose and documents systematic violations of those axioms.
insights.evidence: Apple/banana axiom; prospect theory published in Econometrica as descriptive model built from a dozen observed facts.

insights.claim: Large changes in preference can result from inconsequential variations in how a choice problem is worded.
insights.evidence: Mentioned as the subject of Kahneman and Tversky's Science paper two years after prospect theory.

insights.claim: Subjective intensity tracks ratios rather than absolute amounts: multiplying a stimulus by a fixed factor yields the same psychological increment, so money changes are felt relative to current wealth.
insights.evidence: Fechner's law (10→100 and 100→1,000 add equal intensity); Bernoulli: 10 ducats to someone with 100 feels like 20 to someone with 200; '30% raise'.

insights.concept: expected value vs expected utility (risk aversion from diminishing marginal utility)
insights.claim: People evaluate gambles not by weighted-average money outcomes but by weighted utilities; because each extra unit of wealth adds less utility, people prefer a sure thing even over a gamble of slightly higher expected value, paying a premium to avoid uncertainty.
insights.evidence: Most prefer $80 sure over 80% $100/20% $10 (EV $82); Table 3: 1M→4M adds 50 utility, 4M→7M adds 24, so sure 4M (60) beats 50/50 1M/7M (47).

insights.concept: insurance as risk transfer (wealth-dependent risk attitude)
insights.claim: The same loss hurts a poorer party much more in utility than a richer one, so the poorer party rationally pays a premium to transfer risk to the richer one.
insights.evidence: Losing 1 million costs 4 utility points at 10M but 18 points at 3M; St. Petersburg spice-shipment insurance (5 of 100 ships lost).

insights.claim: Happiness and evaluations depend on changes relative to a reference point, not on absolute states; theories that ignore the reference point make wrong predictions. Errors of a theory hide in what it tacitly assumes.
insights.evidence: Jack (1M→5M) is elated and Jill (9M→5M) despondent despite equal wealth; same sound feels loud after a whisper, faint after a roar.

insights.claim: People evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point (often current state), not as absolute final states; the same end state can feel great to one person and terrible to another.
insights.evidence: Anthony (1M) vs Betty (4M) choosing a sure 2M vs a 50/50 gamble for 1M or 4M; Jack and Jill; loudness and gray patch perception.

insights.concept: risk seeking in the domain of losses (reflection)
insights.claim: People are risk averse when choosing among gains but become risk seeking when all options are losses, preferring a gamble over a sure loss.
insights.evidence: Get $900 sure vs 90% of $1,000 (most take sure); lose $900 sure vs 90% to lose $1,000 (most gamble); Betty; entrepreneurs and generals with all-bad options; alimony example.

insights.concept: evaluate changes, not states (gains and losses framing)
insights.claim: To predict how people will choose or feel, model outcomes as changes (gains/losses) from a reference, since utility of a change cannot be derived from final wealth and losses weigh differently than equal gains.
insights.evidence: Utility theory treats losing $500 as merely the negative of winning $500, yet the loss hurts more; people cannot even assess their wealth within tens of thousands of dollars.

insights.claim: Once a theory is accepted and used as a thinking tool, its flaws become very hard to notice; contradicting observations are explained away by assuming a good explanation exists somewhere.
insights.evidence: Bernoulli's utility theory survived ~200 years despite obvious counterexamples like Anthony/Betty; gain-loss risk asymmetry was ignored because the theory couldn't accommodate it.

insights.concept: outsider/naive questioning to break theory-induced blindness
insights.claim: Ignorance of a dominant theory plus knowledge from another field (psychophysics) let Kahneman see an absurd assumption experts accepted; a sign of real progress is no longer understanding why the obvious was missed.
insights.evidence: Kahneman questioned measuring utility of wealth with penny gambles; Tversky recalled Markowitz's neglected idea of utility of changes in wealth.

insights.claim: Outcomes are judged as gains or losses relative to a reference point, not as final states. The reference point can be the status quo, an expectation or an entitlement such as colleagues' bonuses. Options that are identical in final terms get different choices when the reference point moves.
insights.evidence: Problems 3 and 4: given $1,000 vs $2,000, the same final options produced a sure-thing preference in one and a gamble preference in the other. Three bowls of water: the same lukewarm water feels hot to one hand and cold to the other.

insights.claim: The same absolute change feels smaller the further it is from the reference point, for both gains and losses. This makes people risk seeking when every option is a loss: a sure loss hurts more than its probability-weighted share of a larger loss.
insights.evidence: A light turned on in a dark room vs a bright room. $900 vs $1,000 feels like a smaller gap than $100 vs $200. Most prefer a 90% chance to lose $1,000 over a sure loss of $900.

insights.claim: Losses loom larger than gains, roughly 1.5–2.5 times as large, so people reject mixed gambles with positive expected value. The ratio rises with the stakes and becomes infinite when the loss could be ruinous.
insights.evidence: A coin toss where you lose $100 or win $150 is rejected by most people. The smallest gain that balances a $100 loss is usually about $200.

insights.claim: When a possible loss is ruinous or threatens one's way of life, loss aversion becomes very large or infinite. No upside justifies some risks.
insights.evidence: A self-test asking what gain offsets 50-50 losses of $10, $500 and $2,000: the ratio rises with stakes and is unbounded for ruinous losses.

insights.concept: think like a trader (reducing loss aversion)
insights.claim: Taking the perspective of a professional risk taker, who does not react emotionally to every fluctuation, lowers loss aversion and the physiological arousal caused by losses.
insights.evidence: Participants told to 'think like a trader' became less loss averse and showed sharply reduced emotional arousal to losses.

insights.claim: A dominant theory can hide obvious anomalies for a very long time. Rabin proved that explaining small-stakes risk aversion through utility of wealth implies absurd rejection of very favorable large gambles.
insights.evidence: Anyone who rejects a 50% chance to lose $100 against a 50% chance to win $200 would, under utility theory, also reject a 50% chance to lose $200 against a 50% chance to win $20,000. Bernoulli's flaw went unnoticed for over 250 years.

insights.claim: Once a model is accepted, people stop seeing its flaws. This happened with expected utility, with prospect theory, and with textbook indifference curves that never show the reference point.
insights.evidence: Indifference maps have been in textbooks for a century and leave out the current position. Prospect theory's own flaws went unseen while it was accepted.

insights.claim: When a large gain is very likely, the expectation becomes a new reference point, so getting nothing feels like a big loss rather than zero. Disappointment is real, and people anticipate it when they choose.
insights.evidence: Winning nothing barely matters with a one-in-a-million chance at $1M, but stings with a 90% chance at $1M. Compare an informally promised raise that never comes.

insights.claim: An outcome is felt partly against the option that was rejected. A gamble that loses after a large sure thing was turned down brings regret on top of the loss. Options are not judged independently.
insights.evidence: A 90% chance of $1M versus a sure $50, compared with a 90% chance of $1M versus a sure $150,000. Losing in the second case means regretting a 'greedy' choice.

insights.claim: Realism alone does not make a model worth using. Add a more complex tool only when it gives new predictions that come true and the simpler one cannot.
insights.evidence: Regret theories were realistic but had little impact because they added few distinctive predictions. Prospect theory won because the reference point and loss aversion predicted things expected utility could not.

insights.concept: loss aversion / status quo bias (reference point)
insights.claim: People judge changes as gains or losses from where they stand now, and the losses count about twice as much. So they hold on to the status quo, find concessions painful, and turn down good offers.
insights.evidence: The Albert and Ben hedonic twins both prefer to keep the job they ended up with. Unemployed workers want about 90% of their previous wage, a demand that drops less than 10% in a year. Labor talks center on the existing contract.

insights.concept: status quo bias (loss aversion favoring the reference situation)
insights.claim: Once an option becomes the current state, moving away is evaluated as losses vs gains, and since losses loom larger, people favor staying put and favor small over large changes; preferences shift with the reference point.
insights.evidence: Hedonic twins Albert (raise) and Ben (extra vacation) were indifferent at first but each refuses to switch after adapting.

insights.claim: Models that represent value only as current states (indifference curves, Bernoulli wealth) omit the reference point and history, so they fail to predict status quo preference.
insights.evidence: Standard indifference maps omit current income/leisure; unemployed accept min wage ~90% of prior wage.

insights.claim: Owning an item raises the price required to give it up well above the price one would pay to acquire it, because giving up is coded as a loss; the gap is about 2:1.
insights.evidence: Professor R's wine ($35 max buy vs $100 min sell); concert ticket; mugs: Sellers $7.12 vs Buyers $2.87, trades less than half predicted; pen/chocolate swap ~10%.

insights.concept: held for use vs held for exchange
insights.claim: Loss aversion and the endowment effect appear for goods held for use but not for goods held as proxies for exchange (money, merchant stock, tokens), and experienced traders lose the effect.
insights.evidence: $5 bill for five singles, shoe merchant, Vernon Smith token markets trading as theory predicts; John List's baseball-card traders lose reluctance with experience.

insights.claim: Sellers and Choosers face identical final outcomes yet value the item very differently; reframing a give-up decision as a neutral choice between two options removes the loss emotion.
insights.evidence: Mug study: Choosers valued the mug at $3.12 vs Sellers $7.12 though both could leave with mug or money.

insights.claim: Across riskless and risky domains, losses weigh about twice as much as equivalent gains; e.g., price increases reduce purchases about twice as much as decreases raise them.
insights.evidence: Seller price ~2x Chooser/Buyer price; household responses to egg, orange juice, fish price changes.

insights.claim: Rationally only current market value matters, but owners who bought high set higher asking prices and hold out longer in a down market because they code selling as a loss vs purchase price.
insights.evidence: Boston condo downturn study: owners with higher purchase prices asked more, waited longer, eventually got more.

insights.concept: endowment effect (and its disappearance with trading experience)
insights.claim: Owning a good, especially having held it physically for a while, makes people reluctant to trade it; experienced traders who treat goods as exchangeable show no such effect.
insights.evidence: List's mug/chocolate swap at baseball-card conventions: 18% of novices vs 48% of experienced traders swapped; Knetsch found the effect needs prior physical possession.

insights.concept: living below the reference point (decision making under poverty)
insights.claim: When one is below the reference point, all choices are between losses: small gains feel like reduced losses and every expenditure is the loss of another good, so costs feel like losses.
insights.evidence: Studies of decision making under poverty; misers who treat any dollar spent as a loss; US vs UK students differ in buy/sell price gaps.

insights.claim: Veteran traders avoid the endowment effect by asking how much they want the item compared with other things they could have instead, which makes the get/give-up asymmetry irrelevant.
insights.evidence: Experienced traders at List's conventions traded freely; Kahneman says they learned to ask the Econ's question.

insights.claim: Each side weighs its concessions as losses and the counterpart's concessions as gains, so trades that are fair feel unfavorable and negotiations stall.
insights.evidence: 'Speaking of' example: negotiations going nowhere because both sides struggle to concede even for something in return; refusing to sell a house below purchase price.

insights.concept: negativity dominance (bad is stronger than good)
insights.claim: System 1 prioritizes threats and bad information: they are detected faster, processed more thoroughly, form impressions faster and resist disconfirmation more than good ones; loss aversion is one manifestation.
insights.evidence: Masked fearful eyes activate the amygdala unconsciously; angry face pops out of happy crowd; bad words grab attention faster; Rozin's cockroach in cherries; Gottman's 5:1 good-to-bad ratio; friendship ruined by one act.

insights.claim: Because bad interactions weigh far more, stable relationships need good interactions to outnumber bad ones by at least 5 to 1; avoiding the negative matters more than adding positives.
insights.evidence: Gottman's marital research; a friendship built over years can be ruined by a single action.

insights.claim: A goal acts as a reference point: falling short is a loss felt much more strongly than exceeding it is a gain, so people push to reach a target and then ease off, sometimes against economic logic.
insights.evidence: NY cabdrivers with daily earnings targets work long on slow days and quit early on rainy, high-demand days; golfers putt harder to avoid bogey than for birdie (par as reference).

insights.claim: A goal or target acts as a reference point: falling short feels like a loss and is fought harder than exceeding it, so effort is front-loaded to hit the target and slackens after.
insights.evidence: Pope & Schweitzer: 2.5M PGA putts, success 3.6% higher putting for par than for birdie; Tiger Woods would gain ~1 stroke and ~$1M/season.

insights.claim: In renegotiating existing terms, every change is a concession; each side feels its own concessions as losses weighing more than the other's concessions as gains, so agreements stall, especially over a shrinking pie.
insights.evidence: Labor, trade and arms-limitation renegotiations; negotiators feign attachment to bargaining chips and invoke reciprocity for 'painful' concessions.

insights.claim: Because losers fight harder than winners, incumbents usually win and reforms with net benefit end up diluted, costlier and less effective, often via grandfather clauses protecting current stakeholders.
insights.evidence: Territory holders almost always win challenges within seconds; reorganizations, tax simplification, and cost cuts protected by attrition or future-only cuts.

insights.claim: A well-understood theoretical concept can generate precise, surprising predictions worth testing that intuition alone would never propose.
insights.evidence: Loss aversion predicted the par-vs-birdie putting gap, which surprised even professional golfers.

insights.claim: Existing price, wage or rent is a reference entitlement; imposing losses on others relative to it purely because one can is judged unfair and punished, while passing on one's own threatened losses or not sharing gains is accepted.
insights.evidence: Snow shovel $15→$20 after storm: 82% unfair; cutting current worker $9→$7: 83% unfair, paying a replacement $7: 73% acceptable; cutting wages when profits fall seen as fair.

insights.concept: actual losses vs foregone gains asymmetry
insights.claim: People and legal systems treat out-of-pocket losses as far weightier than foregone gains; possession and the reference point carry moral status.
insights.evidence: Cohen & Knetsch: merchants compensated for incurred costs of goods lost in transit but rarely for lost profits; 'possession is nine-tenths of the law'; Zamir's justification.

insights.claim: Fairness violations have real costs: victims and even bystanders retaliate (altruistic punishment is neurally rewarding), and customers who feel they paid more than the new reference price buy less.
insights.evidence: Catalog showing lower price for recently bought items cut future purchases 15% (~$90 per customer), exceeding gains from the lower price; fMRI of altruistic punishers.

insights.claim: Rationally, each outcome should be weighted exactly by its probability (expected value/utility); von Neumann and Morgenstern proved any other weighting yields inconsistencies, even though it is poor psychology.
insights.evidence: EV of '20% win $1,000 and 75% win $100' is $275; four equal 5% improvements should add equal utility.

insights.concept: System 1 automatic weighting of global evaluations
insights.claim: When forming an overall judgment of a complex object or prospect, System 1 silently assigns weights to features or outcomes; we are mostly observers of the resulting evaluation rather than deliberate weighers.
insights.evidence: Evaluating a car (economy, comfort, looks) or a son-in-law (rich, handsome, reliable).

insights.claim: Near-certain outcomes are underweighted relative to true certainty, so people pay a large premium to turn 95–98% into 100%. It is even stronger than the possibility effect.
insights.evidence: 95% lawsuit worth $950k EV, yet a $910k sure offer is tempting (structured settlements); 98% weighted 87.1; anxiety of 1% chance of not winning exceeds hope of 1% chance to win.

insights.claim: Moving from impossibility to a small chance is a qualitative shift, so unlikely outcomes get far more decision weight than their probability (2% weighted ~8). This drives lottery buying and paying heavily to eliminate small risks.
insights.evidence: 0→5% chance at $1M feels far bigger than 5→10%; Table 4: 2% chance has decision weight 8.1; 5% amputation risk feels more than half as bad as 10%.

insights.claim: Attention to a threat produces worry not proportional to probability, so reducing risk feels inadequate and people pay far beyond expected value to bring it to exactly zero.
insights.evidence: People pay much more than expected value to eliminate small risks; overweighting small probabilities makes insurance attractive.

insights.claim: Preferences flip when a common improvement is added to both options, revealing the certainty effect; restating choices as an urn of marbles exposes the inconsistency, which even expert economists missed.
insights.evidence: A: 61%/$520k vs 63%/$500k → left; B: 98%/$520k vs 100%/$500k → right; B equals A with 37 white marbles turned red in each urn.

insights.concept: insensitivity to intermediate and small probabilities
insights.claim: Decision weights compress the 5–95% range into roughly two-thirds of its rational span, and people barely distinguish among tiny risks; very rare events are either ignored (weight zero) or, when attention is drawn to them, overweighted.
insights.evidence: 5–95% maps to weights 13.2–79.3; cancer risk 0.001% vs 0.00001% feels the same though it is 3,000 vs 30 US cases; nuclear meltdown ignored until focal.

insights.claim: People pay far more to eliminate a risk completely than to reduce it by the same or a larger proportion. Removing the worry, not lowering the risk, is what they value.
insights.evidence: Parents paid $2.38 to cut insecticide poisonings from 15 to 5 per 10,000 bottles but $8.09 to eliminate them.

insights.claim: Risk attitude depends on two things: whether the outcome is a gain or a loss, and whether its probability is high or low. People are risk averse for likely gains and unlikely losses, and risk seeking for unlikely gains and likely losses.
insights.evidence: Figure 13: a 95% chance to win $10,000 vs a sure $9,500 (risk averse); lotteries (risk seeking); insurance (risk averse); a 95% chance of a loss (risk seeking).

insights.claim: Small probabilities get far more weight than they deserve. This makes people gamble on long shots for big gains (lotteries) and overpay to insure against unlikely large losses. They are buying a dream or peace of mind, not expected value.
insights.evidence: Lottery tickets bought for the right to dream; insurance bought for more than its expected value; a minuscule gas-explosion risk people still want mitigated.

insights.concept: risk seeking in the domain of losses (desperate gambles / failure to cut losses)
insights.claim: When every option is bad, people reject a sure loss and take a gamble that will probably make things worse in the hope of escaping entirely. Two causes work together: diminishing sensitivity makes the sure loss feel nearly as bad as the bigger loss, and a 90% probability gets a decision weight of only about 71. This turns manageable failures into disasters.
insights.evidence: A loss of $900 feels more than 90% as bad as a loss of $1,000. Businesses waste their remaining assets chasing a superior technology, and losing sides keep fighting wars after defeat is certain.

insights.concept: bargaining asymmetry from the fourfold pattern (gambling in the shadow of the law)
insights.claim: You can predict negotiation outcomes from each side's cell. A strong-case plaintiff (likely gain) is risk averse and a weak-case defendant (likely loss) is risk seeking, so the defendant has the stronger hand. In frivolous suits the roles reverse, and plaintiffs get more than the statistics justify.
insights.evidence: Guthrie's analysis was confirmed with law students, practicing judges, and real settlement negotiations.

insights.concept: long-view policy over repeated decisions (avoid systematic deviations from expected value)
insights.claim: Each fourfold-pattern choice can feel reasonable, but when the same type of decision repeats, systematic deviations from expected value (in either direction) add up to real losses. Decide by a policy applied to the whole class of cases, not case by case.
insights.evidence: NYC faces 200 frivolous suits a year, each with a 5% chance of a $1M loss. Litigating all of them costs $10M; settling all for $100K each costs $20M.

insights.claim: A vivid threat that media and conversation keep repeating becomes very easy to call to mind. It sets off automatic emotion and an urge to protect yourself that has nothing to do with the real, tiny probability. Knowing the facts through System 2 does not switch this off.
insights.evidence: Israel had 23 bus bombings and 236 deaths against 1.3M daily riders, yet people avoided buses. Kahneman himself sped away from buses at red lights.

insights.concept: possibility effect / insensitivity to probability level
insights.claim: When an outcome is emotional, people respond to whether it is possible at all, not to how likely it is. Halving the risk barely changes how anxious people feel, and fear of a shock is unrelated to the chance of getting it.
insights.evidence: One bomber versus two bombers: risk halved, but people do not feel safer. Heart-rate fear of an electric shock was uncorrelated with the shock's probability. Lottery buyers enjoy the fantasy of winning.

insights.concept: overestimation vs overweighting of unlikely events
insights.claim: Judging the probability of a rare event (overestimation) and the weight it gets in a choice (overweighting) are separate things. Both come from focused attention, confirmatory retrieval and cognitive ease, so the judged probability tracks how fluently a plausible scenario comes to mind.
insights.evidence: Asking for the probability of a third-party US president, compared with asking what you would pay for a $1,000 bet on it. When asked about a baby's hospital discharge, attention moves to the unusual alternative (medical problems).

insights.claim: A rare event's probability is most often overestimated when its alternative is left vague. Judging each specific option one at a time inflates each one, and the totals go well beyond 100%. Making the alternatives equally specific removes the inflation.
insights.evidence: Fox's NBA fans: probabilities for the eight teams summed to 240%, and cash equivalents summed to $287 for a $160 payoff, which guarantees a $127 loss. The East-vs-West question summed to 100%.

insights.concept: decision weights flatter than probabilities (prospect theory)
insights.claim: In prospect theory, decision weights respond weakly to probability: a 90% chance gets a weight of about 71 and a 10% chance about 19, a ratio of 3.8 rather than 9. For non-money outcomes like roses or chores, sensitivity is even lower because there is no expected-value anchor. Stating a dollar value does not fix this.
insights.evidence: Measured weights of 71.2 and 18.6. Princeton studies: for 84% vs 21% chances, roses were valued with less sensitivity than $59. Painting an apartment vs cleaning bathroom stalls showed similar weights, so emotional intensity is not the cause.

insights.concept: planning fallacy via specific success vs diffuse failure
insights.claim: Success for a plan is a single specific story that is easy to imagine, while failure is spread over countless ways things can go wrong. So entrepreneurs and investors both overestimate their chances and put too much weight on those estimates.
insights.evidence: Kahneman extends Fox's focal-event finding to project forecasts and to entrepreneurs or investors judging prospects.

insights.claim: People focus on the number of winning or bad cases and pay little attention to the total, so they judge by numerators rather than ratios.
insights.evidence: 30-40% of students chose urn B (8 red of 100) over urn A (1 red of 10), despite 8% < 10%.

insights.claim: A rich, fluent mental image of an outcome, emotional or not, makes decision weights insensitive to probability by enhancing both the possibility and certainty effects.
insights.evidence: Roses prize valued similarly at 21% and 84% even with price given; predicted same for a blue cardboard envelope holding $59.

insights.claim: The same risk carries more decision weight when stated as relative frequency (1 of 1,000) than as an abstract probability or percentage, because it evokes a concrete individual; this format can be used to manipulate.
insights.evidence: '1,286 of 10,000' judged more dangerous than '24.14%'; clinicians denied discharge 41% vs 21% with frequency vs probability format; DNA false match '1 in 1,000' vs '0.1%'.

insights.concept: salience-driven overestimation and overweighting of rare events
insights.claim: Focal attention and salience, raised by mere mention, vividness, explicit description or obsessive concern, make unlikely events both overestimated and overweighted; memory's confirmatory bias tries to make the considered event true.
insights.evidence: Explicit '99% win / 1% nothing' guarantees attention; bus in Jerusalem, roses, '1 of 1,000'; tourists overestimate tsunamis.

insights.concept: underweighting of rare events in choice from experience
insights.claim: When decisions are based on accumulated experience rather than descriptions, rare events are underweighted or neglected, often because they were never experienced; global impressions are biased toward typical and recent instances.
insights.evidence: Button experiments show no overweighting, frequent underweighting; Californians and earthquakes, bankers before 2007, tepid response to environmental threats; Adele vs Brian.

insights.concept: disaster cycle / single-scenario focus debiasing (make probabilities add to 100%)
insights.claim: Focusing on a single scenario inflates its probability; laying out specific alternatives and forcing their probabilities to sum to 100% counters this, and one should expect a cycle of exaggeration followed by neglect.
insights.evidence: Speaking of Rare Events: 'set up specific alternatives and make the probabilities add up to 100%'; familiar disaster cycle.

insights.claim: Stating a risk as a frequency of people (e.g., 1 death per 1,000) makes it feel larger than the same probability stated as a percentage. Communicators can use this to raise worry.
insights.evidence: 'Speaking of' quote: a risk described as 1 death per 1,000 because the speakers are counting on denominator neglect.

insights.concept: inconsistent risk attitudes: risk averse for gains, risk seeking for losses (fourfold pattern cost)
insights.claim: System 1 is drawn to sure gains and repelled by sure losses. People therefore pay a premium to lock in gains and also pay a premium to avoid sure losses. Both premiums come out of the same pocket, so holding both attitudes at once is costly.
insights.evidence: Large majorities prefer a sure $240 over a gamble worth $250 (EV), yet prefer a 75% chance to lose $1,000 over a sure loss of $750.

insights.claim: People decide on several concurrent choices one at a time, as each comes up. The resulting combination can be dominated by another combination. Looking at all the decisions together as one choice is never worse and is usually better.
insights.evidence: Decision i (A sure +$240 vs. B 25% of $1,000) and decision ii (C sure -$750 vs. D 75% of -$1,000): 73% chose A+D, yet B+C (25% win $250 / 75% lose $750) dominates A+D (25% win $240 / 75% lose $760). Only 3% chose B+C.

insights.claim: An option dominates another when it is better or equal on every outcome. Once a decision is restated as a single combined choice, the dominance is easy to spot, even though it was invisible in the separate parts.
insights.evidence: BC (25% +$250 / 75% -$750) vs. AD (25% +$240 / 75% -$760): this is an 'easy' choice once combined, but most people picked the dominated AD when it was split up.

insights.claim: A small favorable gamble that feels unacceptable alone because of loss aversion becomes clearly attractive when bundled with many similar ones. Aggregation lowers the chance of any loss quickly, so loss aversion matters less.
insights.evidence: Lose $100/win $200 coin toss rejected once but accepted x100. 100 bets give an expected $5,000 with a 1/2,300 chance of losing. Sam (losses weighted x2) values 1 toss at 0, 2 tosses at $50, and 5 tosses at a $203.125 cash equivalent with an 18.75% loss chance.

insights.concept: WYSIATI and effort aversion drive sequential, as-they-arise decisions
insights.claim: Because only the problem in front of us comes to mind, and combining problems takes effort, people decide as problems come up. They do this even when told explicitly to consider the problems together, so consistent preferences cannot be expected unless they are enforced.
insights.evidence: Respondents who were told to examine both decisions first still did not compute the four combinations. With 5 binary decisions, the broad frame has 32 options and the narrow sequence is only one of them.

insights.concept: risk policy / 'you are not on your deathbed' mantra
insights.claim: To counter loss aversion on small bets, treat each small favorable gamble as one of the many such opportunities you will meet. Do not treat it as a one-off final decision. Adopt a standing policy of accepting them when stakes are small relative to total resources.
insights.evidence: Kahneman's sermon to Sam: 'Are you on your deathbed?' Small attractive gambles will keep recurring, and seeing them as a bundle is a large financial favor.

insights.concept: broad framing / 'think like a trader' (you win a few, you lose a few)
insights.claim: Treating a small favorable risk as one of many in a portfolio reduces the emotional sting of losses and the loss aversion that would reject it; valid only if bets are independent, small relative to total wealth, and not long shots.
insights.evidence: Students told to 'imagine yourself as a trader' vs 'as if it were the only one' showed blunted skin-conductance responses to losses and took more risks.

insights.claim: Each manager is loss averse within their own domain, so the organization as a whole takes too little risk; viewing all bets together from the top reveals the aggregate is favorable.
insights.evidence: 25 division heads all refused a 50/50 lose-X/gain-2X bet; the CEO wanted all of them accepted.

insights.concept: outside view + risk policy as opposing correctives
insights.claim: The planning fallacy (overoptimism) and loss aversion (overcaution) push in opposite directions; the outside view fixes the first, the risk policy the second, and combining both should be the goal rather than relying on them canceling.
insights.evidence: Conceptual discussion linking earlier planning-fallacy chapter with risk policies.

insights.claim: Frequently monitoring short-term outcomes amplifies loss aversion because frequent small losses hurt more than equal gains please, causing churning; aggregated, infrequent feedback and commitments not to change position improve decisions and results.
insights.evidence: Investors checking daily vs quarterly; aggregated feedback recipients are less risk averse and end up richer; 'locking in' investments improves performance.

insights.claim: Instead of constructing a fresh preference for each risky choice, adopt a standing rule applied whenever the category recurs; it is a broad frame that accepts occasional losses for long-run advantage.
insights.evidence: 'Always take the highest deductible'; 'never buy extended warranties'.

insights.claim: People keep separate emotional accounts and score gains and losses in them; this narrow framing aids self-control but causes refusal to cut losses, regret aversion, an omission/commission asymmetry, and agent conflicts of interest.
insights.evidence: Earmarked savings vs credit-card debt held simultaneously; golfers keep a separate account per hole.

insights.claim: Investors prefer selling winners over losers to close accounts as gains, a narrow-framing error; a rational agent looks at the whole portfolio and future prospects.
insights.evidence: Need cash for wedding: sell Blueberry Tiles (+$5,000) or Tiffany Motors (-$5,000)? Most sell the winner.

insights.claim: Past unrecoverable costs make closing an account at a loss feel worse, pushing people to persist; System 2 must ask whether it would choose the same if the cost had not been paid.
insights.evidence: Fan who paid for his ticket is more likely to drive into a blizzard than one who got it free.

insights.claim: People sell winning assets to 'close the account' at a gain and keep losers, even though taxes and momentum make selling losers better. It is narrow framing through mental accounts.
insights.evidence: Selling the loser Tiffany instead of the winner Blueberry gives about 3.4% extra after-tax return. US investors sell more losers only in December.

insights.concept: escalation of commitment / agency problem (fresh-eyes replacement)
insights.claim: The person who 'owns' a failing project has a personal reason to keep gambling with the organization's resources. Someone without those mental accounts can judge current opportunities better, and formally teaching the sunk-cost error helps people walk away.
insights.evidence: Boards replace CEOs who are tied to prior decisions. Not because the new CEO is more competent, but because she carries no old accounts. Economics and business graduate students abandon failing projects more readily.

insights.claim: Putting more resources into a failing effort to justify what was already spent, when better options exist. Only future consequences should count.
insights.evidence: A company spent $50M on a project that is now behind schedule and needs $60M more, while a better new project exists. Driving into a blizzard because the tickets are paid for.

insights.claim: Regret is strongest when an alternative is easy to imagine, which is usually after an abnormal or out-of-character act. Blame from others is judged against social norms instead, so the two can diverge.
insights.evidence: Brown rarely picks up hitchhikers and Smith often does; both are robbed. 88% say Brown feels more regret, but 77% say Smith is blamed more. Plane-crash stories about last-minute passengers.

insights.claim: People expect more regret and blame from bad outcomes that follow leaving the default than from the same outcome reached by staying put. What matters is the deviation from the default, not commission as such.
insights.evidence: Paul (stayed) vs George (switched) end with the same loss, and 92% say George feels worse. In blackjack, saying 'yes' to either 'hit?' or 'stand?' brings more regret. A coach is expected to act after a loss.

insights.claim: The fear of future regret and blame pushes decision makers toward conventional, risk-averse options, even when an unconventional one probably has better expected value.
insights.evidence: Reminding consumers of regret makes them favor brand names. Fund managers clean out unconventional stocks at year end. A physician avoids a promising but unusual treatment.

insights.concept: responsibility-amplified loss aversion (WTA/WTP gap for safety)
insights.claim: Loss aversion, usually about 2:1, becomes far stronger for health or safety and when giving something up would make you responsible for a bad outcome. This creates incoherent 'never trade' stances that can lower total safety.
insights.evidence: Thaler: people ask about 50 times more to accept a 1/1000 disease risk than they will pay for a vaccine against it. Over two-thirds of parents would not accept any discount for an insecticide risk that rises from 15 to 16 per 10,000.

insights.claim: People refuse to accept even a tiny increase in risk in exchange for money or other benefits. This wastes a limited safety budget that could reduce bigger risks elsewhere, and it may come more from fear of regret than from a wish to optimize safety.
insights.evidence: More than two-thirds of parents would not buy a slightly less safe insecticide at any price. Money saved could have bought a safer car seat or socket covers.

insights.claim: A rule that bans any action that might cause harm puts the whole burden of proving safety on the innovator. In its strict form it is costly and can paralyze action, but it rests on loss-averse moral intuitions from System 1.
insights.evidence: Sunstein lists innovations that would have failed the test: airplanes, antibiotics, X-rays, vaccines, refrigeration.

insights.claim: To reduce regret later, say explicitly what you might regret before you decide. Avoid the half-considered middle, which feeds hindsight: either be very thorough or deliberately casual. Also, people expect more regret than they actually feel (the psychological immune system), so do not overweight it.
insights.evidence: Kahneman's own policy is to be very thorough or completely casual on long-term decisions. Gilbert's psychological immune system research.

insights.claim: Separate mental accounts lead people to hold losing positions so they don't close an account at a loss. Fear of regret also keeps people repeating a known option instead of exploring.
insights.evidence: 'Speaking of' quotes: holding a stock to avoid realizing a loss, always ordering the same dish, separate accounts for cash and credit.

insights.claim: Options judged one at a time are driven by System 1's emotions and salient anchors. Judged side by side, attention shifts to features that matter and System 2 applies principles, so preferences can reverse between the two modes.
insights.evidence: Miller & McFarland: a crime victim shot in an unfamiliar store gets more compensation in single evaluation but equal compensation in joint evaluation. Lichtenstein & Slovic: people choose safe bet B but price bet A higher.

insights.concept: anchoring on the prize in pricing
insights.claim: When people price a single gamble, the size of the prize becomes the anchor, so risk gets underweighted compared with when they choose between gambles.
insights.evidence: Bet A (11/36 win $160) gets a higher selling price than bet B (35/36 win $40) even though B is chosen in direct choice.

insights.concept: poignancy / counterfactual emotion via intensity matching
insights.claim: An 'if only' story makes a case feel more poignant. Through substitution and intensity matching, System 1 turns that emotional strength into numbers, such as bigger awards, even though the factor has no moral relevance.
insights.evidence: The extra award for a victim shot in a store he rarely visited reflects 'if only he had gone to his usual store'.

insights.claim: Established theoretical beliefs are robust: one embarrassing finding rarely leads to revision, even when a careful attempt to refute that finding fails.
insights.evidence: Grether & Plott tested 13 explanations meant to discredit preference reversals. Only 'the psychologists were right' survived, yet economic theory barely changed.

insights.claim: System 1 automatically judges an item against the norm of its own category. Judgments are coherent within a category but can be incoherent across categories, because each category uses a different reference scale.
insights.evidence: John (6 years old, 5') is 'very tall' and Jim (16, 5'1") is not; apples vs peaches has a stable answer but apples vs steak does not; agency fines are sensible within each agency but globally incoherent.

insights.claim: When asked for a hard number such as a donation amount, System 1 answers an easier question (how much do I like this?) and maps that feeling onto a dollar scale. The number tracks the item's rank within its category, not its real importance.
insights.evidence: Dolphins rank high among endangered species, so they get relatively large contributions; farmworker skin cancer ranks low among public-health issues, so it gets smaller ones in single evaluation.

insights.claim: An attribute that cannot be evaluated on its own (a bare number without a reference) gets little weight in single evaluation. Once a comparison makes it evaluable, it can become the most important factor.
insights.evidence: Hsee's dictionaries: A (10,000 entries, like new) beats B (20,000 entries, torn cover) alone, but B wins in joint evaluation; BTU ratings meant nothing until compared across air-conditioning units.

insights.concept: preference reversal between single and joint evaluation
insights.claim: Options judged one at a time can be ranked in the opposite order when judged side by side. Joint evaluation reveals features that are invisible when each option is seen alone, such as human vs animal.
insights.evidence: Dolphins beat farmworkers in single evaluation, but farmworkers win clearly in joint evaluation; the jurors' burned-child award rose to exceed the bank's in joint evaluation, and personal-injury awards more than doubled.

insights.concept: anchoring on salient magnitude in single evaluation
insights.claim: In single evaluation, a large salient number such as a dollar loss anchors the judgment and can outweigh moral severity. Side-by-side comparison lets the moral factors correct the anchor.
insights.evidence: Mock jurors gave a bank that lost $10 million higher punitive damages than a child burned by flammable pajamas, until they saw both cases together.

insights.concept: broad framing via joint evaluation (with manipulation caveat)
insights.claim: Broader frames and comparative judgment, which use System 2, are usually more stable and rational than isolated judgments, which reflect System 1's emotional intensity. Be wary when whoever controls the comparison set has a stake in your choice.
insights.evidence: Jurors who are barred from considering other cases make inconsistent awards; salespeople manipulate the context in which a product is seen; the closing quote says broadening the frame yields more reasonable decisions.

insights.claim: Logically equivalent descriptions of the same outcome produce different choices because System 1 reacts to the words' associations and emotions, not to the underlying state of the world.
insights.evidence: 10% chance to win $95/90% lose $5 vs paying $5 for a lottery with 10% chance of $100: the lottery version gets far more acceptances; 'Italy won' vs 'France lost'.

insights.concept: reality-bound vs frame-bound preferences (Econs vs Humans)
insights.claim: A rational agent's preferences attach to states of the world, not descriptions; human choices are frame-bound because System 1 is not reality-bound and emotional words trigger approach/avoid tendencies that leak into choice.
insights.evidence: KEEP £20 vs LOSE £30 from £50: sure option favored under KEEP, gamble under LOSE; amygdala active when choices conformed to the frame, anterior cingulate active when resisting it.

insights.concept: costs are not losses (cost vs loss framing)
