insights.claim: An outcome labelled a cost (ticket price, foregone discount) is accepted more readily than the identical outcome labelled a loss or surcharge, though they are economically equivalent.
insights.evidence: Thaler's card 'costs are not losses'; credit-card lobby insisted price differences be called a 'cash discount' not a 'credit surcharge'.

insights.claim: The defense against framing is to translate all options into one common frame, which takes alert, effortful System 2; most people passively accept problems as framed and never discover their preferences are frame-bound.
insights.evidence: In repeated KEEP/LOSE trials a few 'rational' participants likely converted LOSE amounts into KEEP equivalents; the one-shot physicians had no cue to suspect the frame.

insights.claim: Stating the same statistic as survival rate versus mortality rate shifts expert choices sharply, and expertise gives no protection against the frame.
insights.evidence: Physicians: surgery chosen by 84% with '90% one-month survival' but 50% favored radiation with '10% mortality'; physicians as susceptible as patients and business students.

insights.claim: Identical outcomes described as lives saved produce risk-averse choices; described as lives lost they produce risk-seeking choices. Preferences are frame-bound, not reality-bound, and experts are just as susceptible.
insights.evidence: Program A (200 saved) preferred over gamble; A' (400 die) rejected for gamble B'; public-health officials showed the same reversal.

insights.claim: Moral intuitions attach to descriptions relative to an arbitrary reference point, not to actual states of the world; when shown the contradiction, System 2 has no intuition of its own to resolve it, so one must reason about the substantive outcome directly.
insights.evidence: Schelling's students rejected both a larger child exemption for the rich and an equal childless surcharge for the poor, which are logically incompatible.

insights.claim: A loss posted to a narrow account (the lost tickets) feels like doubling the price, whereas the same loss as cash goes to general wealth; the broader frame is better because sunk costs are irrelevant and only current options matter.
insights.evidence: Most think a woman who lost $160 tickets goes home but one who lost $160 cash still buys tickets; advice: would you buy if you had lost equivalent cash?

insights.claim: Ratio metrics like miles per gallon mislead intuition because savings are nonlinear; converting to the quantity actually consumed (gallons per mile) reveals the true size of improvements.
insights.evidence: Adam 12→14 mpg saves 119 gallons per 10,000 miles; Beth 30→40 mpg saves only 83.

insights.claim: Because System 2 is lazy, people unprepared for a question accept whatever happens without action; the default designation is the best single predictor of the choice, so choosing a formulation is never neutral.
insights.evidence: Organ donation ~100% in Austria vs 12% in Germany, 86% Sweden vs 4% Denmark, explained by opt-out vs opt-in forms.

insights.claim: Whichever option is adopted without action tends to win, because people who have not already decided avoid the effort of choosing (System 2 laziness); defaults are design choices, not neutral.
insights.evidence: Mailing-list remark: list would shrink if opt-in instead of opt-out; organ donation default carried from prior page.

insights.concept: inconsequential framing features / sensitivity to formulation
insights.claim: Important choices are often controlled by trivial features of how the choice is formulated; believers in rational agents assume formulation cannot matter and so never test it, leaving inferior outcomes.
insights.evidence: Organ donation rates driven by opt-in vs opt-out form; theory survives falsifying evidence.

insights.concept: reframing by changing the reference point
insights.claim: Evaluations shift with the reference point; deliberately reframing (e.g., imagine you do not own it; count what was kept rather than lost) exposes endowment and loss-framing distortions.
insights.evidence: Speaking-of lines: 'Imagine we did not own it; how much would we think it is worth?'; frame outcome as money kept vs lost; charge a loss to 'general revenue' mental account.

insights.claim: Decision utility (what people want/choose) can diverge from experienced utility (actual pleasure/pain); paying different amounts for the same gain in experienced utility is a mistake.
insights.evidence: Injection puzzle: people pay more to cut injections 6→4 than 20→18 though each removes two identical painful injections.

insights.concept: hedonimeter totals / area under the curve
insights.claim: Total experienced utility of an episode is the integral of momentary pleasure or pain over time, so duration matters: doubling time at the same intensity doubles the total.
insights.evidence: Edgeworth's hedonimeter; Redelmeier–Kahneman colonoscopy study, pain rated 0–10 every 60s; patient B (24 min) suffered more than A (8 min).

insights.claim: The length of an episode has almost no effect on how good or bad it is remembered; memory ignores how long pain or pleasure lasted.
insights.evidence: Procedure duration (4 to 69 minutes) had no effect on total-pain ratings; rats' fear depended on shock intensity, not duration.

insights.claim: Global retrospective evaluation of an episode is predicted by the average of its worst (or best) moment and its final moment, not by the total.
insights.evidence: Colonoscopy: both patients peaked at 8; A ended at 7 (peak-end 7.5), B ended at 1 (4.5); A remembered the procedure as worse though B suffered longer.

insights.claim: The experiencing self lives moments ('does it hurt now?'); the remembering self keeps score and makes decisions, so we optimize future memories rather than future experiences.
insights.evidence: Listener whose symphony disc screeched at the end said it 'ruined the whole experience', ignoring 40 minutes of bliss.

insights.concept: objective clarification: reduce remembered vs experienced harm
insights.claim: The best design depends on whether the goal is reducing memory of pain (lower the peak, end gently) or reducing actual pain (finish fast even with a higher peak).
insights.evidence: Colonoscopy implications: gradual relief vs swift procedure.

insights.claim: People choose the option they remember least badly, even when it means more actual suffering; known facts (duration) are not used in the choice.
insights.evidence: 80% who felt relief in the 90s trial chose to repeat it, accepting 30s of needless pain; they knew which trial was longer.

insights.concept: System 1 represents sets by averages/prototypes, not sums (less-is-more)
insights.claim: System 1 summarizes a set by a typical or average element rather than its total, which produces less-is-more errors where adding positive items lowers judged value.
insights.evidence: Hsee dinnerware set with broken dishes valued less; Linda the feminist bank teller; cold-hand episode stored as a prototypical moment.

insights.claim: Preferences based even on very recent personal experience can be wrong because memory is distorted; inconsistency between decision and experience signals an error.
insights.evidence: Injections puzzle (diminishing sensitivity: 20→18 vs 6→4) and cold-hand study (memory shaped within 15 minutes).

insights.concept: duration neglect in narratives / life as a story
insights.claim: The remembering self stores episodes and whole lives as stories built from key moments and endings. How long something lasted carries almost no weight, and the ending largely defines the whole.
insights.evidence: La Traviata: Violetta's age at death (27 vs 28) does not matter to the audience, but missing the last 10 minutes of reunion would change the whole story.

insights.claim: People judge the total value of a life or an episode by its typical (average) slice instead of summing over time. So adding a positive but weaker period lowers the judged total, which is absurd for an additive quantity.
insights.evidence: Diener's Jen study: doubling a very happy life from 30 to 60 years had no effect. Adding 5 'slightly happy' years cut judged total happiness, even within-subject and among older adults.

insights.claim: Decisions about repeating an experience follow the final remembered evaluation, even when it misrepresents the experience as it was lived moment to moment.
insights.evidence: Diener's spring-break study: plans to repeat a vacation were entirely set by the end-of-break global rating, not by the daily diary ratings. The same pattern appears in the cold-hand experiment.

insights.concept: remembering self vs experiencing self (amnesic thought experiments)
insights.claim: People value experiences mainly for the memories they will leave. They discount pleasure or pain they will not remember and treat their experiencing self almost like a stranger.
insights.evidence: Thought experiments: a vacation whose photos and memories will be erased loses much of its value. Many people are indifferent to surgery pain that an amnesia drug will wipe out. Tourists photograph scenes as future memories.

insights.concept: experienced well-being measure (rather continue than stop; hedonimeter)
insights.claim: Global life-satisfaction questions ask the error-prone remembering self. Well-being can instead be measured as a profile over moments, as the share of time in states one would rather continue than stop, rather avoid, or does not care about.
insights.evidence: 'Helen was happy in March' definition; flow (Csikszentmihalyi) and resistance to interruption as signs of a good time; Edgeworth's hedonimeter; colonoscopy profiles.

insights.claim: Instead of asking for one global judgment, rebuild the recent period as a sequence of episodes. Rate each episode's feelings on a scale and weight it by how long it lasted, which gives a duration-weighted measure that approximates live sampling.
insights.evidence: Women relived the previous day as film-like scenes and rated feelings 0–6 for each episode. The results agreed with experience sampling.

insights.claim: Moment-to-moment mood depends mostly on the current situation and on what one attends to, not on global factors such as status or benefits. Pleasure from an activity is diluted when it is not the focus.
insights.evidence: Mood at work depends on coworkers, noise, time pressure, and the boss's presence, not on job benefits. French women were twice as likely to make eating focal and enjoyed it more.

insights.claim: Bad experience is unevenly distributed. About half of people report no unpleasant episodes in a day, while a small minority carries most of the distress. Poverty also amplifies the effect of other misfortunes.
insights.evidence: With a headache, sadness/worry rises from 19% to 38% for the top two-thirds by income, and from 38% to 70% for the poorest tenth.

insights.claim: Measure bad experience as the percentage of time spent in an unpleasant state, where an episode counts as unpleasant if its strongest feeling is negative. Because it measures time and not a rating, changes in it can be read in proportion and compared across activities.
insights.evidence: 4 of 16 waking hours unpleasant gives a U-index of 25%. Values by activity: commute 29%, work 27%, child care 24%, TV 12%. A drop from 20% to 18% means a tenth less suffering.

insights.claim: Temperament is hard to change, but time allocation can be changed. Shifting time away from high-U activities (commuting, passive leisure) toward socializing and active leisure is the most practical way to improve experience.
insights.evidence: Proposals such as better transportation, child care, and socializing for the elderly. Even a 1% drop in the U-index equals millions of hours of avoided suffering.

insights.claim: How people evaluate their lives and how they actually feel while living are different constructs. Education and income raise evaluation, while illness and children affect daily feeling more. Do not treat one as a proxy for the other.
insights.evidence: Gallup data comparing the Cantril ladder with emotions felt the previous day: education raises evaluation but also stress, and illness hurts experience much more than evaluation.

insights.claim: Beyond a satiation point (about $75k household income in high-cost areas), more money adds zero to experienced well-being, though it keeps raising life satisfaction. Wealth may reduce enjoyment of small pleasures.
insights.evidence: Analysis of more than 450,000 Gallup-Healthways responses. Students primed with wealth showed less pleasure while eating chocolate.

insights.claim: People mispredict how much a change in their circumstances (marriage, climate, a new car) will change their well-being. They also treat base rates such as divorce statistics as if they did not apply to them.
insights.evidence: Newlyweds know divorce rates are high but don't apply them to themselves. Kahneman's wife believed Californians were happier, and he argued it is preposterous to forecast life on a warmer planet.

insights.claim: A quick global score comes from a small sample of highly available ideas, not from carefully weighing every domain. As a salient event loses novelty over time, it is retrieved less often, which looks like a change in the underlying quantity.
insights.evidence: Figure 16 can be read as the probability of thinking about a recent marriage when asked about one's life, not as a happiness curve.

insights.claim: When asked a hard global question such as 'how satisfied are you with your life', System 1 answers an easier one instead: current mood or whatever is salient at the moment. Small irrelevant events can therefore shift the answer.
insights.evidence: Schwarz's study: finding a planted dime on the copier raised reported life satisfaction. A question about dating made dating dominate the happiness answers that followed.

insights.claim: A circumstance can have little average effect because it makes some things better and others worse, or helps some people and hurts others. Satisfaction also depends on the goals people set: hard-to-reach goals predict dissatisfaction.
insights.evidence: In DRM data, married and unmarried women had equal experienced well-being. Income raised satisfaction by .57 for those who rated money as essential vs .12 for those who said it was unimportant. Wanting a performing-arts career was the least promising goal.

insights.claim: Whatever aspect you are attending to gets far too much weight in a global evaluation, and all the other factors get too little (WYSIATI). Nothing is as important as it seems while you are thinking about it.
insights.evidence: Students in both California and the Midwest believed Californians were happier because of the climate. Measured life satisfaction was the same in both regions.

insights.concept: duration neglect in valuing possessions (attention-time test)
insights.claim: Asking 'how much pleasure do you get from X' is really answered as 'how much pleasure when you think of X', ignoring how rarely you think of it. Asking WHEN you get pleasure corrects this.
insights.evidence: Car example: you enjoy your car only when you think about it, which is rarely, even while driving.

insights.claim: People adapt to a new good or bad situation mainly by thinking about it less and less, so most long-term circumstances affect mood only when they are attended to. The exceptions are conditions that keep demanding attention: chronic pain, constant loud noise and severe depression.
insights.evidence: Paraplegics are in a fairly good mood more than half the time one month after the accident. People who know a paraplegic estimate 41% bad mood a year later, while others estimate 68%. Lottery winners show the same pattern.

insights.claim: Whatever you are thinking about seems more important to well-being than it really is. An aspect that is salient now, or vivid because a contrasting alternative comes to mind easily, gets too much weight in judgments of your own happiness, other people's happiness and your future happiness.
insights.evidence: Californians vs Midwesterners: both groups assume Californians are happier because of the climate, yet life satisfaction is the same. Recent movers from Ohio report themselves happier because the question reminds them of the climate.

insights.claim: Bad choices come from errors in predicting how outcomes will feel. The focusing illusion favors goods that are exciting at first but later stop drawing attention, and undervalues activities that keep demanding attention, such as social commitments or skills.
insights.evidence: A new car versus a weekly poker or book club: the car stops being noticed, but the club stays engaging. Tennis and cello are other attention-demanding activities. Also a fancy car or a larger house that did not make the owner happier.

insights.concept: remembering self vs experiencing self divergence (evaluation-context effect)
insights.claim: Global life evaluations can differ sharply from moment-to-moment experience. Asking for an evaluation brings to mind comparisons and recent salient events, so the answer depends on what the question makes people think about.
insights.evidence: Colostomy patients feel no less happy than healthy people in experience sampling, yet would trade years of life to be rid of the condition. A cheerful person says she is very unhappy because the question reminds her of her divorce. A broken-down car colors a rating of job satisfaction.

insights.concept: duration neglect / peak-end and transition focus
insights.claim: The remembering self tells stories: it represents an episode by a few moments (beginning, peak, end) and a state by the transition into it. It ignores how long things last and how people adapt. The mind handles stories well but time poorly.
insights.evidence: The cold-hand experiment and Violetta's story (referenced). In prospect theory, a lottery win is valued as the reaction to the news, not as the lasting state of wealth.

insights.concept: duration neglect + peak-end rule (remembering self bias)
insights.claim: The remembering self judges episodes by their peak and their end and ignores how long they lasted. So people prefer short intense joy over long moderate happiness and fear short intense pain more than long mild pain. Kahneman calls the resulting choices mistakes.
insights.evidence: In the cold-hand study, people chose to repeat the longer, more painful trial because it ended better. Similar effects show up in opera endings and judgments of Jen's life.

insights.claim: Advice like 'you will regret it' sounds wise because it is the remembering self's verdict. That self neglects duration, overweights peaks and ends, and is prone to hindsight, so its judgment should not be taken as final.
insights.evidence: The common admonition 'Don't do it, you will regret it', compared with what an objective observer of the hedonimeter profile would advise.

insights.claim: Weight every moment by its duration. A moment gains weight only from time spent dwelling on it or from how it changes later moments. Claims that something is memorable or meaningful are predictions that are often false.
insights.evidence: An hour of violin practice enhances many later hours of music. A brief trauma causing PTSD should be weighted by the long misery that follows. Many things people say they will always remember are forgotten ten years later.

insights.claim: How severe a condition looks depends on the measure you use: how much people fear it, how much they actually suffer, or how much they would sacrifice for relief. Each measure can rank conditions differently, so priorities must consider both selves.
insights.evidence: Blindness vs deafness and colostomy vs dialysis may rank differently depending on the measure. Some governments are interested in a national suffering index.

insights.concept: rationality as coherence vs reasonableness (Econs vs Humans)
insights.claim: In decision theory, rationality means only internal consistency, which a finite mind cannot achieve. Humans are not irrational, but they are not described well by the rational-agent model either. They fall reliably for priming, WYSIATI, narrow framing, the inside view and preference reversals, so they need help to judge and decide.
insights.evidence: A coherent believer in ghosts counts as 'rational'. Kahneman objects to the claim that his work showed human choices are irrational.

insights.concept: look for good reasons before psychological explanations
insights.claim: When people act in ways that seem odd, first check whether they have a good reason. Invoke psychological explanations only when the rational reasons become implausible.
insights.evidence: Gary Becker half-jokingly explained the obesity epidemic by people's belief that a diabetes cure was coming. The point was valid even though that explanation is implausible.

insights.concept: nudge / choice architecture / default option (libertarian paternalism)
insights.claim: Framing and defaults strongly shape choices. People see the default as the normal choice, and leaving it is an act of commission that takes effort, carries responsibility and invites regret. Setting good defaults helps people without removing their freedom to opt out.
insights.evidence: Making the pension plan the automatic default with a simple opt-out box (Thaler & Sunstein, Nudge).

insights.concept: protection from exploitation of System 1 quirks and System 2 laziness
insights.claim: Humans, unlike Econs, need protection from people who deliberately exploit System 1's quirks and System 2's laziness. Rational-agent models wrongly assume that important decisions are always made carefully.
insights.evidence: This sets up the argument for regulation that protects people from others who exploit their weaknesses.

insights.claim: Behavior change sticks when it requires no immediate loss, ties the change to future gains so losses become foregone gains, and runs automatically unless the person opts out, aligning System 2 laziness with long-term interest.
insights.evidence: Thaler & Benartzi 2003 plan: savings contribution rises automatically with each pay raise until opt-out; raised savings of millions.

insights.concept: Simplicity over disclosure (choice architecture for Humans)
insights.claim: Disclosing information is not enough for Humans, who skip fine print; communication must be clear, simple, salient, meaningful, and framing-balanced (show both the gain and loss frame).
insights.evidence: Nudge's simple-contract recommendations; OMB 2010 report on clear disclosures; USDA rule that '90% fat-free' must be shown with equally prominent '10% fat'; Food Plate replacing Food Pyramid.

insights.claim: System 2 often endorses feelings generated by System 1 and, when asked, fabricates presentable reasons that it then believes.
insights.evidence: Being optimistic about a project because its leader resembles your sister, or disliking someone who looks like your dentist, then finding reasons.

insights.claim: Intuition is trustworthy only when skill was acquired in a regular environment with ample practice and rapid, unequivocal feedback; otherwise fast confident answers may be heuristic substitutes.
insights.evidence: Skilled responses like walking around a stone or defusing an angry customer, versus 17x24 requiring System 2.

insights.concept: Recognize the cognitive minefield, slow down, call System 2
insights.claim: System 1 is barely educable, so debiasing works by recognizing situations where errors are likely (e.g., 'this number will be an anchor', 'reframing could change this') and deliberately invoking slow checks; this is easier for observers than for actors under stress.
insights.evidence: Müller-Lyer illusion: knowing not to trust length impressions when fins appear; Kahneman's own intuitions stayed overconfident and prone to planning fallacy.

insights.concept: Substitution / no warning signal of unreliability
insights.claim: System 1 answers related, more accessible questions in place of the one asked and gives no alarm when unreliable; skilled and heuristic answers feel equally confident, so the only remedy is slowing down to construct the answer.
insights.evidence: Bat-and-ball problem casually endorsed; operative features WYSIATI, intensity matching, associative coherence yield anchoring, nonregressive prediction, overconfidence.

insights.concept: Organizational decision quality control (frame / collect / review)
insights.claim: Organizations, as decision factories, should run routine quality control at three stages—problem framing, information collection, and reflection/review—using checklists, reference-class forecasting and premortems rather than post-disaster reviews.
insights.evidence: Factory analogy: design, fabrication, final inspection; note on lack of training for efficient meetings.

insights.concept: Precise bias vocabulary and process-based evaluation
insights.claim: Naming errors precisely (anchoring, narrow framing, excessive coherence) works like a diagnosis that retrieves causes and cures; decisions improve when judged by how they were made, not only by outcome, and when imagined sophisticated critics are anticipated.
insights.evidence: Medical diagnosis analogy; 'more precise gossip at the watercooler' leads to better decisions.

insights.concept: heuristics and biases (judgment by simplifying heuristics)
insights.claim: People answer hard probability questions with a small set of heuristics. These are usually useful but produce severe, systematic errors, the way judging distance by clarity misleads in fog or in very clear air.
insights.evidence: Perceived distance depends on how sharp an object looks: distances are overestimated when visibility is poor and underestimated when it is good.

insights.claim: The chance that A belongs to class B (or comes from process B) is judged by how much A resembles B. Similarity ignores several factors that should change the probability.
insights.evidence: Steve, shy and tidy with 'a passion for detail', is judged likely to be a librarian. People rank occupations by probability exactly as they rank them by similarity to a stereotype.

insights.claim: When a specific description is given, people ignore how common each category is, even though Bayes' rule says base rates should strongly shift the answer. They use priors correctly only when they have no description at all.
insights.evidence: Descriptions drawn from 70 engineers/30 lawyers vs 30/70 got essentially the same probability judgments, although the odds should differ by a factor of 5.44. With no description, people correctly answered .7 and .3.

insights.claim: People judge how likely a sample result is by how similar it is to the population value, so their answers barely depend on sample size. Yet small samples swing to extremes much more often.
insights.evidence: The probability of an average height above 6 feet was rated the same for samples of 10, 100 and 1,000 men. In the hospital problem (45 vs 15 births a day, days with over 60% boys), 53 of the subjects chose 'about the same' and 21 chose 'the larger hospital'; the correct answer is the smaller one.

insights.claim: People act differently when given no evidence and when given worthless evidence. A description with no relevant information makes them drop the base rate and fall back to 50/50.
insights.evidence: The bland 'Dick' description (30, married, able, well liked) produced a .5 judgment whether engineers were 70% or 30% of the group.

insights.claim: Intuitive posterior odds are far less extreme than Bayes implies; people under-update on strong, large-sample evidence while being swayed by proportions.
insights.evidence: Urn problem: correct odds 8:1 and 16:1, yet intuitive estimates are much milder and favor the 4:1 sample.

insights.claim: People judge how likely a sample result is by how similar it is to the population, ignoring that small samples stray from the mean far more often than large ones.
insights.evidence: Hospital problem: most said 45-births and 15-births hospitals have equally many >60%-boy days; the small one has far more. Urn: 4/5 red judged stronger than 12/20 red though odds are 8:1 vs 16:1.

insights.claim: People expect short random sequences to look locally representative and treat chance as self-correcting; deviations are only diluted, not corrected.
insights.evidence: H-T-H-T-T-H judged likelier than H-H-H-T-T-T; after long red run on roulette, black felt 'due'.

insights.claim: People predict outcomes as extreme as the favorability of the description, ignoring how reliable the evidence is; normatively, lower predictability should shrink predictions toward the average (nil predictability = same prediction for all).
insights.evidence: Subjects' percentile predictions of student teachers' standing 5 years later were identical to their evaluations of a single practice lesson.

insights.claim: Even expert researchers believe small samples are highly representative, over-trust their results, overestimate replicability, and choose inadequate sample sizes.
insights.evidence: Survey of experienced research psychologists' statistical intuitions.

insights.claim: Confidence tracks how well the input fits the predicted outcome and how consistent the inputs are, not real accuracy; redundant correlated inputs raise confidence while lowering accuracy, and the illusion persists even when one knows the limits.
insights.evidence: Librarian stereotype from scanty description; interviewers confident despite literature on interview fallibility; all-B record predicted more confidently than mixed A/C record.

insights.concept: regression toward the mean (misconceptions of regression)
insights.claim: Extreme scores on one measure are followed by less extreme scores on another; people fail to expect this and invent causal explanations for it, e.g. concluding punishment works better than reward.
insights.evidence: Top/bottom children on two aptitude test versions; flight instructors saw praise followed by worse landings and criticism by better ones.

insights.claim: People estimate frequency or probability by how easily instances come to mind; useful because frequent classes are recalled faster, but recall is affected by other factors, causing predictable biases.
insights.evidence: Judging heart-attack risk by recalling acquaintances; judging venture failure by imagining difficulties.

insights.claim: Classes whose instances are familiar, salient or recent are recalled more easily and therefore judged more frequent than equally frequent classes.
insights.evidence: Lists of famous men/women: subjects judged the sex with more famous names as more numerous; seeing a burning house or overturned car raises felt risk.

insights.claim: When instances must be constructed, ease of constructing them substitutes for frequency/probability; easily imagined dangers inflate risk, unimagined ones are ignored.
insights.evidence: Committees of 2 from 10 people judged far more numerous (median 70) than committees of 8 (median 20); correct is 45 for both. Expedition risk judged by vividly portrayed contingencies.

insights.claim: Frequency judgments follow how easy memory search is for a category, not true frequency; categories indexed conveniently (first letter, abstract contexts) seem more common.
insights.evidence: Words starting with r/k judged more common than r/k in third position though the reverse is true; abstract words judged more frequent than equally frequent concrete words.

insights.claim: People overestimate co-occurrence of events that are strongly associated in meaning, and this persists even against contradictory or negative data, hiding real relationships.
insights.evidence: Chapman & Chapman draw-a-person: judges saw suspiciousness co-occur with peculiar eyes far more than in data, even when correlation was negative.

insights.claim: Estimates starting from an initial value, even arbitrary or from partial computation, are adjusted too little and stay biased toward the start; accuracy payoffs did not remove it.
insights.evidence: Wheel of fortune 10 vs 65 gave UN African country estimates 25 vs 45; 8x7x...x1 estimated 2,250 vs 1x2x...x8 at 512, true 40,320.

insights.claim: Numerosity, likelihood and co-occurrence are estimated by the ease of retrieval, construction or association; usually valid but produces systematic errors.
insights.evidence: Summary of the preceding examples: fame lists, letter positions, committees, illusory correlation.

insights.claim: People anchor on the single-stage probability, so they overestimate chains that need every step to succeed and underestimate risks where any one failure suffices; this produces plan optimism and underrated system-failure risk.
insights.evidence: Bar-Hillel bets: conjunctive (0.9^7≈.48) preferred to simple .50; simple preferred to disjunctive (.52). New product development is conjunctive; reactor/body failure is disjunctive.

insights.concept: conjunctive vs disjunctive event bias (chain vs funnel)
insights.claim: Because people anchor on the probability of one stage, they overestimate the success of multi-step chains (plans) and underestimate failure of systems that break if any component fails. The direction of bias can be inferred from the event's structure.
insights.evidence: Marble bets: subjects preferred a .48 conjunctive bet over a .50 simple one and a .50 simple over a .52 disjunctive one; applied to product development and nuclear reactors/human body.

insights.concept: overconfident (too narrow) subjective probability intervals from anchoring
insights.claim: When asked for percentile bounds, people start from their best estimate and adjust insufficiently, so their intervals are far too tight; true values fall outside a stated 98% interval about 30% of the time, for experts and novices alike, even with scoring incentives.
insights.evidence: Dow Jones X01/X99 elicitation studies; 24 quantities (e.g., New Delhi–Peking air distance): events judged at .10 actually occurred 24% of the time.

insights.concept: biases are cognitive, not motivational; experts prone when intuitive
insights.claim: The heuristic biases persist even when people are rewarded for accuracy, and statistically trained experts show them too when judging intuitively in less transparent problems.
insights.evidence: Errors occurred despite payment for correct answers; statistically trained people neglected prior probability in intuitive predictions.

insights.claim: Formally equivalent ways of asking for a probability distribution give different answers because they supply different anchors: asking for percentile values anchors on the best estimate (too extreme/narrow), asking for odds on a stated value anchors on that value or 50-50 (too conservative).
insights.evidence: Second group given first group's median X10/X90 values gave median odds 3:1 instead of 9:1; their .34 events occurred 26% of the time.

insights.concept: calibration tally (grouping predictions by stated probability)
insights.claim: People rarely learn statistical rules or their own miscalibration from experience because events are not coded the right way; keeping a tally of how often predictions at each stated probability came true would reveal miscalibration.
insights.evidence: People never notice lines vary more in average word length than pages; someone may not discover only 50% of their .9 predictions came true.

insights.concept: coherence is not enough: compatibility with the web of beliefs
insights.claim: A set of probabilities can be internally consistent yet irrational if it conflicts with other knowledge; a rational judge checks probability estimates against subject knowledge, the laws of probability, and known heuristics/biases.
insights.evidence: A gambler's-fallacy believer's coin probabilities can be coherent but contradict the belief that a coin has no memory.

insights.concept: three judgmental heuristics (representativeness, availability, anchoring and adjustment)
insights.claim: Judgment under uncertainty relies on three economical heuristics—representativeness for class membership, availability for frequency/plausibility, and anchoring-and-adjustment for numeric prediction—which usually work but cause systematic, predictable errors.
insights.evidence: Summary of the 1974 article.

insights.claim: The same decision problem described in different ways produces different preferences, violating the rational invariance criterion.
insights.evidence: Abstract: multiple framings of one decision problem yield different preferences.

insights.concept: mental accounting: cost vs uncompensated loss
insights.claim: How people organize transaction outcomes into mental accounts changes acceptability; a negative outcome feels acceptable as a cost but aversive as an uncompensated loss.
insights.evidence: Abstract: mental accounting explains consumer anomalies; acceptability depends on cost vs loss coding.

insights.concept: normative vs descriptive analysis; decision vs experience values
insights.claim: Decision study separates how choices should be made (logic of rationality) from how people actually choose; also the values used at decision time may differ from values experienced later.
insights.evidence: Introduction of Appendix B contrasting normative and descriptive questions and noting decision vs experience values.

insights.claim: Decision weights overweight sure things and improbable events relative to moderate-probability events, distorting choices away from expected value.
insights.evidence: Abstract: 'psychophysics of chance' induces overweighting of certainty and rare events.

insights.concept: reflection of risk attitudes (gains vs losses)
insights.claim: The psychophysics of value make people risk averse when outcomes are framed as gains and risk seeking when outcomes are framed as losses.
insights.evidence: Abstract of Appendix B summarizing the value-function findings of prospect theory.

insights.concept: reference dependence (changes vs. states of wealth)
insights.claim: People evaluate outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point such as the status quo, not as final states of total wealth; value carriers are changes.
insights.evidence: A $20 coin bet is felt as win/lose $20, not as moving from W to W±20.

insights.claim: With gains, the concave value curve makes people prefer a sure outcome over a gamble with higher expected value.
insights.evidence: Majority prefer sure $800 over 85% chance at $1,000 (EV $850).

insights.claim: The value function is much steeper for losses than for gains, so a loss of X hurts more than a gain of X pleases; people reject fair or even favorable bets.
insights.evidence: Most undergraduates refused to stake $10 on a coin toss unless they could win about $30.

insights.concept: risk seeking in the domain of losses
insights.claim: Because the value function is convex for losses, people gamble to avoid a sure loss even when the gamble has worse expectation; this holds for money, pain and lives.
insights.evidence: Most prefer an 85% chance to lose $1,000 (EV -$850) over a sure loss of $800.

insights.concept: dominance and invariance as rationality checks
insights.claim: Any rational choice must satisfy dominance (prefer an option at least as good everywhere and better somewhere) and invariance (preference unaffected by description); framing can make people violate both.
insights.evidence: Problem 3: F (25% win $250 / 75% lose $750) dominates E (win $240 / lose $760).

insights.concept: framing effect / invariance violation (Asian disease problem)
insights.claim: Equivalent options described as lives saved vs lives lost reverse preferences; invariance fails robustly, even for sophisticated people and after reflection, like a perceptual illusion.
insights.evidence: '200 saved' chosen by 72%; equivalent '400 die' chosen by only 22% (78% gamble).

insights.concept: narrow framing of concurrent decisions (violation of dominance)
insights.claim: When several decisions are made at once but evaluated separately, people pick risk-averse in gains and risk-seeking in losses, and the combined portfolio they choose can be strictly dominated by the one they rejected.
insights.evidence: Problem 4: 73% chose sure +$240 and 75% chance to lose $1,000; combined this equals option E, which everyone rejected versus F in Problem 3.

insights.claim: Since frame invariance cannot be guaranteed and confidence in a choice does not show it survives another frame, deliberately restate the problem in multiple frames (gains vs losses, total states vs changes) and check that the preference holds.
insights.evidence: Advice to judge in terms of total assets rather than gains/losses (Schlaifer); Fischhoff, Slovic & Lichtenstein recommendation to reframe; disease problem with lives saved vs lives lost.

insights.concept: decision weights / probability weighting function (category-boundary effect)
insights.claim: People weight probabilities nonlinearly: moving from impossible to possible or from possible to certain matters far more than an equal change mid-scale; moderate/high probabilities are underweighted, low ones overweighted or ignored.
insights.evidence: Lottery ticket for $300: 0→5% and 95→100% feel bigger than 30→35%; Figure 2 hypothetical weighting function; explains lottery tickets and insurance purchases.

insights.claim: Invariance is normatively essential and intuitively compelling yet psychologically unfeasible; confidence in a choice does not ensure it would be made under another frame.
insights.evidence: Respondents stay inconsistent even when facing their conflicting answers; total-asset and actuarial fixes are impractical for health, safety, or concurrent decisions.

insights.concept: fourfold pattern of risk attitudes (from decision weights)
insights.claim: Because low probabilities are overweighted, people become risk seeking for unlikely gains and risk averse for unlikely losses, reversing the usual pattern for moderate/high probabilities.
insights.evidence: Attractiveness of both lottery tickets and insurance policies explained by overweighting small chances.

insights.claim: In multi-stage situations people ignore a shared uncertain first stage and treat a conditional sure outcome as truly certain, overweighting it and reversing preferences versus the equivalent single-stage gamble.
insights.evidence: Problem 5 (two-stage, 25% to reach stage 2): 74% chose sure $30 over 80% of $45; Problem 6 (identical 25% $30 vs 20% $45): 58% chose the $45.

insights.claim: An advisor can steer a decision without distorting or hiding information, simply by choosing how outcomes are framed. This can happen by accident or on purpose, and it is common in marketing and politics.
insights.evidence: A physician or presidential advisor could steer a choice through framing alone; the credit-card industry pushed to label the price gap a 'cash discount'.

insights.claim: People accept the description of outcomes as given and judge them as gains or losses against the reference point the wording implies. Equivalent statements in different words shift choices, and System 1 does not recode the two framings into one common form.
insights.evidence: 'Lives saved' vs 'lives lost' in the public health problem; surgery looks worse when outcomes are stated as mortality rather than survival (McNeil et al.); lobbyists insisted on 'cash discount' rather than 'credit card surcharge'.

insights.concept: probabilistic insurance / elimination vs reduction of risk (certainty effect at low probabilities)
insights.claim: Decision weights rise steeply near zero, so cutting a hazard from p to p/2 feels worth much less than cutting it from p/2 to 0. People undervalue partial risk reduction and overpay for full elimination, so the same protection looks better when framed as eliminating a specific risk.
insights.evidence: Half-price earthquake insurance that covers only odd days is seen as unattractive. A vaccine that cuts disease risk from 20% to 10% appeals less as 'effective in half the cases' than as 'fully effective against one of two strains'.

insights.concept: topical mental accounts (relative vs absolute evaluation of savings)
insights.claim: Options can be judged in a minimal, topical or comprehensive account, and people default to the topical one, the context of the purchase at hand. Combined with the concave value function, this makes the same absolute gain or cost look large or small depending on the size of its topic.
insights.evidence: 68% would drive 20 minutes to save $5 on a $15 calculator, but only 29% to save $5 on a $125 one. Price spread across stores is proportional to average price. Add-ons like a car stereo are easier to buy alongside a car.

insights.concept: minimal vs comprehensive account reframing (debias mental accounting)
insights.claim: Whether an option is accepted depends on which account it is posted to. Recasting the decision as a minimal account (only the differences) or a comprehensive account (total wealth or the whole budget) exposes the inconsistency, and showing an equivalent case side by side helps people see a lost ticket as lost cash.
insights.evidence: The two calculator versions are identical in both minimal and comprehensive accounts. Willingness to replace a lost ticket rose after subjects first saw the lost-cash version, but not the other way around.

insights.concept: cost posting to topical account (lost ticket vs lost cash / sunk-cost-like double payment)
insights.claim: People post a loss to the account of the activity it belongs to. Replacing a lost ticket feels like paying twice for the play, while losing the same cash feels like being slightly less rich. Such effects may partly reflect real secondary consequences like regret, but those feelings may change on reflection.
insights.evidence: Only 46% would buy another $10 ticket after losing one, but 88% would buy a ticket after losing a $10 bill (N=200/183).

insights.claim: When the status quo is the reference point, an alternative's advantages count as gains and its disadvantages as losses. Because losses loom larger, people stick with what they have, and the lowest price they would sell an asset for is well above the highest price they would pay for it.
insights.evidence: In the job choice (salary vs workplace temperature), subjects assigned to either job refused to switch to the other. Studies also find large gaps between willingness to pay and willingness to accept (Knetsch & Sinden, among others).

insights.concept: loss aversion favors stability (adaptation to reference point)
insights.claim: Once people adapt to whatever state they are in, they evaluate other states as gains and losses relative to it, so they prefer to stay where they are. Unstable preferences end up producing a preference for stability, which also dampens regret and envy.
insights.evidence: Hedonically identical twins who were indifferent between two environments each come to prefer the one they were placed in.

insights.claim: Two problems with the same primary consequences need not get the same answer. Still, deliberately recasting a decision in other frames shows which preferences come from secondary feelings (regret, saving $5) and whether those feelings hold up on reflection.
insights.evidence: Saving $5 on a $15 item feels less satisfying once you realize you wouldn't make the same effort to save $10 on a $200 item.

insights.claim: The same money feels less aversive framed as a cost (a payment, an insurance premium) than as an uncompensated loss. This breaks invariance and can reverse preferences between objectively identical options.
insights.evidence: 80% chose a 25% chance to lose $200 over a sure $50 loss, yet only 35% refused to pay $50 to insure against it. Among 132 students, 42 rejected the 10% win $95 / 90% lose $5 gamble but accepted the identical $5 lottery ticket.

insights.claim: People keep using something they have paid for, even when doing so hurts, because stopping would force them to admit the payment as a dead loss rather than a cost.
insights.evidence: Thaler's example: a man develops tennis elbow after paying his club fee and keeps playing in pain so as not to waste the investment.

insights.claim: How attractive an outcome seems at the moment of choice often differs from how it actually feels when experienced. Some factors that drive the experience are hard to foresee, and some framings sway the choice without changing the experience at all (mortality vs survival). Sometimes framing changes the experience as well.
insights.evidence: Ordering a large meal while ravenous and regretting it by the fifth course. Mortality vs survival framing of lung cancer therapies affects the choice but not the experience.

insights.concept: hedonic reference point and hedonic treadmill
insights.claim: Whether an outcome feels like a gain or a loss depends on a reference point set by the status quo, expectations and social comparison. Rapid adaptation means the boost from any objective improvement fades quickly.
insights.evidence: An employee who gets a raise smaller than everyone else's experiences it as a loss. Brickman and Campbell's hedonic treadmill.

insights.concept: collecting too few observations (law of small numbers / statistical power)
insights.claim: The note for the Introduction says researchers, Kahneman and Tversky included, tend to collect too few observations and do not justify their sample sizes. It points to statistical power analysis as the fix.
insights.evidence: Note citing Jacob Cohen's Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (1969), a book that criticized psychologists for using small samples.

insights.claim: When an automatic response (reading a word) conflicts with the instructed task (naming the ink color), performance becomes very hard; the conflict shows System 2 must actively suppress System 1.
insights.evidence: Stroop task: name ink colors when the words are themselves color names (GREEN printed in red).

insights.concept: Limited general capacity of attention and effort
insights.claim: Attention and mental effort are a limited general resource shared across very different tasks, so concurrent demanding tasks interfere with each other; practice can reduce the effort a task needs.
insights.evidence: Pupil dilation and heart-rate rise during mental tasks; perceptual deficit for flashed letters during a mental task; brain studies showing less activation after practice; high-SAT scorers show smaller pupil dilation on same task.

insights.claim: People avoid cognitive demand: effort is registered as a cost when valuing an action, so the cheaper path tends to be chosen even if it is worse.
insights.evidence: Kool et al. on avoidance of cognitive demand; neural region that counts invested effort as a cost when evaluating a completed action.

insights.claim: People judge an argument as valid when its conclusion is believable, confusing plausibility of the conclusion with logical soundness.
insights.evidence: Syllogisms with believable but invalid conclusions are accepted as valid (Evans, dual-processing accounts).

insights.claim: Some problems evoke a fast intuitive answer that is wrong; checking it with deliberate thought is needed to override it.
insights.evidence: Frederick's Cognitive Reflection Test (2005) on intuitive but incorrect answers.

insights.concept: Ego depletion / depletion effects in judgment
insights.claim: Exerting self-control draws on a limited resource; after depletion, judgments drift toward default, low-effort decisions.
insights.evidence: Hagger meta-analysis on ego depletion; Gailliot on glucose; Danziger et al. on extraneous factors (timing) in judicial parole decisions.

insights.concept: Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) as predictor of bias susceptibility
insights.claim: A note cites research finding that CRT scores predict how people do on heuristics-and-biases tasks better than standard IQ measures do. Reflectiveness is a different thing from intelligence.
insights.evidence: Toplak, West & Stanovich: CRT as a predictor on heuristics-and-biases tasks.

insights.claim: People fall back on a vague sense of familiarity only when they cannot recall specifics like where or when. The fallback is better than nothing but imperfect, so familiarity alone can be mistaken for knowledge or fame.
insights.evidence: Jacoby's 'Becoming Famous Overnight' study; the note's example of being greeted by someone who only looks vaguely familiar.

insights.concept: processing fluency inflates belief and weight (repetition, rhyme, simple wording, easy names)
insights.claim: Inputs that are easy to process feel truer, more credible and more important. This covers repeated statements, rhyming sayings, plain wording and pronounceable names. Needlessly complex wording lowers credibility. Easy-to-pronounce stock names had a small short-term advantage.
insights.evidence: Repeated statements believed more ('body temperature of a chicken'); rhyming aphorisms judged more accurate; fictitious Turkish companies with fluent names weighted more; Alter & Oppenheimer on stock tickers; Oppenheimer on long words.

insights.claim: When processing feels hard (for example, a hard-to-read font), people move into a more engaged, analytic mode and make fewer intuitive errors.
insights.evidence: Alter, Oppenheimer, Epley & Eyre (2007), 'Overcoming Intuition: Metacognitive Difficulty Activates Analytic Reasoning'.

insights.concept: good mood increases gullibility and reliance on intuition
insights.claim: Positive mood, cognitive ease and intuitive reliance go together. Happy people are less skeptical and worse at detecting deception. Even people who fail to solve a word-association triad can sense whether a solution exists.
insights.evidence: Bolte, Goschke & Kuhl, where mood changed the accuracy of coherence intuitions; Forgas & East, 'On Being Happy and Gullible'.

insights.claim: The cited sources show that people automatically infer causes and intentions from sparse input. Infants perceive causality, and observers see bullies and victims in moving shapes.
insights.evidence: Hassin, Bargh & Uleman on spontaneous causal inferences ('pickpocket'); Michotte; Heider & Simmel's animated shapes; Leslie & Keeble on infants.

insights.claim: Gigerenzer's fast-and-frugal heuristics (e.g., pick the recognized city as larger) can be accurate in some settings, but people use more than the recognition cue, and expertise usually means handling much information quickly rather than using less.
insights.evidence: Which of two cities is larger; Oppenheimer (2003) showed subjects use cues beyond recognition; chess-master research on skill.

insights.concept: substitution (mood as answer to happiness question) and its undoing by naming the cause
insights.claim: When asked about overall happiness, people substitute their current mood, so weather correlated with reported happiness; asking first about the weather gave them an explanation for their mood and erased the effect.
insights.evidence: German telephone survey: weather correlated with happiness reports, but not when respondents were asked about current weather first (Schwarz/Strack line of work).

insights.concept: law of small numbers / low statistical power
insights.claim: Researchers trusting statistical intuition chose samples so small that their studies ran about a 50% risk of failing to detect real effects.
insights.evidence: Jacob Cohen's 1962 review of statistical power in abnormal-social psychology; Tversky & Kahneman 'Belief in the Law of Small Numbers'; small-schools example (Wainer & Zwerling).

insights.concept: anchoring effect in expert and negotiation judgments
insights.claim: Arbitrary or strategic numbers pull expert estimates: listing prices shifted real-estate valuations, dice rolls shifted judges' sentences, purchase limits raised quantities, and damage caps acted as anchors in settlements.
insights.evidence: Northcraft & Neale real-estate study (anchors 12% above/below list price); Englich et al. dice and criminal sentences; Wansink 'limit per person'; Pogarsky & Babcock damage caps.

insights.concept: resisting the anchoring effect (perspective-taking in negotiation)
insights.claim: A first offer's anchoring pull can be resisted by deliberately focusing on the other party's position and on one's own alternatives.
insights.evidence: Galinsky & Mussweiler (2001), first offers as anchors and the role of perspective-taking and negotiator focus.

insights.claim: Posterior odds equal prior odds (from the base rate) multiplied by the likelihood ratio of the evidence; even strong evidence moves a rare hypothesis only modestly.
insights.evidence: Rare disease 1/600 with a 25:1 test gives only ~4%; Tom W 3% base rate × LR 4 gives ~11%; cab problem (.15/.85)×(.80/.20)=.706 → 41% Blue.

insights.concept: negative correlation of costs and benefits among competing options
insights.claim: When options compete to solve the same problem, the ones offering the largest benefits should also tend to cost the most; judging that good options are also low-risk/cheap (as affect suggests) is suspicious.
insights.evidence: Note to the affect-heuristic studies: technologies studied were not alternatives, but in realistic choices cost and benefit must correlate negatively.

insights.claim: An impressive-looking correlation may account for little: removing a factor with correlation r shrinks spread only to sqrt(1-r^2) of the original; also correlations depend on the environment and should not be read as causation.
insights.evidence: Jencks: equalizing education would cut income inequality (SD) only about 9%; parent–child height correlation would drop where nutrition varies.

insights.claim: Moderate (regressed) predictions are optimal when errors are penalized by squared deviation; a different loss function can justify a different prediction, so the loss criterion should be stated.
insights.evidence: Note to ch.18: proof of standard regression as optimal assumes the least-squares criterion; standard scores (mean 0, SD 1) make variables comparable.

insights.concept: outcome bias / hindsight in judging decisions
insights.claim: People grade a decision by how it turned out instead of by what was knowable when it was made. In hindsight, harms look foreseeable, which inflates blame and liability.
insights.evidence: Baron & Hershey (1988) on outcome bias; Kamin & Rachlinski (1995): ex post judges think the city 'should have hired the monitor'; Fischhoff & Beyth's 'I knew it would happen'.

insights.concept: weak correlation / inversion rate (halo effect in business success)
insights.claim: Even a real link between a practice and success stays weak: at correlations of .20 or .40, the firm with the weaker practice still does better in about 43% or 37% of pairs. So stories of 'what made companies great' overstate what we can learn.
insights.evidence: Steiger's algorithm answering 'How often will you find…' the inverse ranking; Rosenzweig's The Halo Effect; Built to Last.

insights.concept: regression and halo in CEO hiring
insights.claim: Struggling firms hire CEOs away from recently successful firms. The new firm then improves, mostly through regression to the mean, and the CEO gets the credit while the old firm declines. Pay ends up rewarding regression and halo rather than skill.
insights.evidence: Jason Zweig's personal communication (2009) on CEO recruitment and buyout-based pay.

insights.concept: improper linear models / simple scores over unstructured judgment
insights.claim: Simple, equally weighted formulas and checklist scores such as the Apgar score match or beat expert judgment and statistical regression, and sampling accidents don't distort them. Unstructured interviews can actually lower predictive validity.
insights.evidence: Dawes (1979) 'Robust Beauty of Improper Linear Models'; Dana & Dawes (2004); Grove et al. (2000) meta-analysis; DeVaul et al. on rejected medical students; Apgar (1953); Gawande's Checklist Manifesto.

insights.concept: inconsistency of expert judgment / extraneous factors
insights.claim: Experts give different judgments when shown the same case twice, and irrelevant factors such as when they last had a food break sway their decisions.
insights.evidence: Hoffman, Slovic & Rorer on radiologists; Brown on auditors; Shanteau's 41 studies; Danziger et al. on parole judges and food breaks.

insights.claim: Experts can reach the same intuitive verdict quickly while being unable to explain it, and each offers a different, vague reason. Agreement on the conclusion paired with disagreement on the reasons is suspect.
insights.evidence: Getty Museum kouros: experts felt 'intuitive repulsion' and cited fingernails, the word 'fresh', and 'never been in the ground'.

insights.concept: hindsight bias in failure (illusion of learning)
insights.claim: Entrepreneurs who failed stay confident because they believe, probably wrongly, that the failure taught them a lot. Their optimism survives evidence that should temper it.
insights.evidence: Cassar and Craig study of hindsight bias in nascent venture activity.

insights.claim: People answer the easy question (when is demand highest?) instead of the harder one (when is demand highest relative to competitors?). Sellers who account for competition do better.
insights.evidence: eBay sellers mostly end auctions around 7pm EST, when bidder numbers peak. Noon actually draws more bidders per auction, and sellers who avoid prime time get higher prices (Simonsohn 2010).

insights.claim: Perceived value tracks proportional change, not absolute change. Doubling income adds about the same satisfaction for rich and poor, and the slow growth of utility explains why people pay little for the St. Petersburg gamble despite its infinite expected value.
insights.evidence: Deaton's plot of life satisfaction against log GDP across countries; Nicholas Bernoulli's coin-doubling St. Petersburg game.

insights.claim: People typically weight losses about 1.5 to 2.5 times as heavily as equal gains. Taking a trader's broad, detached perspective reduces both the emotional reaction to losses and loss aversion.
insights.evidence: Novemsky and Kahneman 2005 on the boundaries of loss aversion; Sokol-Hessner et al. 2009, 'Thinking Like a Trader'.

insights.claim: People anticipate how the options they did not take will affect their future feelings. Their choices change depending on whether they expect to learn how the forgone option turned out.
insights.evidence: Regret theories of Bell and of Loomes and Sugden (1982); Mellers' emotion-based choice; Ritov on anticipating uncertainty resolution.

insights.claim: Rejecting small favorable gambles cannot be explained by the curvature of utility over total wealth. It would require an absurdly steep drop in the value of money, so small-stakes risk aversion comes from loss aversion relative to a reference point.
insights.evidence: Someone who rejects a 50/50 bet to win $11 or lose $10 would, under concave wealth utility, value $1 over 9% less across a $21 range. Kahneman also notes that mathematical proof persuaded an economist more than common sense had.

insights.claim: Owning something makes people demand far more to give it up than they would pay to get it. Standard theory predicts the two prices should be almost the same.
insights.evidence: Super Bowl lottery winners: 94% would not buy at $3,000 and 92% would not sell at $3,000.

insights.concept: loss aversion as affective forecasting error
insights.claim: Loss aversion runs on how much pain we expect a loss to cause, and those expectations can be wrong. The actual loss often hurts less than predicted.
insights.evidence: Kermer et al. (2006), 'Loss Aversion Is an Affective Forecasting Error'.

insights.claim: Losses weigh roughly twice as much as equal gains. Market data from 16 countries over 100 years gave about 2.3, close to lab estimates. Demand also reacts more to price increases than to decreases.
insights.evidence: Levy (2010), price of risk estimated at 2.3; asymmetric demand response to telephone price changes.

insights.claim: A test that teaches participants the behavior the experimenter expects can make an effect disappear for the wrong reason. Removing the conditions that cause an effect, like physical possession, also hides it. Each side may reject the other's methods.
insights.evidence: Plott and Zeiler trained participants in both buyer and seller roles and removed physical possession, and the endowment effect vanished.

insights.claim: A goal acts as a reference point: falling short feels like a loss, so effort is shaped by the target, not by marginal returns. Cabdrivers may quit early on high-earning days once they reach their target.
insights.evidence: NYC cabdrivers' daily income targets (Camerer et al., disputed by Farber); Zurich bicycle messengers field experiment (Fehr & Goette).

insights.claim: Bad events, threats and losses are detected faster, weigh more, and resist disconfirmation more than equal good ones. People also treat actual losses as worse than foregone gains, including in fairness and legal judgments.
insights.evidence: Angry faces 'pop out' in a crowd; amygdala damage removes loss aversion; Rozin & Royzman; 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good'; fairness rules for merchants, employers and landlords.

insights.claim: People pay much less to reduce a risk partway than a rational model predicts compared with what they would pay to eliminate it entirely; removing the worry completely carries a large premium.
insights.evidence: Viscusi et al.: willingness to pay to cut accident frequency from 15 to 5 units was well below two-thirds of what people paid to eliminate the risk.

insights.concept: subadditive probability of event and complement
insights.claim: When people know little about a topic, their separately judged probabilities for an event and its complement can add up to less than 100%, so the probability judgments are not coherent.
insights.evidence: Asking for the probability that Bangkok's temperature tops 100° at noon tomorrow, and separately for the opposite.

insights.claim: Investors sell winners too early and hold losers too long, avoiding a realized loss on a mental account; more sophisticated investors are less prone to it, and the fallacy can be reduced through training.
insights.evidence: Shefrin & Statman; Odean on reluctance to realize losses; Dhar & Zhu on sophistication; Lehman et al. on the effect of graduate training on reasoning.

insights.claim: Having paid for something makes people more likely to use it, because skipping it feels like closing a mental account at a loss; past cost should not drive future choice.
insights.evidence: Arkes & Blumer field experiment: students who paid full price for theater season tickets went to more shows than those given discounted tickets, especially early in the season.

insights.claim: Unusual events prompt both causal explanations and counterfactual thoughts. The same event compared to a personal norm or to other people's norm gives different causes and different emotions (regret or blame).
insights.evidence: Hart & Honoré: a wife blames eating parsnips for her husband's indigestion, while the doctor names the ulcer as the cause and the meal as a mere occasion.

insights.claim: Some attributes can be evaluated only when options are compared side by side, so judging options one at a time and judging them together can reverse preferences; preferences are built from the context of choice.
insights.evidence: Bazerman, Loewenstein & White on allocation reversals; Hsee's joint/separate terminology; Lichtenstein & Slovic bid-vs-choice gamble reversals, replicated by Grether & Plott.

insights.claim: When people judge an entire life, its length of misery barely matters, but how it ends weighs heavily: adding a few mildly bad years at the end changes the verdict more than doubling the miserable span.
insights.evidence: Diener, Wirtz & Oishi 'James Dean effect': Jen living miserably 60 vs 30 years not judged twice as unhappy; adding 5 mildly miserable years before death made her seem considerably happier.

insights.claim: Life satisfaction (thoughts when you reflect on your life) and happiness (feelings while living) are different quantities; conflating them produces wrong conclusions, and different survey questions mix them in different degrees.
insights.evidence: Kahneman admits he confused the two when asking about Californians; GSS 'very happy' question mixes both while the Cantril ladder is a pure life-evaluation measure.

insights.concept: vivid retrieval reinstates feelings (Day Reconstruction Method)
insights.claim: Recalling a past situation in enough vivid detail lets people re-experience its feelings, which is why reconstructing a day episode by episode yields better reports of experience than global questions.
insights.evidence: Robinson & Clore accessibility model; basis of the Day Reconstruction Method and Ecological Momentary Assessment.

insights.claim: An apparent difference between two groups can vanish once you control for a differing mix of subgroups within them.
insights.evidence: California vs Midwest students: lower-satisfaction Asian students were a larger share in California; adjusting for this, life satisfaction in the two regions was identical.

insights.claim: A salient attribute predicts how people say they enjoy something when asked directly, yet has no effect on their actual mood during ordinary use, because it is only attended to when focused on.
insights.evidence: Xu & Schwarz: car Blue Book value predicted stated enjoyment and joyride pleasure, but not mood during normal driving.

insights.claim: A global evaluation of something, like how much you enjoy your car, follows its salient quality. Moment-by-moment experience during ordinary use may not follow it at all. Global judgments and lived experience can come apart.
insights.evidence: Xu and Schwarz: a car's Blue Book value predicted owners' general enjoyment ratings and their pleasure on joyrides, but had no effect on their mood during normal commutes.

insights.claim: People misjudge how they will feel about future states. They often want things that won't satisfy them, and they misestimate how they will adapt to outcomes. The cited colostomy study found that former patients rate the condition worse than current patients do.
insights.evidence: Smith et al., 'Misremembering Colostomies?': former patients gave lower utility ratings than current patients. Gilbert and Wilson coined the term 'miswanting'.

insights.concept: organizational cognitive repairs (checklists, decision review, shared vocabulary)
insights.claim: An organization can put procedures in place and enforce them to make up for individual biases. Examples are checklists, structured reviews before big decisions, and a shared, distinctive vocabulary for naming biases.
insights.evidence: Notes cite Gawande's Checklist Manifesto, Kahneman, Lovallo and Sibony's 'Before You Make That Big Decision' (HBR 2011), and Heath, Larrick and Klayman's 'Cognitive Repairs' for distinctive vocabulary.

insights.concept: what you see is all there is (WYSIATI)
insights.claim: The index ties WYSIATI to several phenomena in the book: overconfidence, optimistic bias, the premortem as a countermeasure, and problems like Tom W and the Julie problem. It reads as a central mechanism, with judgments built only from the evidence at hand. These pages are index only, so the substance is in the chapters the index cites.
insights.evidence: Index cross-references: confidence, curriculum team, Julie problem, optimistic bias, premortem, professorial candidate, soldiers' performance, Tom W.
